# 2  
Learning Panorama Under TinyML

*Ikechukwu Ignatius Ayogu, Euphemia Chioma Nwokorie, Juliet Nnenna Odii, Francisca Onyiyechi Nwokoma, and Chidi Ukamaka Betrand*

*Department of Computer Science, Federal University of Technology, Owerri, Nigeria*

 

## 2.1 Introduction

Tiny machine learning (TinyML) pushes the frontiers of machine learning (ML) applications to resource‐constrained, battery‐operated devices, with the potential to enable the ubiquity of artificial intelligence and increase the scale of innovation in ML applications. TinyML combines the gains of decades of intensive research and development in the domain of embedded systems, ML, Internet of Things (IoT), and software development \[[1](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0001), [2](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0002)\] to provide effective solutions that facilitate effective data processing at the edge, leveraging the IoT framework \[[3](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0003)–[6](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0006)\]. It has made significant positive impacts in many areas of application within the IoT and edge computing domains, including smart homes \[[7](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0007)–[9](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0009)\], smart agriculture \[[10](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0010)–[15](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0015)\], automobiles [\[16\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0016), wearable devices \[[17](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0017)–[19](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0019)\], and smart cities [\[20\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0020).

The key drivers for the accelerated development of TinyML include, in part, the unprecedented improvement in microcontroller units (MCUs), which continue to grow in computational power, memory capacity, and energy efficiency, as well as accelerated developments within the two fundamental building blocks: the ML algorithm and the hardware architecture. The rapid improvements in both algorithmic approaches and hardware architectures have led to improved performance of various ML models in the context of edge computing, especially in the TinyML domain. Algorithmic approaches, such as growing attention‐based models for sequence data processing, do not rely on backpropagation for training and thus work on simpler algorithms and simpler hardware architectures, which are special considerations for edge ML.

However, developing and deploying TinyML on microcontrollers presents significant challenges relating to design, optimization, and learning. Other challenges arise from the dearth of development frameworks – currently, TensorFlow Lite for MCUs and uTensor, and Edge Impulse are among the popular options available – as well as programming language restrictions, the lack of good support for various development boards, the choice of suitable sensors, the absence of standardized benchmarks, sensor selection issues, and the scarcity of development datasets \[[21](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0021)–[23](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0023)\]. These challenges need to be resolved in order for TinyML to realize its full potential. In Africa, where the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) and embedded systems is still in its infancy, TinyML could address issues related to connectivity, energy, and costs [\[24\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0024). Moreover, its potential to facilitate computation at the edge, reducing dependence on cloud‐based operations, opens up new areas for energy‐efficient, secure, and private data processing. It also ushers in a new era of novel localized applications in all sectors.

 

### 2.1.1 Chapter Contribution

This chapter presents a comprehensive examination of the processes by which ML models for tiny devices, a class of computational devices with limited computing, memory, and power resources, are created and deployed. A sequential knowledge presentation approach was adopted, highlighting challenges in TinyML design, opportunities for model design improvements, model compression and optimization techniques, development frameworks, tools, TinyML hardware, and opportunities for algorithmic innovations for emerging TinyML applications. The major contributions of this chapter are as follows:

1.  It presents a clear outline of the major issues that are of importance to the design, training, and deployment of ML models on resource‐constrained edge devices, as well as the opportunities for an improved model design using already established techniques. Thus, it serves as a resourceful and handy information source for experienced and upcoming TinyML practitioners. More importantly, it reduces the time required for a novice reader to get acquainted and also develop interest in the subject matter.
2.  The chapter identifies the frontiers for TinyML development through model optimization approaches and also provides a detailed cost–benefit analysis of the major model compression techniques that are currently under active research. This elucidation further provides new entrants with balanced information and reasoning for selecting a given technique in a given application scenario.
3.  This chapter presents an in‐depth, informative discussion of the learning frameworks and tools for TinyML development. It devotes significant attention to the discussion of the key features, strengths, weaknesses, examples, and use cases of the more popular tool framework currently used for developing models for tiny devices and key hardware platforms for deploying tiny models.
4.  The chapter highlights avenues for algorithmic innovations for improved learning for TinyML. The chapter forecasts the importance of meta‐learning and multimodal learning in developing TinyML applications that are both adaptive and extensible in the near future.

 

### 2.1.2 Chapter Organization

[Section 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0004) presents an in‐depth discussion of the major challenges facing the TinyML model design as well as the available avenues for overcoming them. In particular, the section analyzed the prominent challenges of TinyML design before delving into the opportunities for overcoming the identified bottlenecks using state‐of‐the‐art Tiny model development techniques, including neural architecture search (NAS), neural attention mechanisms, depth‐separable convolutions, and rational activation functions. [Section 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0009) presents a detailed account of the frontiers in model optimization for TinyML development and deployment, viewing model compression as the principal paradigm for model development for TinyML. It examined quantization, knowledge distillation (KD), pruning, and low‐rank decomposition as principal examples of learning a tiny model from large parameter models. It also presents a balanced cost–benefit analysis of these major model compression techniques. [Section 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0014) provides a detailed discussion and analysis of learning frameworks and tools for TinyML development, focusing on the various development frameworks, tools, and major edge hardware. The section presents a detailed analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of representative TinyML development frameworks as well as key features, weaknesses, and use cases for some popular TinyML hardware systems. [Section 2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0015) discusses the frontiers of algorithmic innovations for TinyML, identifying multimodal learning and meta‐learning as key contenders. [Section 2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0018) presents a high‐level summary of the TinyML development process, highlighting model training, conversion, and inference as the major phases in the TinyML development process. [Section 2.7](#c02.xhtml#c02-sec-0019) concludes the chapter by summarizing the main issues facing TinyML model development in the context of learning, compression, and inference.

 

## 2.2 Challenges and Opportunities for Improved TinyML Model Design

TinyML is a maturing field of study within the domain of AI and ML, with significant capacity for commercial impact. However, the design and deployment of effective ML models in the TinyML space present many challenges, mainly limited computational capacity, hardware resources, and power deficiencies \[[5](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0005), [25](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0025)\]. This peculiarity compromises lightweight models, where trade‐offs between model accuracy and computational complexity/efficiency need to be made. Efficient inference in resource‐constrained environments depends on a number of factors, including model complexity. Within the context of important applications such as healthcare and agriculture, there are further challenges arising from a dearth of high‐quality datasets \[[26](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0026)–[28](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0028)\].

Designing ML models for edge devices is a challenging problem. TinyML model design involves working with devices with limited energy resources; to be of practical use, the new designs must be small and energy‐efficient. Restricted energy resources usually motivate the use of less complicated algorithms, leading to considerable loss and poor application‐level performance. Some of the main challenges affecting the applications of TinyML are captured in [Figure 2.1](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0001), including lack of standards to promote interoperability, limited tooling and community support, computing, energy, data protection, scalability, and post‐deployment management challenges.

![Figure 2.1 An overview of the major challenges of TinyML.](images/c02f001.png)

**Figure 2.1** An overview of the major challenges of TinyML.

Although TinyML enables the deployment of ML models on resource‐constrained edge computing devices, its development continues to face several challenges. A brief outline of the key obstacles and examples is presented in [Table 2.1](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0001).

**Table 2.1** The scope of some of the key challenges of TinyML.

| **Key challenges** || **Explanation** || **Example** || **References** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Compute and memory constraint || Current TinyML models are constrained to run on microcontrollers with kilobytes to a few megabytes of RAM and low processing power. This renders the execution of complex models infeasible. || Running MobileNet on an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense requires extreme optimizations, such as quantization and pruning, to reduce the model's computing and memory requirements. || \[[29](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0029), [30](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0030)\] |
| Acute power constraints || TinyML applications typically run on battery‐powered or energy‐harvesting devices. This necessitates that the operations performed be minimally power‐consuming. || A typical sensor must consume microwatts of energy while processing computations for extended battery life. || \[[31](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0031), [32](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0032)\] |
| Model size‐performance trade‐off || Striking a good balance between model miniaturization and performance (accuracy) is a challenge since excessive simplification leads to a remarkable loss in accuracy, a principal performance measure. || Quantizing FP32 to INT8 on a TinyML gesture recognition model reduces the memory requirement, but it has been noted to result in a significant number of misclassifications. || \[[33](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0033), [34](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0034)\] |
| Scarcity of dataset || The scarcity of data at the edge is a significant issue for TinyML applications. Collecting and using data on a device is challenging because it seems impossible to provide labels in real‐time applications. || Critical but resource‐challenged applications, such as speech recognition for low‐resource languages, face performance issues due to the unavailability of labeled data. || \[[35](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0035), [36](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0036)\] |
| Complexity‐induced challenges for on‐device learning || The lack of cloud connectivity makes adapting models to new data difficult. This is due to memory‐related limitations and the lack of complicated training algorithms on microcontrollers. || A personalized speech application that runs on an embedded device must learn from a user's voice samples without sending data to the cloud. || \[[37](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0037), [38](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0038)\] |
| Lack of standardized frameworks || TinyML deployment requires custom optimizations for different hardware, making portability and scalability difficult. || A model optimized for TensorFlow Lite Micro may not run efficiently on Arm CMSIS‐NN without further tuning. || \[[31](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0031), [39](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0039)\] |
| Security and privacy issues || On‐device ML models are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Thus, when sensitive information is involved, data privacy concerns naturally arise. || A TinyML‐powered baby monitor could be attacked with adversarial noise, triggering false alarms. || \[[40](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0040), [41](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0041)\] |
| Hardware compatibility issues || The diversity of TinyML model architectures, such as ARM Cortex‐M, RISC‐V, and ESP32, makes universal ML model deployment complex. || A LoRa‐based TinyML sensor for air quality monitoring may require different optimizations compared to ESP32‐based AI cameras. || \[[32](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0032), [42](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0042)\] |

In addition to devising innovative solutions to mitigate the shortage of computational resources, memory constraints must also be considered when designing TinyML models. The RAM is required to store the model and input data processed by the model as it is run. ML models that run on devices with tight memory constraints run the risk of memory thrashing, which occurs when limited memory is used inefficiently, resulting in model slowdown [\[43\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0043). Addressing these challenges is vital for successfully deploying deep learning models on edge devices. A successful TinyML model design must deliver the processing capabilities required while minimizing resource requirements, complexity, and computational effort. Some of the most popular techniques for improved TinyML model design are discussed in this section.

 

### 2.2.1 Neural Architecture Search

TinyML has drawn markedly high research interest in the past few years. However, searching for very accurate and resource‐efficient models is still a manual investigation involving domain knowledge and assumptions [\[44\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0044). This renders training and deployment of TinyML models difficult, resource‐inefficient, and significantly more expensive in terms of training and development time. NAS is an effective method for automatically engineering various high‐performance deep neural network architectures [\[45\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0045).

NAS aims to automate the design of neural network models by directly searching for optimal neural architectures. NAS typically has three components – the search space, the search strategy, and the evaluation strategy. A search space, normally very large, describes the set of all architectures available for the NAS algorithm to choose from. A search strategy, which may be black‐box, is an optimization method for identifying a high‐performing neural architecture within the defined search space. A performance estimation strategy, such as learning curve extrapolation, is used to speed up the process of evaluating the performance of neural architectures without completing the training of the model. NAS searches for the network architecture from scratch with parameters, layers, modules, and more fine‐grained operations or connections [\[46\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0046). TinyML, as an increasingly important paradigm, represents a potential, albeit critical, application area for NAS. As such, NAS is a promising method to remove the performance‐resource bottleneck in TinyML by designing TinyML models that autonomously optimize model architectures through extensive searching. NAS has been applied to thoroughly search for a TinyML neural network for object detection [\[47\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0047).

The recent advancements in NAS could come in handy in offloading the challenges associated with the traditional heuristic approach to TinyML design, thus revolutionizing the TinyML landscape with the possibilities of more innovative solutions – the YOLO‐NAS example is classic. The transformations built for optimizing tiny designs using NAS are agnostic and could be used for many TinyML applications. Tools and frameworks are increasing support and gaining popularity, attracting academic and industry professionals to engineer and design miniature ML models.

However, there are some drawbacks to using NAS to optimize TinyML. First, it requires a large amount of computational resources [\[48\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0048). The implementation of NAS makes it necessary to train and evaluate millions of different designs sequentially to determine the highest‐performing model. Secondly, scalability issues exist when applying the NAS methods [\[49\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0049). The search space explodes quickly, such that the possibilities of selecting a suboptimal model increase significantly. Despite these challenges, the successful applications of NAS to TinyML design have been validated by a broad range of case studies, and the feasibility of improving the design of TinyML models has been demonstrated \[[50](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0050)–[53](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0053)\]. These applications entail developing models that can perform well in real‐world circumstances when the models have been designed and pretrained. The application of NAS to TinyML design is operationalized in [Figure 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0002). The first step is to define a search space, setting conditions and constraints for possible network architectures. In the second step, the search strategy is selected – popular choices are reinforcement learning, evolutionary or gradient‐based techniques. Next is the actual architectural search, during which several candidate models are trained and evaluated. Upon the search's conclusion, the model that gives the best trade‐off between efficiency and accuracy is selected and deployed on suitable hardware.

![Figure 2.2 Typical workflow for NAS in TinyML development.](images/c02f002.png)

**Figure 2.2** Typical workflow for NAS in TinyML development.

 

### 2.2.2 Neural Attention Mechanisms

Attention mechanisms are a key part of most modern deep learning research. The basic principle of attention is written into its name; these mechanisms allow the network to *pay attention* to specific parts of its input data points. This has applications in numerous domains and purposes, from localizing objects or parts of objects in visual inputs, weighting different parts of text inputs based on perceived importance, or altering the network structure used to process different sections of longer sequences [\[54\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0054). In all of these cases, the underlying concept is to allow the network to focus on the most important parts of its input data for whatever task it is carrying out in order to optimize information processing, reduce errors, and improve accuracy. However, understanding and properly utilizing these concepts can be complex.

The TinyML community has demonstrated that attention mechanisms can be integrated within TinyML frameworks to obtain value not only in terms of model accuracy but also in terms of interpretability, as they reveal which input features the model actually *focuses on* to make its prediction. However, integrating attention in the TinyML domain also presents unique challenges: top‐attention TinyML models with increased performance often come attached with proportionally higher computational and memory requirements [\[55\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0055). This tightly constrains the feasibility of its real‐world applications on devices with strict resource limitations and severe hardware constraints, especially compared to their non‐attentional TinyML counterparts. It is, therefore, crucial to understand these trade‐offs and weigh the costs versus the benefits with every decision around the model design when it comes to integrating attention.

When implementing attention, the TinyML community predominantly adopts the transformer and gated attention models for TinyML [\[56\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0056). In the future, the TinyML community will need to research new adaptations to attention mechanisms for resource‐constrained conditions, focusing on achieving more resource‐efficient attention‐driven TinyML models for cutting‐edge applications in which there is the predominance of large‐scale deep learning architectures. For instance, in the application of TinyML to the burgeoning object detection domain, consideration of the attention mechanism design and makeup of the visual architecture is of high importance; research needs to elucidate how adaptations change the visual representation of the system, trade off the level of accuracy improvement for a decrease in efficiency, or find an ideal compromise between both.

Adding attention mechanisms to TinyML models has benefits and challenges [\[57\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0057). The integration of the attention mechanism benefits TinyML by making tiny models more adaptable and enabling them to focus on data features relevant to the application for better performance. Correctly infusing attention into tiny models makes the overall model size smaller because it does not require all data features at each layer level. However, it is essential to balance the benefits of adding attention with the computational demand and improvements to the accuracy of the model. As [Figure 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0003) illustrates, the challenges of low model adaptability in basic TinyML models can be significantly overcome by incorporating attention technology – gated or transformer models. However, achieving the trade‐off between high model adaptability and high computational demand is a delicate balance, as the performance of edge devices is severely degraded with increasing computational demand. Hence, it is imperative to carefully weigh the objectives and motivation for adopting TinyML prior to adoption for a given application scenario or use case.

![Figure 2.3 Balancing benefits and challenges of attention mechanisms in TinyML.](images/c02f003.png)

**Figure 2.3** Balancing benefits and challenges of attention mechanisms in TinyML.

 

### 2.2.3 Depth‐Separable Convolution

The convolution operation is a fundamental component of modern deep learning architectures. Depth‐separable convolution was first introduced to boost the efficiency of convolution by dividing it into two steps called depthwise and pointwise convolutions. This is differentiated from the commonly used (two‐dimensional) 2D convolutional filters that process all the input, which they share across the output channels simultaneously. As a result, 2D convolutional filters tend to have a large number of learned parameters. In contrast, pointwise convolution uses 1 × 1 filters across the channels that lie in the output space of the depthwise convolution operations and consequently reduces the computational burden in training and in the subsequent forward and backward passes drastically.

The advantage of using depthwise separable convolution is quite manifold. Firstly, it requires relatively fewer parameters \[[58](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0058), [59](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0059)\]. Hence, it reduces step computation and offers a quicker design implementation. Furthermore, depthwise separable convolution reduces the computational cost of initialization and increases the speed of convergence and the validation accuracy of the model. It splits the convolution into two steps, reducing the number of multiply‐accumulate (MACs) operations to compute. These two approaches use significantly fewer parameters than traditional convolution to process images. Furthermore, by conveniently separating each output index for each input at the convolution output map, the depth‐separable convolution strategies can have progressive advantages for TinyML‐related applications [\[59\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0059). This method of breaking down the standard convolutions, step by step, makes training the larger model and its inference more efficient in terms of the amount of memory and computational power used [\[60\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0060). [Figure 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0004) outlines the most essential points about applying depth‐separable convolution for TinyML.

![Figure 2.4 Depth‐separable convolution for TinyML.](images/c02f004.png)

**Figure 2.4** Depth‐separable convolution for TinyML.

The interest, in most instances, is in reducing the number of MAC operations and the amount of memory required to keep each layer of the network while maintaining accuracy. Because depthwise convolutions and especially pointwise convolutions require fewer operational resources, spending more convolutions of the model's input data on these iterations leads to a proportionally lower amount of MAC convolutions, which account for a disproportionate amount of the computational power required, for instance [\[58\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0058). Therefore, one benefit of depthwise and pointwise separable convolutions is enabling efficient training of larger models in high‐capacity hardware and platforms. Moreover, since the use of depth‐separable convolution allows designing smaller models with the same feature maps and operations, the approach is beneficial for reducing memory footprint and decreasing the amount of convolution operations on resource‐constrained platforms for TinyML as well. The most significant advantages of using depth‐separable convolutions in creating TinyML models are the efficient reduction of the number of parameters in the model, the number of floating‐point operations necessary for inference, and finally, the amount of memory needed to store the weights of the neural network.

 

### 2.2.4 Rational Activation Functions

Activation functions are mathematical functions that can be applied to weighted sums of inputs and biases of neurons before they are used as inputs to other neurons or the output of a neural network [\[61\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0061). The use of activation functions is a key part of deep learning systems. Rational activation functions (RAFs), expressed as ratios of polynomials, are innovative alternatives to the traditional activation functions such as the Sigmoid, ReLU, GeLU, and tanh. The nonlinearity offered by RAFs has the promise to be of significant benefit to TinyML – it represents researchers' attempts to optimize the activation mechanisms [\[62\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0062).

Traditional activation functions are known to suffer from several important issues, including high computational cost and the very popular vanishing gradients problem. RAFs are an emerging, promising alternative – they are flexible and have the potential for efficient approximation.

Given some numbers *a*[0], …, *a*[*m*], *b*[0], …, *b*[*m*] ∈ *ℝ*, RAFs are mathematically defined as in [equation (2.1)](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0001) [\[63\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0063):

(2.1)![f left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis equals StartFraction upper P left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Over upper Q left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis EndFraction equals StartFraction a 0 plus a 1 x plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus a Subscript m Baseline x Superscript m Baseline Over b 0 plus b 1 x plus midline-horizontal-ellipsis plus b Subscript n Baseline x Superscript n Baseline EndFraction](images/c02-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo form="postfix">+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo form="prefix">+</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>x</mi><mo form="postfix">+</mo><mo>&#8943;</mo><mo form="prefix">+</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msup><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow></mfrac></math> 

where *P*(*x*) and *Q*(*x*) are polynomials of varying degrees; *b*[*j*] ≠ 0 for at least one *j*.

RAFs offer the flexibility of modeling complex nonlinearity without losing computational efficiency. Other motivations for RAFs in TinyML applications include compactness, efficient hardware implementation, and flexibility in designing TinyML models. RAFs are compact because they use fewer coefficients than piece‐wise linear or transcendental functions; RAFs are compatible with fixed‐point arithmetic and are, thus, well‐suited for hardware‐based acceleration, leading to possibilities of efficient hardware implementation. The RAF approach has the potential to significantly reduce overreliance on traditional activation functions and thus avoid computationally expensive operations that are associated with their use. Unlike the traditional activation functions, RAFs do not use extensive lookup tables – a memory‐hungry structure – thus lowering memory requirements, which is critical for TinyML. RAFs facilitate faster inference since they predominantly perform addition and multiplication. This property enables RAFs to better adapt to scenarios where model size and parameter counts are limited. Computationally, the simplicity of RAFs also translates to lower energy requirements.

Although RAFs have significant chances to contribute to the design of an efficient TinyML system, there are a number of considerations that must be given careful attention while implementing RAFs [\[63\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0063). First, the division operations inherent in RAFs are a potential source of numerical instability, which risk increases as the denominator approaches zero. To mitigate this, researchers have sought to constrain the polynomial coefficients. Secondly, parameter optimization is somewhat challenging with RAFs; there is no straightforward way to determine the optimal degrees of *P*(*x*) and *Q*(*x*) and their coefficients. A third concern is dependency on target hardware. The efficiency of RAFs depends on the capabilities of the target hardware; hardware that does not natively support division is bound to suffer performance bottlenecks with the use of RAF. The challenges and prospects of RAFs for TinyML are further expressed in [Figure 2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0005).

![Figure 2.5 Benefits and challenges of RAFs for TinyML.](images/c02f005.png)

**Figure 2.5** Benefits and challenges of RAFs for TinyML.

Although research on RAFs for TinyML is still in its infancy, there is evidence to suggest speedy development and adoption of RAF‐based approaches for TinyML in the near future. The focus will be on developing automated design tools capable of generating and optimizing RAFs for specific hardware constraints, increasing framework integration by including RAFs as a standard option in deep learning libraries, exploring hybrid approaches, and developing methods to dynamically adjust the degrees of coefficients of RAFs during training or inference in changing workload scenarios.

RAFs promise compelling solutions to the challenges currently undermining the wide adoption and deployment of TinyML systems. Their promise lies in their ability to combine computational efficiency, representational power, and adaptability. While challenges like numerical stability and ecosystem support remain, ongoing research and development could make rational activation functions a cornerstone of future TinyML applications.

 

## 2.3 Frontiers in Model Optimization for TinyML

Model optimization is at the forefront of learning for TinyML at the moment. Emerging approaches in the development of the TinyML model significantly leverage the optimization and miniaturization of large parameter learning models that are primarily developed on regular, high‐capacity computing hardware systems. In the last five years, model miniaturization techniques such as pruning, quantization, low‐rank decomposition, and (KD) have greatly advanced, following major breakthroughs in optimization research. These techniques have been used to facilitate the development of accurate, resource‐efficient, lightweight ML models that have shown good performance on resource‐constrained devices. The literature has a rich account of research that illuminates the subject of ML model optimization for TinyML development and its bourgeoning applications in resource‐limited environments. Model compression is a principal technique in the context of TinyML; many researchers have emphasized and demonstrated its growing importance for edge computing applications. This section examines the techniques of model pruning, quantization, low‐rank decomposition, and KD as a high‐level summary of the major neural network model compression for the development of TinyML systems. The major strengths of these four techniques are highlighted in [Figure 2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0006).

![Figure 2.6 Model optimization techniques for TinyML.](images/c02f006.png)

**Figure 2.6** Model optimization techniques for TinyML.

The efficiency and suitability of each of these popular model compression techniques vary according to application requirements. The choice of model compression approach impacts the cost, performance, and complexity of the final model. Before delving into the main discussion of the four major compression techniques discussed in this section, a brief cost–benefit analysis is presented in [Table 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0002) to serve as a background to the reader.

**Table 2.2** A cost–benefit summary of the major model compression techniques.

 
| **Compression technique** || **Benefits** || **Costs/challenges** || **References** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quantization – lowering the precision of weights and activations. || 

*   Can reduce model size and memory requirement by up to a factor of 4.
*   Significant increase in inference speed on hardware that supports low‐bit operations.
*   Lowers energy requirement, thus improving battery life for edge devices.

 || 

*   Degrades model accuracy, especially significant in the aggressive case (FP32 to INT 4).
*   Often needs hardware‐aware optimization since not all devices can perform efficient low‐bit operations.
*   Sensitive to model architecture. Quantizing transformers is more challenging than CNNs.

 || \[[33](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0033), [34](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0034), [64](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0064)\] |
| Knowledge distillation (KD) (Based on teacher‐student model. Transfer of knowledge from a large, complicated to a small, simple model). || 

*   Derives a smaller, efficient model that retains the accuracy of the larger model.
*   More robust and generalized since the student model learns from soft labels.
*   It can be combined with other compression techniques (e.g., KD‐quantization setup) to produce better models.

 || 

*   KD incurs additional training costs as both the teacher and the student model must be trained.
*   Optimizing KD models is challenging. Performance is affected by the choice of teacher‐student pair and the loss function.
*   Performance gain is task‐dependent.

 || [\[65](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0065)–[67\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0067) |
| Pruning (Reduces complexity by removing redundant connections and weights). || 

*   Achieves a significant reduction in model size. A 90% weight reduction can be achieved with structured pruning.
*   Improves inference speed on sparsity‐optimized hardware.

*   Sparse models can be pretty slow on some hardware due to workload requirements for sparse matrix computations.

*   Creates a more efficient model by reducing parameter count.
*   Favors lower latency in resource‐limited environments.
*   It is well‐suited for fully connected layers and transformers.

 || 

*   It requires careful selection of decomposition rank. If the decomposition rank is too low, an approximation error is introduced, resulting in a significant loss in accuracy.
*   Pruning is less effective for already compact models.

### 2.3.1 Pruning

Liu et al. [\[74\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0074) extensively discussed model compression techniques, with a focus on using pruning techniques to facilitate the deployment of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for edge applications. Pruning is a key approach to reducing the size of neural networks for TinyML applications; it creates a toned‐down version of larger models by systematically dropping off nonessential or redundant neurons, thereby reducing model complexity at a small cost to model performance. One major issue common to all model compression techniques is the trade‐off between accuracy and model complexity; therefore, it is important to carefully consider alternative options and employ the most promising approach, given a set of predefined objectives \[[75](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0075), [76](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0076)\]. A helpful pruning algorithm is expected to strike a good balance between efficiency in model size reduction, improved inference speed, and model performance. Focusing on these three issues is crucial in edge applications, which often necessitate real‐time processing capabilities [\[76\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0076).

The process of pruning a large neural network involves, as shown in [Figure 2.7](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0007), identifying redundant neurons, applying the chosen pruning technique, evaluating trade‐offs, and optimizing the model to generate a simpler model.

![Figure 2.7 Pruning approach for TinyML.](images/c02f007.png)

**Figure 2.7** Pruning approach for TinyML.

Typically, a neural network model has a significant number of non‐influential or redundant parameters that do not contribute significantly to the generalization capacity of the model. Hence, the main objective of model pruning is to exploit this opportunity to reduce the space and time complexity of the model while preserving model performance. This is achieved by removing unimportant parameter weights from a deep learning model. Neural network parameter counts can be reduced by over 90% through pruning without significant performance losses [\[69\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0069). This makes pruning an essential approach.

In general, pruning focuses on the weights of the parameters; the biases are not dropped. Research has shown that pruning biases negatively affect the resulting lightweight model [\[76\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0076). Frankle and Carbin [\[69\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0069), in the *lottery ticket hypothesis*, have shown that pruning can be conceptualized as a search for subnetworks that have optimal initial weights that facilitate effective training in a similar number of iterations and with better performance than the original large parameter networks but with only about 10–20% of the size of the fully connected CNN. Pruning is preferred in situations where a balance between model size and accuracy is desired.

Pruning techniques are generally categorized into two, namely, train‐time pruning and post‐training pruning. Train‐time pruning (TTP) removes less important connections in the network during training using L1 and L2 regularization, while post‐training pruning (PTP) removes less important connections after training has been completed. While PTP is simple to implement, it is susceptible to suboptimal decisions. TTP, on the other hand, is more efficient because it often incorporates sparsity by default. Regarding implementation, PTP can be achieved via a structured or unstructured approach.

Structured pruning drops specific weight structures. In contrast, unstructured PTP, a simpler approach, drops individual model weight parameters by selecting individual parameters to prune using minimum threshold values of weights or their activations. This approach works by setting parameter weight values below the set threshold to zero, thus removing them from the active connections. The weight‐zeroing operation necessitates recomputation of the weights each time, and thus, unstructured pruning does not have a significant positive impact on latency. It, however, has a positive impact on the reduction of noise from the model weights, thus facilitating more efficient inference performance. Unstructured pruning is reported to achieve up to 50% model compression with less than 1% performance degradation [\[77\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0077).

Structured pruning offers greater improvements in model inference speed and model size compared to unstructured pruning. Structured pruning removes an entire group of weights, simplifying the architecture in fewer steps. The approach usually reduces the computations typically made in the forward pass through the neural network's weight matrices. Structured pruning has a strong capability for increased inference speed while maintaining accuracy in an architecture‐agnostic fashion [\[78\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0078). In spite of this, observed performance gains, experience, and good planning are key requirements for success when using structured pruning.

Pruning techniques are further categorized into local and global pruning depending on the focal point of the pruning operation on the network. Local pruning is targeted at individual neurons, weights, or connections within a layer of the neural network architecture. Low weight magnitude, low importance in the context of the given layer, or low contribution to the network's inference performance are the main yardsticks for local pruning. Local pruning methods such as unit magnitude‐based pruning, weight magnitude pruning, and connection sensitivity‐based pruning follow an iterative process that prunes weights or connections, one at a time, based on the set criteria. Global pruning removes entire neurons, layers, or sections of the neural architecture simultaneously. Thus, the global pruning approach considers the overall importance of neural nodes or layers over the entire network simultaneously. Furthermore, unlike local pruning, global pruning considers interactions and interdependencies between model segments. It considers the overall importance of neurons or layers across the entire network rather than focusing on specific parts within individual layers. Global pruning often involves more sophisticated techniques that consider the interactions and dependencies between different parts of the network. A typical example is the iterative magnitude pruning approach [\[79\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0079). Although global pruning makes more impactful decisions than local pruning, given that it has more context, it can lead to suffering specific layers. [Table 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0003) summarizes the main points about global, local, structured, and unstructured pruning approaches.

**Table 2.3** Comparative analysis of pruning strategies.

 
| **Pruning strategy** || **Method** || **Advantages** || **Disadvantages** || **References** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Global pruning || It uses a global threshold to delete the lowest‐magnitude weights across the entire network (model). || 

*   There are no strict layer constraints; hence, it maximizes compression.
*   Produces very sparse models.

 || 

*   The risk of removing essential weights from critical layers is a significant concern.
*   Fine‐tuning is required for optimal performance.

 || \[[70](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0070), [80](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0080)\] |
| Local pruning || Removes a specific percentage of weights per layer, thereby maintaining relative sparsity across layers. || 

*   Prevents over‐pruning of critical layers; it maintains structured sparsity.
*   Easier to implement than global pruning.

 || 

*   Achieves lower compression than global pruning.
*   Requires manual layer‐wise tuning.

 || \[[81](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0081), [82](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0082)\] |
| Structured pruning || Drops entire neurons, channels, or filters rather than individual weights. || 

*   Highly efficient for hardware acceleration such as CPUs, GPUs, and MCUs.
*   Ease of implementation.

 || 

*   Offers lower flexibility than unstructured pruning.
*   Has the potential to degrade accuracy more than unstructured pruning.

 || \[[83](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0083), [84](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0084)\] |
| Unstructured pruning || Drops individual weights without considering structure. It uses magnitude‐based thresholds. || 

*   Achieves extreme model compression by maximizing sparsity.
*   Well‐suited for applications deployed on memory‐constrained devices.

 || 

*   Difficult to accelerate on standard hardware.
*   Inefficient inference due to the influence of irregular weight patterns.

 || \[[69](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0069), [85](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0085)\] |

 

### 2.3.2 Quantization

Quantization, like other model compression techniques, aims to shrink the model size and enhance efficiency without significantly sacrificing performance. Quantization is a numerical approach for converting high‐precision, compute‐ and memory‐intensive data to low‐precision, compute‐ and memory‐light versions \[[86](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0086), [87](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0087)\]. Quantization can reduce power consumption by over 94% and increase the speed with which the quantized model transfers data by up to four times the full‐parameter model [\[88\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0088). Neural quantization is, therefore, an important technique for accelerating the deployment of high‐performing AI innovations on embedded devices ([Figure 2.8](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0008)).

![Figure 2.8 Strengths and weaknesses of neural model quantization.](images/c02f008.png)

**Figure 2.8** Strengths and weaknesses of neural model quantization.

The primary problem of quantization lies in minimizing the loss of precision resulting from the lowering of numerical bitwidth [\[87\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0087). A substantial body of research has been undertaken to identify quantization strategies appropriate for various network architectures and application contexts, along with the best quantization parameters for distinct quantization methods. However, quantization approaches still face significant challenges in a number of important ways, including how to optimally allocate quantization bitwidth, balance computational speed with accuracy, and optimize quantization parameters based on disparities in model and data distribution [\[88\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0088).

Researchers have developed various techniques to quantize neural network models, each geared toward addressing the identified challenges. The post‐training quantization (PTQ) method quantizes a model post‐training without necessitating retraining, thus facilitating swift deployment. Nevertheless, PTQ may result in significant accuracy degradation, particularly in models sensitive to precision [\[89\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0089). In contrast, quantization‐aware training (QAT) incorporates quantization into the training phase, thus creating better optimized models with minimal accuracy loss. However, QAT is computationally intensive and more time‐consuming; it necessitates retraining. PTQ is applied to neural network models after training is completed. PTQ works best for Gaussian‐like distributions, especially for complicated applications with higher accuracy requirements. The key issues for PTQ lie in determining the appropriate clip range for the optimal quantization parameters. Typically, the range of activations is computed using a series of input calibrations \[[33](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0033), [90](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0090)\]. A very common choice of the clip range is the use of the min/max value of the input data [\[33\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0033). This has been shown to often increase the range to the detriment of quantization resolution. Other more intelligent approaches include the use of the *i*th largest or smallest value in the data and the use of information loss between original and quantized values [\[91\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0091), such as information derived using mean squared error (MSE), entropy, or Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. The challenges associated with computing optimal model quantization parameters and reducing the loss of accuracy after quantization remain key problems to be addressed by research.

In QAT, the quantization steps are integrated into the model training stage. In contrast to PTQ, QAT allows the model to learn and adapt the effects of quantization during training. The QAT procedure produces models that optimally adapt and preserve accuracy, notwithstanding reduced precision. However, the majority of QAT methods are susceptible to the effect of gradient error, which results from the use of a straight‐through gradient estimation technique. Research has proposed a number of approaches to address this problem, including activation value trimming [\[92\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0092), the use of a differentiable tanh function to approximate the quantization function, pre‐quantization tailoring of weight range [\[93\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0093), and in‐training use of gradient update and weight adjustment process. QAT methods deliver superior quantitative performance. However, they require huge training datasets alongside high demand for compute resources, with excessively long training times, exceeding 100 GPU hours [\[94\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0094).

The quantization process applied to a neural network model involves constraining the activation and weight values to a discrete set of numbers, which exhibit various distributions, including uniform and nonuniform types [\[95\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0095). The inference of neural network models on hardware platforms necessitates processing quantized computational results through specific inverse quantization steps to achieve an accurate floating‐point output. Nonuniform quantization methods exhibit intricate inverse quantization computation processes, which may pose challenges for compatibility with hardware platforms. Current hardware predominantly supports uniform quantization methods. The predominant quantization scheme employed is the uniform distribution method, characterized by a consistent step size.

The primary concern in quantization involves developing an appropriate quantization mapping function and a practical approach for calculating quantization parameters. In the context of uniform quantization, most current methodologies employ either asymmetric or symmetric quantization mapping functions \[[96](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0096)–[98](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0098)\]. The literature appears to have been predominantly focused on symmetric quantization, while the investigation of asymmetric quantization has only recently gained research interest \[[99](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0099)–[101](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0101)\].

The distinction between the two strategies is based on treating positive and negative values. Symmetric quantization guarantees that both positive and negative values utilize an identical quantization resolution, whereas asymmetric quantization permits distinct scales for positive and negative values. As a result, symmetric quantization can result in increased quantization error, whereas asymmetric quantization may require additional resources to maintain two sets of parameters \[[97](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0097), [102](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0102)\]. Asymmetric quantization demonstrates superior performance in classification tasks, whereas symmetric quantization is favored for object detection and image‐to‐image regression applications \[[103](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0103)–[105](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0105)\].

The configuration of the quantization strategy is essential for optimizing the effectiveness of both quality preservation and resource efficiency. In the context of various natural language processing and computer vision models, the appropriateness of the scenario is significantly influenced by the model architecture and the dataset being utilized \[[97](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0097), [106](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0106)\]. Additionally, the implementation of various quantization strategies can result in a cascading impact on performance concerning precision‐aware layers, necessitating a trade‐off based on the permissible decline in these layers.

To understand the asymmetry characteristics in neural network quantization, it is important first to outline the distinctions between symmetric and asymmetric quantization methods. In symmetric quantization, both weights and activations are represented uniformly. This can be accomplished in a feedforward network by normalizing weights or activations. In contrast, asymmetric quantization permits the quantization of weights and activations through distinct methods \[[97](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0097), [102](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0102)\], potentially enhancing information encoding within the network. Furthermore, it facilitates enhanced reconstructions of prior activations based on the forward activations and weights, which can be utilized since the network weights can be identified.

The distinction between symmetric and asymmetric quantization can be analyzed through the lens of information‐preserving quantization error, highlighting the limitations inherent in various representations. This error, associated with an approximation under constant top‐norm, is commonly employed to measure the spectrum of feasible degrees of approximation attainable through quantization. In practical applications, this extreme approximation is rarely utilized, and the selection of quantization resolution is determined by the acceptable level of this approximation. The asymmetry in quantization can be addressed by adjusting the bias direction to minimize error, shifting focus from activations to weights, and ensuring fairness through the top‐norm constraint on network depth \[[107](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0107), [108](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0108)\]. By permitting one of these dimensions to be significantly deeper, the theoretical difference can be minimized if the quantization of the other dimension is increased. Consequently, quantizing the larger dimension of weights may lead to more significant relative differences when the associated activations are quantized to the same level.

Quantization of neural networks represents a thoroughly researched area, with numerous optimization algorithms developed to enhance this process. These methods can primarily be categorized into gradient‐based and heuristic‐based \[[109](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0109)–[111](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0111)\]. The choice of optimization algorithm is critical during the quantization process, as both accuracy and speed directly impact the resulting quantization outcome. Several widely utilized optimization techniques for quantization include SGD, LBFGS, Adam, and Proximal Mapping \[[112](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0112)–[114](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0114)\]. However, the predominant method employed is quantization‐aware training. In this approach, the loss function deviates from the standard categorical cross‐entropy by incorporating additional quantization functions linked to the model weights. This modification compels the network to enhance its learning efficiency \[[106](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0106), [115](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0115), [116](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0116)\]. The parametrized quantization approach has recently gained significant popularity, attributed to its efficacy in enhancing quantization processes. The application of several standard optimization techniques, such as simulated annealing and k‐means, has been studied for the quantization process \[[97](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0097), [102](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0102), [103](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0103)\]. Novel approaches that integrate optimization techniques with various other concepts are emerging. For example, the combination of the gradient‐based method with the fixed‐point number quantization error principle lowers bounding to streamline arithmetic operations.

Selecting the optimal bitwidth for quantization is a significant challenge. The use of high bitwidth leads to high accuracy with elevated memory and compute requirements. On the other hand, the low bitwidth approach favors memory and compute efficiency at the expense of model performance. Hence, researchers have investigated diverse approaches for selecting quantization bitwidth. Measuring quantization‐induced loss is a significant issue in the quantization literature. There is a need to assess the performance loss due to quantization over a wide range of possibilities. Currently, effectively assessing the degree of accuracy loss of different neural network models in different computational task scenarios after quantization is a significant challenge that begs for a solution.

The above notwithstanding, several researchers have proposed wide‐ranging criteria to assess accuracy losses due to quantization, primarily based on statistical principles. The principles of signal‐to‐noise ratio were extended to the context of quantization by Qualcomm [\[117\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0117). In a similar vein, Feng et al. [\[118\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0118) proposed a method based on the intuition of mean squared error, called quantization mean square error, to determine the quantization coefficients. In [\[119\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0119), an overly computationally expensive predictor for quantization accuracy that is based on the flexible once‐for‐all network described in [\[120\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0120) for a direct prediction of model quantization accuracy is described. Beyond these, the assessment of the nature and scale of losses due to the quantization of deep learning models has not been adequately studied [\[88\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0088), and it requires research attention since developing a clear understanding of the origin and mechanism of losses could aid the development of better quantization approaches.

 

### 2.3.3 Low‐Rank Decomposition

Low‐rank decomposition (low‐rank factorization) is a matrix decomposition technique for reducing the size of neural network models. Similar to other model compression techniques, it strives to achieve optimal model light‐weighting while preserving model performance. This approach decomposes large, dense weight matrices characteristic of deep neural networks into smaller (usually two) low‐rank matrices \[[121](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0121), [122](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0122)\]. The strength of this approach lies in its ability to lower model complexity by approximating the original large, dense matrix through the combination of two low‐rank matrices. Furthermore, by capturing the most relevant information in the model's weights, the low‐rank factorization approach creates a compact representation of the large model without significant loss in performance.

The two most prominent low‐rank decomposition approaches are matrix and tensor decomposition techniques. Within this application, singular value decomposition (SVD) is a very common method for decomposing a dense matrix into three low‐rank matrices and capturing the essential features of the original matrix while reducing storage and compute requirements of the resulting approximate model [\[123\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0123). Tensor decomposition, on the other hand, focuses on tensors (multidimensional arrays) in deep neural networks. A popular and efficient tensor decomposition technique is the canonical polyadic low‐rank decomposition. It optimizes the model by removing redundant weights and activations in the fully connected layers [\[121\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0121).

The potential of low‐rank tensor decomposition to compress weight matrices and reduce the dimensionality of deep neural network model parameters is demonstrated in [\[124\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0124) using the Kronecker tensor decomposition technique. Despite the high potential of low‐rank tensor decomposition, there are known issues with low‐rank decomposition approaches; their applicability is limited to scenarios where there is significant information redundancy in the fully connected layers \[[121](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0121), [122](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0122)\]. Hence, the applicability of low‐rank decomposition is somewhat constrained, showing limitations in neural network models that have varying degrees of architectural complexities or in those architectures that do not have appreciable redundancy in their fully connected layers [\[125\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0125). These are the main issues in low‐rank tensor decomposition that invite interest for ongoing research – there is a need to widen the scope and increase the effectiveness of low‐rank decomposition techniques by exploring schemes that are applicable to a broader spectrum of deep neural network architectures without significantly trading off model performance.

 

### 2.3.4 Knowledge Distillation

KD is a predominant approach for deep neural network model compression and optimization \[[126](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0126), [127](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0127)\]. It is based on teacher‐student knowledge transfer principles where the experienced large‐scale model teaches the inexperienced small‐scale student model. The purpose is to improve the student model's performance without inheriting the computational overheads of the teacher model [\[128\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0128). KD fundamentally involves extracting the informative characteristics of a large model's behavior and transferring this knowledge to a smaller model to facilitate the preservation of excellent accuracy in the student model while markedly decreasing its size and complexity. [Figure 2.9](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0009) presents a high‐level overview of KD, highlighting its basic principles, techniques, challenges, and limitations.

![Figure 2.9 Overview of knowledge distillation.](images/c02f009.png)

**Figure 2.9** Overview of knowledge distillation.

In the teacher‐student model framework underlying distillation, the large‐scale, well‐trained model is utilized to guide knowledge development in a smaller‐scale model; the large‐scale network offers direction to the small‐scale network [\[129\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0129). The objective is to replicate the performance of the large‐scale model in the small‐scale model while using fewer parameters and minimizing computational complexity. The small‐scale model may be trained to align with the softmax output of the large‐scale model or to correspond with its feature representations. Distillation loss is a quantity used to measure the small‐scale model's understanding of the large‐scale model's behavior, extending beyond simple categorical inference. Common loss functions exist to evaluate the alignment between small‐scale and large‐scale outputs [\[126\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0126).

The process of transferring knowledge from a teacher model to a smaller version, the student model, aims to optimally preserve vital information as decision‐making abilities required for applications without jeopardizing the performance levels of the student model. Although small‐scale models may not achieve the same performance as large‐scale models in all tasks, the emphasis lies in attaining comparable performance on specific targeted tasks while leveraging smaller models' efficiency and speed benefits. The objective is to balance model size, computational efficiency, and task‐specific performance rather than replicating the large model's exact performance. This makes KD an important technique for model compression and optimization in practical applications.

Distillation techniques have been shown to markedly improve the performance of smaller models, frequently surpassing those trained using conventional methods [\[130\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0130). KD has been effectively utilized in computational vision, natural language processing, and speech recognition, showcasing its adaptability and efficacy. Intelligent selection of large and small‐scale models is essential; an overly complex teacher can diminish the effectiveness of the distillation process. The architecture of both large and small‐scale models significantly influences the success of the distillation process. Adjusting hyperparameters, including temperature in softmax and the weight of distillation loss, is essential for optimizing performance in the student model [\[131\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0131).

KD, recognized for its ability to condense the capabilities of bigger models into formats suitable for deployment in resource‐constrained environments, encounters a range of complex obstacles and limitations. A significant challenge exists, for instance, in implementing large pretrained language models (PLMs) on devices with constrained memory, requiring a careful equilibrium to enhance performance without depleting system resources [\[132\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0132). The generalization capacity of distillation models may be undermined when employing public datasets that diverge from the training datasets, diminishing the model's relevance and accuracy [\[133\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0133). The limitations of current KD methods in federated learning highlight the necessity for novel strategies to tackle the lack of cross‐lingual alignments for knowledge transfer and the risk of unreliable temporal knowledge discrepancies \[[134](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0134), [135](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0135)\]. These limitations underscore the imperative for research to improve KD methodologies to guarantee their efficacy in minimizing model size and complexity while preserving or potentially improving performance across various applications.

KD is an effective method in CNNs, where it has been used to facilitate model compression and improve the performance of smaller networks. The increasing demand for sophisticated models in resource‐limited environments underscores the significance of KD as a critical area of research, capable of facilitating the advancement of more efficient and accessible AI applications [\[136\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0136).

 

## 2.4 Learning Frameworks and Tools for TinyML Development

The quest to attain the transformational effect of TinyML in edge computing and IoT application domains has led to increased efforts in developing frameworks, libraries, and tools to facilitate the implementation of ML algorithms on constrained platforms.

TinyML development approaches may be grouped into three distinct categories ([Figure 2.10](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0010)). The predominant approach involves converting pretrained models to accommodate MCUs limitations. Consequently, these tools typically utilize inference engines produced by established ML libraries, including TensorFlow, Scikit‐learn, and PyTorch, among others, and adapt their code for execution on resource‐constrained, mostly battery‐powered edge and IoT devices [\[22\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0022). The second approach focuses on embedding ML libraries within MCUs, thereby enabling local model training and analysis. This allows for the immediate development of learning models from data collected by the device itself, thereby potentially enhancing the chances for improved model accuracy and facilitating the application of unsupervised techniques [\[22\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0022). The final approach depends on a dedicated coprocessor to assist the primary computing unit with ML‐specific tasks. This is a strategic way to enhance computational performance, though it is not quite familiar due to the significant increase in cost and complexity of the development platforms.

![Figure 2.10 TinyML development ecosystem.](images/c02f010.png)

**Figure 2.10** TinyML development ecosystem.

Research has explored the space of shallow ML algorithms and deep learning algorithms for developing tools and frameworks for TinyML development, with remarkable achievements. Deep learning has significantly influenced the landscape because of its unprecedented growth and adoption across the ML ecosystem. Tools for converting shallow ML techniques, such as decision trees, Naive Bayes classifier, and *k*‐nearest neighbors (*k*‐NNs), to edge or embedded device executable formats have been developed. MicroML [\[137\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0137) enables the conversion of support vector machine (SVM) and relevance vector machine (RVM) algorithms into C code, facilitating execution on various C‐compatible MCUs. It interfaces with the commonly utilized Scikit‐learn toolkit to modify the models produced by this library for execution on 8‐bit microcontrollers with 2 KB of RAM.

Sklearn‐porter [\[138\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0138) is a tool for the translation of trained estimators into Java, GO, C, Ruby, and JavaScript. Sklearn‐porter is comprehensive due to its support for a wide array of languages and its compatibility with a variety of ML algorithms. Sklearn‐porter can port Scikit‐learn models, including decision trees, SVM, random forest (RF), and AdaBoost classifier, specifically for the C language. m2cgen [\[139\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0139) can also translate models trained with Scikit‐learn into various native code formats, including Java, Python, C, Go, and JavaScript. The number of compatible algorithms and the target programming languages exceed those offered by sklearn‐porter.

Weka‐porter [\[140\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0140) is a more algorithm‐specific tool that converts decision tree classifiers produced by the WEKA tool into C, Java, and JavaScript code. EmbML [\[141\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0141) is another library that enables the translation of models trained by WEKA or Scikit‐learn into C++ source code files, which can then be compiled and executed on resource‐constrained platforms. This library supports various ML algorithms, including decision trees, SVMs, and neural networks. Learn [\[142\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0142) is another shallow ML‐targeted framework that generates portable C code from Python libraries, including Scikit‐learn and Keras. This library supports models generated from various algorithms, including RF, decision trees, Naive Bayes, and linear models.

Major technology companies are facilitating the growth of the TinyML ecosystem by investing in and developing open‐source development libraries. Google, for instance, has introduced TensorFlow Lite, which comprises a collection of tools designed to modify TensorFlow models for the execution of deep learning models on embedded or IoT devices. TensorFlow Lite consists of two primary components: the Converter and the Interpreter. The Converter translates models created with TensorFlow into optimized code suitable for execution on resource‐constrained platforms. The Interpreter executes the code produced by the Converter. The resulting model is optimized and could have been developed using any or a combination of various algorithms from the neural network family and is compatible with diverse platforms, including smartphones, embedded Linux, and MCUs. Added to TensorFlow Lite, Google has also adapted the GO language for microcontrollers, creating TinyGo [\[143\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0143).

Microsoft has contributed the open‐source embedded learning library (ELL) to the development of TinyML [\[144\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0144). ELL enables the design and deployment of pretrained ML models on constrained platforms, such as ARM Cortex‐A and Cortex‐M architectures, including Arduino and Raspberry Pi. ELL functions as an optimizing cross‐compiler operating on a standard desktop computer, producing C++ code prepared for execution on the designated single‐board computer. The ELL API is accessible through C++ or Python. It utilizes pretrained neural network models generated by any of the following: Microsoft Cognitive Toolkit, Darknet, or models in the Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) format [\[145\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0145).

At ARM, the efforts to incorporate ML in its devices have increased in recent times. The ARM‐NN toolkit is a component of Linaro's ML initiative. It facilitates the incorporation of neural network workloads within ARM Mali GPUs, ARM Cortex‐A CPUs, and Ethos neural processing units. The ARM‐NN initiative is driven by an open‐source philosophy and is compatible with popular ML frameworks, including TensorFlow, Caffe, and ONNX. To support its suite of devices, ARM has released the Cortex microcontroller software interface standard‐NN (CMSIS‐NN) [\[146\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0146). CMSIS‐NN facilitates the conversion of floating‐point neural networks produced by widely used libraries such as TensorFlow, PyTorch, and Caffe into a fixed‐point format suitable for execution on Cortex‐M devices.

STMicroelectronics is another electronics manufacturer that has created specialized libraries for its devices. The STM32 Cube.AI toolkit [\[147\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0147) facilitates the integration of pretrained neural networks into STM32 ARM Cortex‐M‐based microcontrollers. The tool produces STM32‐compatible C code from neural network models trained with TensorFlow and Keras. STM32Cube.AI enables the execution of large neural networks by utilizing external flash memory for weight storage and RAM for activation buffers.

The Artificial Intelligence for Embedded Systems (AIfES) library [\[148\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0148) developed by the Fraunhofer Institute for Microelectronic Circuits and Systems, is a C‐based, platform‐independent tool designed for generating neural networks compatible with various MCUs, such as Arduino UNO, STM32 F4 Series, and ATMega32U4. AIfES distinguishes itself from other frameworks by enabling the implementation of the neural network training process on embedded devices. It can also generate efficient codes for Windows, Linux platforms, and Raspberry Pi. Cartesiam's NanoEdge AI Studio is a commercial product that enables the creation of ML static libraries for embedding in Cortex‐M‐based microcontrollers. Like AIfES, it facilitates the execution of the training process, including unsupervised model training, on the MCU. This toolkit includes a microcontroller emulator for testing and debugging the resulting model before deployment. uTensor [\[149\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0149) and TinyMLgen [\[150\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0150) are libraries designed to enhance the compatibility of TensorFlow models by generating C code suitable for integration with various families of MCUs. The former emphasizes Mbed boards, whereas the latter exports the trained model to a standard C array, making it applicable to a broader spectrum of microcontrollers.

The implementation of diverse forms of deep neural networks on ARM Cortex‐M processors is currently widespread. CMix‐NN [\[151\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0151) is another open‐source library designed for the deployment of mixed‐precision quantized deep neural networks on MCUs. This tool provides for convolutional kernels with precisions of 2, 4, or 8 bits for any operand. FANN‐on‐MCU [\[152\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0152) is another open‐source framework developed from the fast artificial neural network (FANN) library [\[153\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0153); it is designed to execute lightweight neural network models on microcontrollers. This toolkit processes multilayer perceptrons trained with FANN. It also generates code operating on the ARM Cortex‐M and parallel ultralow‐power platforms [\[154\]](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0154).

To further increase understanding of the frameworks and hardware tools for TinyML development, [Table 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0004) compares some of these TinyML development frameworks, indicating their key features and weaknesses.
