## 10.2 Fundamentals of TinyML

TinyML refers to any deployment of ML technologies conducted on Cortex‐M class microcontrollers and their connected sensor and actuator peripherals. This new field is an intersection of research in ML, embedded systems, low‐power design, hardware efficiency, communications, and real‐time systems. Fundamentally, the issue that distinguishes TinyML from traditional ML applications is that the latter typically assumes the presence of an internet connection and sufficient computational power to process the data, while also having access to extensive storage capacities for large‐scale model weights. In contrast, TinyML devices must manage with minute fractions of computational time and energy, restricted data storage and network bandwidth, enabling fast decision‐making, often on a microsecond timescale [\[8\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0008).

Elements that enable deployment in this space include model‐efficient algorithmic techniques and compact hardware nodes featuring local processing capabilities alongside energy‐optimized computation and memory elements. As a result, tasks such as decision trees, support vector machines, and k‐nearest neighbors are generally favored over dense, deep learning models. Enabling technologies also include specialized hardware, such as custom digital or mixed‐signal integration of ML cores onto mixed‐signal sensors or processors, and optimized peripheral operation. To enable interoperability across sensors and actuators from different manufacturers, the TinyML community also jointly develops standards for operation, representation, and transmission [\[9\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0009). These elements are stated here to distinguish the key technical drivers of the TinyML domain and not as required knowledge for this review. The means by which raw data is translated to signals for the learning system that motivate the constraints detailed above should be apparent from the outset as a clear, robust deployment with TinyML.

TinyML is defined as developing ML models for resource‐constrained edge devices such as microcontrollers. These machines generally lack dedicated hardware to accelerate mathematical operations, a minimum and fixed amount of random‐access memory (RAM) and read‐only memory (ROM), and a battery‐connected power source with a tiny capacity. TinyML employs specialized model optimization to optimize ML models so that they are light enough to deploy and run on resource‐constrained edge devices. In traditional ML, after data collection and model training on a server or the cloud, we need to deploy models on edge devices “close to sensors and actuators,” usually for real‐time data interpretation and device actuation based on the outcome [\[10\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0010). In other words, only the preprocessed or sensor data are transferred to the model, and the model typically takes only a few seconds to produce an outcome.

TinyML powers today to make edge devices “embedded with intelligence,” as reflected by smart home, energy, building automation, industrial monitoring, predictive maintenance, predictive farming, diagnostics, and healthcare monitoring. Edge devices can use TinyML chips to interpret raw data from the sensors, actuators, and nearby assets in real time, give commands, leverage on‐device intelligence to tag raw data instead of streaming everything to the cloud, and make inferences and suggest possible solutions. The hardware components of a TinyML system typically include microcontrollers, sensors (on‐chip and off‐chip components), and memory. Microcontrollers' memory footprints vary significantly from kilobytes to a few megabytes, limiting the size of the model and the capacity of the learning algorithm due to memory constraints [\[11\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0011). These microcontrollers implement at least one general‐purpose processing core capable of running multiple threads with ultralow standby energy via fast entry‐exit capabilities. The processing cores are optimized for low‐power operation.

Likewise, software components designed to operate in remote settings or battery‐powered nodes consume less energy during operation, providing computational operations compared to their server‐based or cloud variants. The ML community is in the process of designing TinyML algorithms that have low memory footprint and low power consumption, especially as the tiny operations need to run many times in battery‐powered systems. These tiny operations take several shapes and sizes but focus on tiny learning operations with a heavy emphasis on executing predictions with less computational processing, reduced memory access, and thus minimal energy for execution. The software tools, comprising both ML algorithms optimized for low‐power consumption and tools to convert these learning algorithms into lightweight firmware that can operate on tiny microcontrollers, form the essentials of TinyML. Recognizing the potential of edge computing, many software framework players have launched lightweight embedded ML inferencing engines to perform inference directly on microcontrollers by deploying learning models [\[12\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0012). Some prominent open‐source ML deployment frameworks include lightweight versions optimized for operation analysis and are key to understanding the operational dynamics.

 

### 10.2.1 Security Threats in TinyML Devices

The proliferation of TinyML has been encouraging, though TinyML devices bring certain threats that can be a risk for use in commercial settings. For instance, an electronic device, no matter how tiny, is not immune to physical damage or subversion. One of the significant constraints for the security of small electronic devices is anonymity from the rest of the world, such as wireless connectivity. If two or more devices do not communicate with the outside world, the security threat these devices face is minimal. When it comes to security, gaining a digital interface is like opening a can of worms.

Physical attacks, software attacks, and side‐channel attacks are significant threats. Physical attacks center around unauthorized access to both hardware devices and physical systems; if operators can prevent access, the integrity of the device is likely to remain intact. Software attacks usually come in the form of errors or vulnerabilities in operating systems and application software; they aim to use defective code to cause the application to crash or to compromise the device and hardware [\[13\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0013). Therefore, side‐channel attacks purport to empower attackers with knowledge about the physical properties in use or governing the design of a cryptographic algorithm; for example, repeated outputs may enable an attacker to guess if two messages use the same encryption key.

 

#### 10.2.1.1 Physical Attacks

Physical attacks are performed directly on the TinyML device, and attackers can interact with the hardware as well. Unlike software‐based attacks, physical security threats should be prevented at the device level to ensure that every functional component is adequately secured. Some common physical attacks include tampering, where attackers try to modify the device configuration or hardware design parameters to unlock protected features, and probing or reverse engineering, where adversaries try to extract sensitive information to access functionalities that are otherwise protected and prohibit unauthorized access. Most of the time, physical security measures are overlooked in a design due to ignorance of possible threats or the added costs involved in designing tamper‐resistant devices [\[14\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0014). However, with the growing number of secure installations in congested cyberspace, the cost per hack has increased, encouraging both attackers and organizations to invest in technology to follow attackers and defend their infrastructure.

A commercial off‐the‐shelf microcontroller can be physically attacked by a side‐channel analysis that reveals the device's secret decryption key. A COTS flash memory chip could be cleaned out entirely with a laser‐based side‐channel attack. An attacker used chemical stripping, a microscope repair operation, and a reverse engineer's expertise to extract read‐only memory physical unclonable feature secrets from a microcontroller. A successful ROM physically unclonable function (PUF) secret recovery entails the complete functionality invasion of the system, namely, having full access to its flash memory. Once this attack is accomplished, the ability to release the attacks in the future is a matter of reverse engineering efforts and analysis on the COTS microcontroller. Hostile ROM PUF secrets can now be calculated using the broadcast behavior of COTS flash memory storing adversarial prefetched instruction operations and PUF challenges, coupled with programming errors in the soft reconfigurable state [\[15\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0015).

 

#### 10.2.1.2 Software Attacks

The main threat to TinyML devices is software attacks, which exploit flaws in the operating system or application software. Since most of these devices run an embedded operating system and execute some applications to collect and analyze data, software attacks may lead to unauthorized access, data manipulation, or malfunctioning of the device. Software vulnerabilities can be exploited in various ways, such as by infecting the operating system with malware, by infecting the application software, or simply by denying that service. Common attacks include malicious software infections such as ransomware, denial‐of‐service attacks, and code injections [\[16\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0016).

TinyML devices have limited processing capability, which may make them more prone to software attacks. Unauthorized access to these devices may result in data theft, data confidentiality compromise, and user privacy violations. Execution of malicious applications may result in data manipulation, data loss, and performance degradation in the devices. A denial‐of‐service attack may render the TinyML device unavailable to users. Given the vulnerabilities and potential consequences of software security breaches, rigorous software security practices such as secure design, secure coding, and software testing and validation are necessary.

Furthermore, access control, secure communication, and data monitoring can also contribute to thwarting malware and malicious code execution, as well as preventing unauthorized access to and data exfiltration from TinyML devices [\[17\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0017). Recently, there has been a significant push to run sanitizers, static analysis, and formal verification tools on modern IoT devices, and similar methods can likely be used to detect potential security risks when building a TinyML model for deployment. For security‐related issues where verification of code is standard, it should be clear that future software technologies provided for general‐purpose devices, like those embedding TinyML, may lack these same constraints. The conclusion should be that more certain, simplistic, and transparent TinyML constructions may be necessary on these platforms in order to protect sensitive data stored in a deep learning classifier.

 

#### 10.2.1.3 Side‐Channel Attacks

Side‐channel attacks exploit information made available by a system while it performs its regular functions. The information leak usually occurs in unintended ways via the physical implementation of the system, such as power consumption, timing information, and electromagnetic emanations. Such leakage might enable attackers to recover secrets or other sensitive information, including cryptographic keys or the direct output of the TinyML model. One of the most promising paths of side‐channel attacks is ML models, which have been shown to suffer from privacy leakage via inversion attacks and backdoor attacks. Hardware side channels, captured through microarchitectural probes such as data caches and micro‐op caches, can lead to the extraction of full cryptographic keys in the presence of known plaintext attacks and to plaintext exfiltration on encrypted channels even if the attacker only controls the network stack.

In the context of TinyML, powerful side‐channel attacks have been developed to extract the output of binarized, quantized, and pruned models and leverage this information to backdoor ML retraining [\[17\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0017). These types of attacks can provide backdoor reprogramming success rates of up to 99.375% under strong evasion attack scenarios. The adaptive countermeasures to mitigate such attacks can lead to the extraction of TinyML model output with a deviation reduction of up to 76.46% compared to non‐mitigated output extraction. Such attacks, when extended to TinyML, would totally undermine trust in autonomous smart devices. Security analysts have come up with interesting case studies of passive side‐channel attacks against IoT devices. For privacy leakage, the models are recovered by considering physical access to the training data, showing a successful inversion attack scenario. Finally, conducting side‐channel resistance measurements allows the designer to ensure that their proposed design contains appropriate mechanisms to protect against passive observation attacks.

 

## 10.3 Privacy Concerns in TinyML

The introduction of processors with ML capabilities has led to the development of low‐powered TinyML devices, which are gaining extensive interest from the engineering and scientific community. These tiny devices will, most of the time, be used close to the end user. Being the major or sole source of private information being dealt with, the use of such data marks a need for attention. Most applications of TinyML are centered on data from physical sensors or smartphones, and this data is frequently sensitive and personal. Neither the consumer nor the end user knows the extent to which information can be crafted based on the data. A primary concern regarding the use of TinyML is the potential misuse of user data by employers and governments. ML models created using user information might be used to compromise the privacy of the user's data or to block freedom of speech [\[17\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0017).

The definition of privacy is multifaceted and spans various domains, including data acquisition, usage limitations, data sharing, and data deletion, making it essential to define and consider data privacy separately. Consumer confidence is essential when launching new TinyML technologies, and this is an essential issue for those trying to develop secure TinyML devices. User confidentiality and privacy preferences should be taken into account during the TinyML system design, while user experience considerations should be taken into account during the actual implementation of the system. As more and more of such implementations occur, concern for data privacy and security has raised a wave of laws and regulations worldwide [\[18\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0018). Though ML applications are increasingly important, ethics and privacy remain pressing issues.

 

### 10.3.1 Data Privacy and Protection

The first and foremost issue that needs to be addressed, from the security and privacy viewpoint, while considering a data‐driven application, is how to protect the privacy of the data that is collected by the application. Data privacy is involved in all data lifecycle aspects, such as collection, processing, storage, and sharing. Therefore, data collection, the first step in the data lifecycle, is critical since once data are collected, the privacy of the owner of the data is at risk. As a result, it is crucial to protect data and ensure that they are only accessible by authorized users. To achieve this, privacy‐preserving techniques must be put in place at the data collection stage as well as across the rest of the data lifecycle processes to safeguard against unauthorized access. This is critical in TinyML, where devices are built to interact with each other and share data, and so challenges to the privacy of data are increased [\[18\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0018).

This motivates the urgent need for methodologies to protect the data privacy of systems for TinyML. For example, data anonymization techniques can help in hiding the identity of data owners, and encryption can protect sensitive data. In addition, FL and DP can also be utilized to enhance the privacy of the system. Also, users have the right to control the way that the service or entity provider processes their data, such as providing their consent to accept or deny usage of their data for specific purposes or accessing their data. Service providers have a legal obligation to comply with regulations that state the right of users to have full access to and full control of their data in the process. Data privacy, however, doesn't merely refer to protecting the originator's personally identifiable information; it encompasses the protection of all individual data, such as aggregated data [\[18\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0018). Therefore, what is necessary in the context of TinyML applications is the development of frameworks that address the privacy of data across the entire data lifecycle.

 

### 10.3.2 User Privacy and Consent Issues

It is important to acknowledge that the way we collect data can impact the autonomy and possibly trust between users and the organizations deploying such sensing mechanisms. Engaging in data collection without obtaining consent from the users to collect details of a potentially sensitive nature could raise ethical and possibly regulatory issues. The role of transparency is essential. Informed, explicit consent is likely under the control of regulatory frameworks, and there are challenges that the right to give informed consent could impose on embedded devices. What would be even more difficult for an embedded learning scenario is if the inferred properties of an individual were derived as a result of data sharing using cloud platforms. Data sharing and interoperability mandates providing adequate information to allow an individual to make an informed choice prior to consent [\[18\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0018).

One of the overarching issues with a lot of data usage and exchange practices is often the adequacy of transparency and informed consent in this space. There are regulatory frameworks that enforce some level of user rights to understand and question their data sharing. There must be prior consent to transfer personal information to a third party if the jurisdiction is different from the one in which the data was collected and the receiving country does not have similar privacy protections. The consent of the data subject is acknowledged as the legitimate basis for transferring data between jurisdictions with different privacy protections. Specific requirements for consent include that it must be freely given, specific, informed, and explicit. However, managing informed consent is challenging in the space where there is a shortage of capabilities with some of the emerging edge ML [\[19\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0019). It is essential to ensure that the interests and rights of the individual are prioritized in the operation and design of technologies.

 

## 10.4 Security and Privacy Solutions

Developing effective security and privacy solutions that are compatible with the constraints of TinyML is necessary. However, the diminished technical and economic incentives present in the edge and IoT markets mean that many device manufacturers will not undertake security and privacy‐enhancing efforts unless there are external pressures to do so. The dissemination of security and privacy knowledge is therefore necessary so that consumers or regulatory bodies will have the requisite information to qualitatively differentiate these sensor deployments based on their designs or the manufacturer's security posture \[[10](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0010), [19](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0019)\].

There are two primary features of the device design and development process that will have a significant impact on the fundamentals of device security and privacy posture: hardware and software. A range of hardware‐based protections also exists in the data protection and encryption space, but many of these are designed for larger general‐purpose computers and have performance‐speed‐accuracy trade‐offs that make them prohibitive for a small microcontroller. Examples of hardware‐based protections for larger computers include the use of secure enclaves and tamper‐resistant hardware designs. These ensure that if an adversary were to compromise the device and extract the computational secrets physically, it would be infeasible to use the results of that computation as substitutes in a new operating device or to learn the details of what transpired [\[11\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0011).

Practices that can enhance software security on these devices include defect mitigation, for example, Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) and secure coding practices, ensuring that the software (and hardware, when possible) is constructed in a manner that prohibits whole classes of attacks on the system. This could include performing vulnerability assessments to enumerate the potential attack surfaces on a device and then hardening those surfaces to resist attacks. Protection of data in transit and at rest is necessary to ensure the integrity of the data and the privacy of the user. Combine this with ensuring that network traffic associated with these systems can be authenticated to prevent spoofing and depersonalization via encryption so that intermediate parties on the network, with potentially intrusive insight into user traffic, will not have personalized user data that violates user privacy [\[12\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0012).

 

### 10.4.1 Hardware‐Based Solutions

Integrating hardware solutions in TinyML devices is essential to enhancing their security. Key hardware security technologies include secure chips and hardware security modules, which can be used to provide, for instance, encryption functionalities and secure key storage. These modules can also be leveraged to perform relevant security functionalities, including securely identifying a device, secure data storage, secure firmware updates, secure remote access, code and data protection, secure boot procedures, and secure on‐board cryptographic operations. A secure chip can be used for, among other things, establishing a trusted execution and data processing environment, establishing a secure link with the device, and enabling secure registration and verification of the devices [\[13\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0013). Security‐aware training of TinyML Models is presented in [Table 10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-tbl-0001).

For embedded devices in general, and TinyML devices in particular, the combined use of hardware‐based cryptographic operations, hardware‐based encryption tamper protection, and physical security features can be precious in resisting physical attacks. Hardware‐based encryption typically requires a secret or confidential key to be stored securely in a key storage memory or dedicated hardware security module inside or connected to a microcontroller or processor. During the decryption process, minimal or no sensitive data is made available to the software or becomes directly accessible as unencrypted data, reducing the risk of unauthorized data access. A hardware security module can improve the security of key and data operations by integrating functionalities resistant to external active and semi‐invasive physical attack techniques [\[14\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0014). Relevant industry standards and guidelines exist, defining requirements and checking methods for secure cryptographic devices.

The importance of hardware‐level security features is also clearly depicted in real‐world use cases and case studies. For example, a modern approach to secure code storage and execution on a microcontroller in the cloud utilizes the microcontroller's architecture‐based components to make this process as efficient as possible. The solution was also compatible with a growing set of security features that extend over a trust boundary from the silicon to the cloud. The secure chips used in practice acted as a hardware root of trust. Combined with a typically used method for the secure operation of the main processor in the industry, it allowed remote attestation and secure condition detection processes in their protocol. Secure chips were also used to store RSA and symmetric secret keys in a project, focusing on a low‐power IoT‐based facial authentication and identification system [\[15\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0015). This was one of the key security features of the facial recognition solution, respecting the identification standard for driver's licenses and electronic visa systems. Each module was given a unique, secure chip, ensuring that the symmetric keys stored in them always satisfied the requirements provided in the guidelines. This unique hardware feature was verified to give the system software and developers knowledge of whether the module functions under the correct purchased quality level. According to the guidelines, the setup was tested using an obtainment setup that would generate a unique, non‐containing backdoor, data hiding, and a feature for financially identifying the chip [\[16\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0016). A secure reference firmware was created for the security check. Development of the main module system firmware continues.

 

### 10.4.2 Software‐Based Solutions

To bolster the security posture of TinyML devices, companies can also aim to address software‐based issues on both the device and server sides. This includes: Secure Coding Practices: The main focus should be to follow a secure development lifecycle during the development of software for TinyML devices. During the design phase, identify various types of nodes for identification purposes. Frequent Vulnerability Assessment: It is quite likely that companies can easily find or assess vulnerabilities within the TinyML software stack. These identified vulnerabilities can be reported to the developer for fixing, which can be provided to the user through regular software updates. Regular Software Updates: Supply the TinyML software updates in a phased manner to address the known vulnerabilities on a priority basis (where unknown vulnerabilities are not fixed once the device is under deployment) [\[17\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0017).

By developing software, identifying weaknesses, and updating software with added security solutions, ML can be used for real‐time threat detection. Vulnerabilities will continue to exist in the environment from which solutions are derived, and the emphasis will be on addressing these vulnerabilities as quickly as possible. Manufacturers of TinyML devices will be forthcoming in implementing control measures to address the identified vulnerabilities. By implementing software‐based solutions, organizations can demonstrate a prudent level of control to identify and address weaknesses in software through a consolidated known vulnerability document. In this way, developers can fix the known issues well in advance during the development lifecycle.

Organizations that develop TinyML embedded devices must use internal or external known threat intelligence services to find any embedded malware in their solution that resides on the device itself. By providing malware‐free solutions that monitor device memory and constantly look for any embedded malware in the device or solution, manufacturers can win the trust and satisfaction of the consumer. Developers can start providing such exceptions at design time when the device is being developed and functions are being provided [\[18\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0018). This needs to be built in during the initial device design and not as an add‐on feature at the end.

 

### 10.4.3 Encryption and Authentication Techniques

Encryption is a critical component for security on TinyML devices. Data transmitted from these devices to a remote server or database and stored on the device can be intercepted or otherwise breached if left unencrypted. As such, one of the primary tenets of encryption is its ability to prevent unauthorized access or exposure of sensitive (and often private) data. Systems or devices that utilize cryptography will want to be sure that the encryption standards used are intense, challenging to break, and provide protection from techniques such as cryptanalysis.

Moreover, these standards should be able to ensure the integrity and confidentiality of the data being transmitted or analyzed. Some suggested algorithms and standards include the Advanced Encryption Standard, elliptic‐curve cryptography, and protocols such as RSA and hash‐based message authentication code – Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (HMAC‐SHA1) [\[19\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0019). The prime concepts in protecting data include two significant ways of encryption. Authentication, such as encryption, is of equal importance in maintaining a safeguard on devices and data; a valid user identification or device recognition must be enforced before any data is potentially stored or transmitted further.

For these TinyML devices to be secure, robust methods must be used to verify that data is encrypted and that a user's data is held confidential. This often takes the form of some physical device in the user's possession. One of the most common forms of protecting data on a device is the use of cryptographic keys, typically a pair consisting of a public key and a private key. Key management is an essential aspect of security that must be taken into account when developing these systems [\[20\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0020). For that reason, it is necessary to guarantee that privacy policies are transparent, carefully implemented, and routinely updated to deal with arising personal privacy worries and governing needs. ## 10.5 The Implementation of Novel Security Schemes for TinyML Applications

TinyML represents the execution of ML models on ultralow‐power edge devices, including microcontrollers, wearables, and IoT sensors. The use of TinyML is proliferating, particularly in domains like healthcare, autonomous systems, and smart homes. Given the constrained nature of these devices, ensuring security poses significant challenges. Developing and implementing novel security schemes tailored specifically for TinyML applications is critical to protect against cyber threats. This section explores several advanced security techniques specifically adapted to the needs and limitations of TinyML systems.

 

### 10.5.1 Intrusion Detection System (IDS)

As IoT resource‐constrained systems expand, the complexity of cyber threats grows accordingly, making the need for effective threat mitigation more critical. Intrusions, unauthorized activities that compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of these systems, must be detected and countered [\[21\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0021). Intrusion Detection Systems

The SIDS functions by matching network activity to a database of known attack signatures, leveraging supervised ML algorithms to enhance its ability to detect familiar threats. However, these systems face limitations due to their dependence on labeled datasets, which makes it difficult to detect novel or previously unseen threats. Additionally, maintaining the large databases required for SIDSs can be resource‐intensive [\[24\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0024). Traditional SIDS architectures, often centralized, may also introduce vulnerabilities, such as single points of failure and privacy concerns [\[25\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0025).

In contrast, the AIDS uses ML and statistical techniques to establish a baseline of normal system behavior, flagging deviations as potential security threats [\[26\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0026). These systems, particularly those utilizing unsupervised learning, are capable of detecting anomalies and new patterns without relying on predefined criteria. This flexibility enables AIDSs to support sophisticated malware detection, spam classification, and intrusion detection frameworks. To achieve this, AIDSs typically rely on powerful servers with high computational capacity to analyze vast datasets and identify vulnerabilities [\[27\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0027). However, AIDSs, or behavior‐based IDSs, are often plagued by a high False Alarm Rate (FAR), which can lead to unnecessary disruptions, wasted resources, and system downtime while verifying alerts. Furthermore, the growing threat of zero‐day attacks – exploits targeting unknown vulnerabilities poses a significant challenge to AIDSs. These attacks require rapid adaptation, a difficult task given the unpredictable nature of such threats [\[24\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0024).

Several studies have investigated various ML methods for IDSs. For example, authors of [\[28\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0028) present an IDS that employs a deep auto‐encoder along with multiple deep decoders for unsupervised classification. This system processes raw, unlabeled network data, compressing it into a simpler form using the auto‐encoder, while the decoders work to reconstruct the original data. Through this reconstruction process, the IDS learns to identify anomalies in network traffic that could signify potential threats. Also, [\[29\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0029) introduces an IDS using XGBoost, an ML technique renowned for tree‐boosting capabilities. In this system, decision trees are constructed sequentially, correcting errors identified by previous trees. The primary strength of XGBoost lies in its ability to strike a balance between bias and variance, allowing the system to make accurate predictions while minimizing the risk of overfitting. In a different context, the authors of [\[30\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0030) explore the use of several ML classifiers for IDSs in electric vehicle charging stations (EVCSs).

The importance of IDS in electric vehicle charging infrastructure (EVCI) is critical to maintaining both cybersecurity and operational integrity. Authors in [\[31\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0031) demonstrate the effectiveness of ML classifiers in detecting distributed‐denial‐of‐service (DDoS) attacks within EVCS networks by analyzing IoT datasets to detect malicious traffic patterns specific to EVCS environments. In wearable devices, Fyntanidou et al. [\[32\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0032) developed a wrist‐worn device that tracks vital signs such as body temperature, respiratory patterns, and blood oxygen levels to assist in prioritizing COVID‐19 patients in emergency settings.

Utilizing TinyML technology, the device's neural network processes respiratory data locally, eliminating the need to transfer information to the cloud and ensuring the privacy of sensitive patient data. Moving beyond traditional ML approaches, TinyML emerges as a game changer for IDS, particularly in resource‐constrained environments. TinyML enhances both SIDS and AIDS by optimizing ML models for edge devices, enabling real‐time, resource‐efficient anomaly detection. Its adaptive capabilities minimize latency, reduce network dependence, and strengthen cybersecurity resilience, allowing systems to adapt to evolving threats.

 

### 10.5.2 Trusted Execution Environment (TEE)

Trusted execution environment (TEE) refers to a secure, isolated environment within a device that ensures sensitive computations, such as those involving ML models or private data, are performed securely. TEEs are designed to protect data and code integrity from unauthorized access or tampering, even if the primary operating system is compromised. TEEs are becoming more commonly available on modern embedded processors [\[33\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0033). One notable example of such embedded processors is ARM, where a TrustZone security feature is integrated into ARM‐based processors that create a secure execution environment [\[34\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0034). It enables the separation of trusted and untrusted resources on a system, effectively dividing the hardware into two modes: secure and normal. The Secure mode handles sensitive tasks like encryption and authentication with access to both secure and nonsecure resources, while the normal mode runs regular applications with restricted access to ensure the protection of critical operations. Because of its TEE capability in providing a secure environment, it has gained significant attention in the development of speech‐based applications.

VoiceGuard [\[35\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0035), for example, was one of the pioneering efforts to implement Intel SGX, a well‐established TEE solution for automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems. Similarly, Bayerl et al. [\[36\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0036) introduced the Offline Model Guard (OMG), a TEE‐based architecture designed to support keyword spotting (KWS) tasks on ARM‐powered mobile devices. Furthermore, iFlask [\[34\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0034) introduced a security system that isolates the Flask security subsystem from unsafe environments using ARM TrustZone, by placing the security server in a protected enclave. They address mobile runtime security issues and mitigate threats from malicious environments. Implemented on SELinux, which underpins SEAndroid, their prototype successfully protects against all known vulnerabilities, according to experimental results. Similarly, authors in [\[37\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0037) developed a system to prevent sensitive information leakages, like contact lists or private photos, using a fine‐grained access control scheme based on Ciphertext‐Policy Attribute‐Based Encryption (CPABE), and TEE. Their approach supports secure access during critical operations, outperforming traditional access‐control methods.

Moreover, the work [\[38\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0038) proposed PrivateRS, a private recommender system using a client/server framework. Assuming an untrustworthy server, the client randomizes user ratings with DP techniques and replaces them with private symbols, allowing the server to predict item ratings without revealing sensitive data. Their experiments showed that the system can generate accurate recommendations while maintaining privacy. The works \[[39](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0039), [40](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0040)\] propose two notable approaches for ensuring the security of on‐device learning models: ShadowNet and MirrorNet. ShadowNet, designed around convolutional neural networks (CNNs), modifies the linear layer weights before sending them to the untrusted environment and subsequently restores them within the TEE. This enables secure outsourcing of the model's heavy linear layers without exposing the weights.

Alternatively, MirrorNet connects a lightweight mirror network to the base deep neural network (DNN) model, with the mirror network residing in a secure environment. This solution effectively prevents model extraction and addresses the computational and storage constraints of TEEs. Finally, [\[41\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0041) presents STML, a system and algorithm codesign aimed at securing the intellectual property (IP) of TinyML on MCUs equipped with ARM TrustZone, focusing on resource‐constrained devices. The design optimizes both memory utilization and latency while also ensuring the security and accuracy of emerging models. A prototype was implemented and benchmarked using seven models, showing that STML significantly reduces model protection runtime overhead.

 

### 10.5.3 Lightweight Cryptography

TinyML devices typically operate with limited memory, processing power, and battery life, making the use of conventional cryptographic algorithms infeasible. Lightweight cryptography has emerged as an essential approach for securing TinyML applications, offering data protection without overburdening the system's resources. Generally, lightweight cryptography is broadly categorized into symmetric and asymmetric algorithms. Symmetric algorithms are further broken down into two types: Lightweight Block Ciphers (LWBC) and Lightweight Stream Ciphers (LWSC). In contrast, elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) is a form of asymmetric cryptography. The performance of lightweight cryptographic techniques is assessed based on several parameters, including key size, block size, the number of rounds, and the underlying algorithmic structure. In this direction, authors [\[42\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0042) introduced the LWHC system, combining LED and PRESENT ciphers with the SPECK key scheduling algorithm, enhancing security through the RECTANGLE S‐Box. Although resistant to key attacks, the system leaves other vulnerabilities unaddressed. Noura et al. [\[43\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0043) proposed a dynamic lightweight stream cipher (LSC) optimized for IoT, combining CR4, PRNG, and LFSR with high resistance to various attacks but remaining vulnerable to disclosure attacks. Also, [\[44\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0044) developed SAT\_Jo, a lightweight block cipher for IoT, balancing security and resource efficiency through a substitution‐permutation network (SPN). Authors of [\[45\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0045) created a hybrid cryptographic model using PRESENT and Salsa20 with a chaotic logistic map for key generation, providing both speed and complexity.

Notably, Noura et al. [\[46\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0046) presented the One Round Cipher (ORC), a dynamic lightweight encryption model offering high randomness and resistance to critical attacks. Authors in [\[47\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0047) introduced G‐TBSA for energy‐efficient encryption in wireless sensor networks, though it is restricted to sensor devices. The framework in [\[48\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0048) enhanced the PRESENT cipher by reducing rounds, and improving tiny can significantly enhance privacy and security. Register security, though battery consumption remains untested. The KDF scheme [\[49\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0049) introduced dynamic key generation with real‐time applications, ensuring resistance to several attacks while maintaining low computational complexity. Furthermore, authors in [\[50\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0050) proposed Lightweight CA (LCC), a cipher that outperforms DES and 3DES with strong randomness and efficiency.

Zhao et al. [\[51\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0051) developed a modified QARMA architecture, enhancing speed and gate area efficiency but requiring further optimization. Similarly, reference [\[52\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0052) presented MBCT, a block cipher with matrix rotation and XOR functions that reduced memory use and improved speed. Mishra et al. [\[53\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0053) introduced lightweight cryptographic primitives, combining differential logic and random key generation to reduce memory and time while increasing complexity. Authors in [\[54\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0054) developed chaos‐based PRNG encryption for patient data security, demonstrating strong real‐time performance and resistance to attacks. Gyamfi et al. [\[55\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0055) enhanced ECC by integrating Diffie‐Hellman key exchange and AES, making it suitable for resource‐limited IoT systems. Khan et al. [\[56\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0056) proposed IECC, an elliptic curve‐based security framework for medical IoT sensors, offering faster encryption and lower overheads. Mohandas et al. [\[57\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0057) introduced A4, a stream cipher using LFSR and FCSR, with strong resistance to algebraic and brute‐force attacks. Finally, authors of [\[58\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0058) designed NLSC, a chaos‐based stream cipher suitable for resource‐constrained devices, demonstrating resistance to statistical attacks.

 

## 10.6 Privacy‐Enhancing Techniques for TinyML

TinyML, with its ability to perform on‐device ML on edge devices such as IoT sensors and wearables, introduces privacy concerns, especially when dealing with sensitive data in healthcare, smart homes, and autonomous vehicles. To address these privacy concerns, several techniques are employed, each carefully designed to align with the resource constraints and computational limitations of TinyML environments.

 

### 10.6.1 Federated Learning

Data privacy remains a critical concern for individuals, particularly when it involves the transmission and storage of their personal information. FL can address this by enabling TinyML models to be trained locally on devices while data, such as medical records, must remain local, eliminating the need to transfer sensitive raw data to the cloud server [\[59\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0059). Hence, incorporating FL into TinyML can significantly enhance privacy and security. For instance, authors in [\[60\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0060) have introduced TinyFedTL, a decentralized learning mechanism. This approach keeps data processing on the device itself, thereby avoiding the centralization of sensitive information and strengthening security. Federated transfer learning provides a privacy‐respecting solution for the TinyML community, reducing communication overhead and accommodating the hardware limitations of microcontrollers like the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense.

Similarly, Mathur et al. [\[61\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0061) demonstrated FL on TinyML edge devices such as Android phones, Raspberry Pi, and NVIDIA Jetson using the Flower framework. They implemented the clients in Java and Python, allowing on‐device training with TensorFlow Lite. This approach differs from resource‐limited systems, such as the Arduino Nano 33 BLE, where models must be trained off‐device and later transferred to the device for inference [\[62\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0062). Moreover, the authors of [\[63\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0063) review key challenges in TinyML, such as power consumption, limited memory, and computational constraints, while exploring solutions like energy harvesting, optimization techniques, and privacy‐preserving FL. They also examine TinyML's role in enhancing cybersecurity for EVCIs through an experimental case study. This study shows that TinyML reduces delay and memory usage compared to traditional ML, with a minor accuracy trade‐off, and includes a practical demonstration using the ESP32 microcontroller.

Although FL keeps the raw data safe, it is still vulnerable to various privacy and security threats, mainly because sensitive information can still be inferred from shared model updates [\[63\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0063). Similarly, in [\[64\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0064), the authors propose FedLVR, a privacy‐preserving FL framework optimized for fine‐grained vehicle detection in edge‐assisted intelligent transportation systems. This framework deploys a lightweight vehicle recognition model on edge nodes, achieving high accuracy while notably reducing model complexity, as demonstrated in experimental evaluations.

Rahim et al. [\[65\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0065) present the EET‐SAGIN algorithm, leveraging the TinyFDRL framework in a four‐layer aerial system combining ground nodes, low‐ and high‐altitude UAVs, and satellites. Integrating FL, deep reinforcement learning, and TinyML enables distributed UAV applications across diverse environments. Simulations show that while energy consumption increases with more UAVs, TinyFDRL consistently achieves the lowest consumption with 20 drones due to optimized parameter learning.

 

### 10.6.2 Differential Privacy (DP)

This has emerged as a critical privacy‐preserving technique for TinyML, ensuring that sensitive information in local datasets is protected while allowing for collaborative model training and inference. In TinyML, where models are deployed on resource‐constrained edge devices [\[66\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0066), DP can prevent the leakage of private data during model updates and inference by adding controlled noise to the data or model gradients. DP was initially introduced by Dwork [\[67\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0067); it is a statistical model aimed at preserving data privacy. It works by applying carefully calculated random noise to the data through various mathematical techniques to ensure anonymity. There are many types of DP. Global DP (GDP) adds noise after data aggregation, while Local DP (LDP) applies noise directly to individual data, ensuring privacy at the source. Zero‐concentrated DP (zCDP) and Rényi DP (RDP) offer fine control over privacy budgets, particularly in iterative ML processes. Approximate DP (ε, δ)‐DP allows minor privacy breaches for practical use. Group DP extends privacy to groups, and PATE applies DP in model aggregation for sensitive data. Each type balances privacy and utility based on application needs \[[67](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0067), [68](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0068)\].

Conventional DP relies on the assumption of a trusted central authority, a requirement that is frequently impractical [\[69\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0069). Therefore, LDP [\[70\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0070) has been adopted in FL to eliminate the need for a trusted central party, but it struggles with deep learning on heterogeneous IoT data due to the trade‐off between privacy and utility [\[71\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0071). Key challenges include the degradation of model performance from fixed‐range gradient clipping and the rapid accumulation of the privacy budget during iterative training. Sun et al. [\[72\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0072) proposed adaptive weight clipping, though it only adapts at the layer level, and the noise introduced by LDP continues to impair accuracy. For TinyML devices, authors of [\[73\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0073) integrated several LDP mechanisms, including PM‐OPT and PM‐SUB, with FedSGD to form the LDP‐FedSGD algorithm, enabling privacy‐preserving traffic prediction in vehicular crowdsourcing by transmitting noisy gradients.

Experiments show superior performance, with plans to extend this to deep learning tasks. Similarly, an LDP‐based framework for clustered FL on heterogeneous IoT data is proposed in [\[74\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0074). To reduce LDP noise impact, an adaptive layer‐wise perturbation method, along with parameter shuffling and compression, is used to minimize privacy budget issues and communication overhead. This approach effectively balances privacy and utility in FL models. DP is also applied in centralized speech applications to obscure speaker voiceprints, as demonstrated in VoiceMask [\[75\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0075). In contrast, another approach ensures privacy by introducing dummy words into the output transcripts [\[76\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0076). While these techniques focus on centralized training, there is a growing trend of incorporating DP within FL. For example, DP has been applied to mitigate property inference attacks in the training of FL‐based speech‐emotion recognition models [\[77\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0077).

 

### 10.6.3 Homomorphic Encryption (HE)

This is a cryptographic technique enabling computation on encrypted data, ensuring privacy by never revealing the underlying data to the processing entity. For TinyML, which involves ML models deployed on resource‐constrained edge devices, homomorphic encryption (HE) has emerged as a promising solution for privacy‐preserving computations. However, the computational overhead and memory usage associated with HE pose significant challenges in the context of TinyML. Recent innovations focus on reducing this overhead and making HE feasible for real‐time TinyML applications.

Hybrid homomorphic encryption (HHE), which combines the efficiency of symmetric cryptography with HE, has been a key advancement. HHE reduces the computational burden by offloading intensive cryptographic operations to the cloud, allowing edge devices to perform lightweight encryption tasks while maintaining robust privacy [\[78\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0078). In this direction, Xu et al. [\[79\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0079) developed the OpenFHE library, an open‐source tool designed to enhance the performance of fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). The library integrates several hardware acceleration techniques, such as GPU and FPGA support, to make HE more practical for edge computing scenarios like TinyML. This work focused on the bootstrapping mechanism, which is critical for reducing noise and enabling deeper computations on encrypted data.

A HHE framework enables privacy‐preserving ML on edge devices. This framework demonstrated its effectiveness in reducing computational costs by selectively applying encryption only to sensitive parts of the data [\[78\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0078). The proposed solution was tested on a heart disease prediction model, showing that HHE could enable efficient and secure model inference on TinyML devices. Shabir et al. [\[80\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0080) presented an aggregation scheme for FL using HE, designed specifically for TinyML devices. Their study addressed the communication bottlenecks in secure FL environments, showing how efficient homomorphic operations could significantly reduce both computation and communication overhead while maintaining privacy.

Lou and Jiang [\[81\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0081) introduced HEMET, a HE‐friendly privacy‐preserving mobile neural network architecture. This work addressed the challenge of using traditional mobile network architectures for privacy‐preserving neural networks (PPNNs). They found that simply reducing parameters did not lower inference latency due to the increased multiplicative depth in HE. HEMET optimized this architecture, resulting in a 59.3–61.2% reduction in inference latency while maintaining accuracy, which makes it particularly valuable for real‐time TinyML applications. Also, the approach integrates FHE with deep learning, specifically for edge devices. They demonstrated the application of FHE in time‐series analysis using a one‐dimensional convolutional neural network (1D CNN) for predicting dairy herd performance [\[82\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0082). This work highlighted the practical challenges of integrating FHE in real‐world neural network models and laid the groundwork for further optimizations in edge computing scenarios.

 

## 10.7 Future Directions of Security and Privacy in TinyML Devices

As TinyML continues to expand its applications across various industries, the security and privacy of these devices have become critical concerns. TinyML operates at the edge, often processing sensitive information directly on‐device, which presents unique challenges related to the protection of data and model integrity. The resource‐constrained nature of TinyML devices, limited in computing power, memory, and energy, adds further complexity to the implementation of robust security measures. Moving forward, research and development in the security and privacy of TinyML devices are expected to focus on several key areas.

 

### 10.7.1 Secure Model Inference and Execution

Ensuring the security of model inference is a significant challenge for TinyML devices, as adversarial attacks can target both the model's input and output. Future advancements will focus on developing secure inference protocols that protect against adversarial examples, deliberately manipulated inputs designed to deceive the model into making incorrect predictions. Additionally, techniques like HE and secure multiparty computation (SMPC) will evolve to enable secure model inference without revealing sensitive data to external entities, albeit with more efficient and lightweight adaptations suitable for TinyML devices.

 

### 10.7.2 Adversarial Attack and Defense Mechanisms

As TinyML devices become more prevalent, they will become targets for various adversarial attacks, including data poisoning, model inversion, and evasion attacks. Future research will focus on creating robust adversarial defense mechanisms that can be deployed on resource‐constrained TinyML platforms. This includes developing lightweight adversarial training methods to improve model robustness, as well as designing detection systems to identify and mitigate adversarial attacks in real time. Additionally, the concept of “secure by design” will become more prominent, where TinyML models are designed with inherent resistance to adversarial manipulation.

 

### 10.7.3 Federated Learning (FL) with Differential Privacy Security

FL is widely recognized as a privacy‐preserving method of distributed model training, but it faces unique security challenges in the context of TinyML. In the future, secure FL for TinyML devices will focus on mitigating threats like model poisoning, where malicious devices can corrupt the global model. Innovations such as Byzantine‐resilient aggregation techniques, secure model updates, and DP‐integrated FL will be essential to ensure the integrity of the model without relying on computationally expensive operations. Moreover, advancements in hierarchical and decentralized FL architectures will enable more secure, efficient, and scalable deployment of TinyML systems in environments with a large number of devices.

 

### 10.7.4 Tamper‐Resistant Hardware for TinyML

Physical tampering poses a serious risk to TinyML devices, particularly when deployed in untrusted environments, such as industrial settings or remote locations. Future research will focus on developing tamper‐resistant hardware architectures that protect TinyML devices against physical attacks. Secure hardware enclaves, TEEs, and PUFs will become more prevalent in TinyML devices. These hardware‐based security mechanisms will ensure that sensitive data, model parameters, and cryptographic keys are protected even if an attacker gains physical access to the device.

 

### 10.7.5 Energy‐Efficient Security Protocols

One of the critical challenges in securing TinyML devices is balancing the energy efficiency requirements with the computational demands of security protocols. Future directions will emphasize the development of energy‐efficient security solutions specifically designed for TinyML environments. This includes lightweight authentication and authorization protocols, as well as context‐aware security solutions that adapt the security level based on the device's current energy state and threat level [\[83\]](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0083). The rise of energy‐harvesting TinyML devices, which rely on ambient energy sources like solar or kinetic energy, will also drive the need for ultralow‐power security techniques.

 

### 10.7.6 Real‐Time Security Monitoring and Anomaly Detection

TinyML devices often operate in dynamic environments where new threats can emerge at any time. Real‐time security monitoring and anomaly detection will be critical to protecting TinyML devices from attacks or abnormal behavior. Future advancements will include lightweight ML‐based anomaly detection systems that can run directly on TinyML devices, enabling them to detect and respond to security threats in real time. These systems will leverage behavior profiling, context awareness, and unsupervised learning techniques to identify deviations from normal operations without the need for extensive computational resources.

 

## 10.8 Lessons Learned

In the exploration of security and privacy for TinyML devices, several critical lessons have emerged that highlight the importance of adapting security mechanisms to the unique characteristics of resource‐constrained edge devices. Key lessons learned include:

*   TinyML devices have limited computational power, memory, and energy, so security mechanisms must be lightweight yet practical. Traditional cryptographic methods and security protocols must be reengineered to operate within TinyML's constraints without compromising the device's performance.
*   FL has emerged as a promising solution for decentralized model training on TinyML devices. However, FL introduces new attack vectors, such as model poisoning and data leakage, emphasizing the need for secure aggregation methods and privacy‐preserving techniques like DP to ensure both data integrity and user privacy.
*   TinyML systems are particularly vulnerable to adversarial attacks, where small input manipulations can lead to incorrect model predictions. This underscores the need for lightweight adversarial defense mechanisms tailored to TinyML devices, capable of detecting and mitigating such attacks without imposing excessive computational burdens.
*   Tamper‐resistant hardware, secure enclaves, and TEEs are essential to safeguarding TinyML devices from physical attacks. Security needs to be implemented at the hardware and software levels to ensure holistic protection against adversarial threats.
*   Many TinyML devices operate in environments where power sources are limited, making energy‐efficient security protocols essential. Techniques like lightweight cryptography, context‐aware security solutions, and efficient key management are necessary to maintain robust security without draining device power.
*   While DP and HE show promise, their implementation on TinyML devices remains a challenge due to their resource demands. More efficient versions of these techniques are needed to maintain privacy while enabling real‐time, on‐device inference and learning.
*   As TinyML evolves to support on‐device learning, new security challenges arise. Securely updating models and preventing adversarial tampering during training requires new protocols and mechanisms that can operate within the limited resources of TinyML systems.

 

## 10.9 Limitations of this Study

This chapter provides a comprehensive exploration of privacy‐enhancing techniques for TinyML; however, certain limitations persist, and some have been identified. The implementation complexity and computational demands of methods such as SMPC and DP can be prohibitive for resource‐constrained TinyML devices. Moreover, FL, while effective in decentralizing data, remains vulnerable to challenges such as model poisoning and inference attacks, which are not fully mitigated by existing solutions. Privacy‐preserving data augmentation techniques may also affect model accuracy due to the synthetic nature of generated data, potentially limiting the robustness of the models. While methods such as encryption and anonymization are promising, they often involve trade‐offs between security and computational efficiency, which may restrict their practicality for real‐time TinyML applications. Besides the detailed analysis of security and privacy, this study did not consider other aspects of TinyML devices, which are also critical to fostering acceptable technology usage and application, such as ethical and legal considerations, explainability and interpretability, data quality and management, edge device heterogeneity, real‐time processing and latency, deployment and integration challenges, model optimization and compression and energy efficiency.

 

## 10.10 Conclusion

This chapter explored privacy‐aware training methods to boost the discretion of data processed by TinyML models. It begins by exploring differential personal privacy, which adds statistical sound to version outcomes of unknown individual data payments. This makes personal privacy more robust while balancing the compromise between personal privacy and design precision. Federated understanding is looked at for its ability to keep information centered by sharing only model updates and mitigating threats of information breaches, yet encountering difficulties such as version poisoning and reasoning assaults. It was identified that SMPC is scrutinized as a technique that enables collective design training without raw information exchange. It depends on cryptographic methods to preserve information confidentiality, though its complexity and computational demands can be high. Privacy‐preserving data augmentation, which creates artificial information to simulate actual information while protecting personal privacy, is highlighted, noting its possible effect on design performance and the requirement for adequate anonymization. Information minimization, which entails gathering vital information, is a simple strategy to reduce direct exposure risks. Simultaneously, privacy‐enhancing innovations such as encryption and anonymization are reviewed for their duties in safeguarding information. The chapter addresses added methods such as safe and secure design implementation, synthetic information validation, privacy‐aware hyperparameter tuning, encrypted calculation, and anonymized information synthesis, each contributing to a detailed structure for privacy‐aware TinyML version training.
