# 11  
Robust Ground Truth Data Mining for Enhanced Privacy and Accuracy in Noisy TinyML Environments[\*](#c11.xhtml#c11-note-0001)

*Yuichi Sei^([1](#c11.xhtml#c11-aff-0001)) and Agbotiname Lucky Imoize^([2](#c11.xhtml#c11-aff-0002),[3](#c11.xhtml#c11-aff-0003))*

*¹Graduate School of Informatics and Engineering, The University of Electro‐Communications, Chōfu, Tokyo, Japan*

*²Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, University of Lagos, Lagos, Nigeria*

*³Department of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology, Institute of Digital Communication, Ruhr University, Bochum, Germany*

 

## 11.1 Introduction

Recently, tiny machine leasrning (TinyML) has emerged as a groundbreaking technology that enables machine learning (ML) algorithms to operate on microcontrollers and other resource‐constrained devices [\[2\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0002). By integrating the Internet of Things (IoT) with ML, TinyML facilitates intelligent, data‐driven decisions at the edge without relying on cloud‐based processing. This capability is crucial for applications that require low latency, reduced bandwidth, and enhanced privacy. TinyML considerably influences the IoT sector, where numerous devices generate vast amounts of data daily \[[3](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0003), [4](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0004)\]. These devices, ranging from environmental sensors to wearable health monitors, operate with limited computational power, memory, and energy \[[5](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0005)–[7](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0007)\]. Despite these constraints, they must perform reliably and accurately to support applications such as predictive maintenance, anomaly detection, and real‐time monitoring. TinyML brings advanced ML capabilities to edge devices that traditionally could not handle such complex computations. The benefits of TinyML include the following aspects.

First, local data processing minimizes delays associated with cloud data transmission, which is crucial for time‐sensitive applications such as autonomous driving and industrial automation \[[8](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0008), [9](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0009)\]. Second, local data processing keeps sensitive information on edge devices, reducing the risk of data breaches [\[10\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0010). Third, processing data at edges limits the data sent to the cloud, leading to lower bandwidth usage and costs [\[11\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0011). Fourth, TinyML models are designed to be lightweight and efficient, thereby extending the battery life of portable and remote devices.

Despite its potential, TinyML faces challenges due to resource constraints, necessitating innovative approaches for designing, training, and deploying TinyML models. Techniques like model quantization and pruning have been developed to reduce the size and complexity of ML algorithms without compromising accuracy, making them suitable for edge devices. Integrating ML with IoT also requires robust frameworks for seamless deployment and operation. Frameworks such as TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers and Edge Impulse provide necessary tools and libraries for efficient TinyML model development, training, and deployment. TinyML applications are extensive. In health care, TinyML‐powered wearables monitor vital signs and detect anomalies in real‐time, providing timely alerts to patients and healthcare providers. In agriculture, TinyML‐based sensors monitor soil conditions and crop health, optimizing irrigation and fertilization practices. In smart homes, TinyML enhances security, optimizes energy consumption, and offers personalized user experiences. As TinyML continues to evolve, future developments will likely focus on enhancing edge devices by improving algorithms, hardware support, and data processing efficiency. Integrating TinyML with emerging technologies like 5G and edge computing will further expand its potential, enabling previously unimaginable innovative applications.

Nevertheless, sensing data related to individuals or their surroundings can contain personally identifiable information [\[12\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0012), risking privacy breaches. To address this issue, data can be anonymized using ![epsilon](images/c11-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐differential privacy (DP) \[[13](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0013), [14](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0014)\], a well‐established privacy framework. In ![epsilon](images/c11-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐DP, the privacy budget ![epsilon](images/c11-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> balances data utility and privacy preservation. This approach has been widely used in various studies \[[15](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0015)–[17](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0017)\] and is crucial for data analysis.

Local DP (LDP) is a variant of DP designed for data collection from individuals. In this context, “DP” refers to “local DP.” To achieve DP, numerical values are typically protected by adding Laplace noise [\[13\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0013). For categorical values, category identifiers (IDs) can be disguised with a certain probability to ensure privacy preservation \[[18](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0018), [19](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0019)\]. While these methods ensure ![epsilon](images/c11-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐DP, they do not address errors in the data.

This chapter introduces a novel privacy model, inferred ground truth DP (GDP), which distinguishes between “true” values (original, error free, and possibly unknown to the data owner or anonymizer) and “measured” values (potentially containing errors). Unlike traditional DP, which focuses on sensor data protection, GDP aims to safeguard the ground truth values. We acknowledge that ground truth values are often unknown and assume they follow a specific probability distribution, such as a normal distribution (ND), based on the knowledge or error theory of the data owner or anonymizer \[[20](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0020), [21](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0021)\].

By leveraging GDP, the noise added to sensor data can be reduced because GDP accounts for the inherent errors in the sensor data, thereby requiring less additional noise for privacy preservation. The effectiveness of GDP relies on the anonymizer's ability to estimate the measurement error distribution ([Figure 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0001)). However, even with inaccurate estimates, GDP remains valid provided the errors are not overestimated. Therefore, GDP can still be applied with uncertain error distributions by conservatively estimating the error amount. When no error is anticipated, GDP defaults to traditional DP.

![Figure 11.1 Inferred ground truth differential privacy (GDP). The goal of GDP is to add noise to the ground truth values rather than to the sensor data.](images/c11f001.png)

**Figure 11.1** Inferred ground truth differential privacy (GDP). The goal of GDP is to add noise to the ground truth values rather than to the sensor data.

In scenarios with no information about the error distribution available, the proposed method cannot be applied. However, we believe that in several real‐world scenarios, reasonable error estimates can be made, enabling the GDP to be used effectively by underestimating the error amount. A more detailed discussion on this issue is available in [Section 11.6](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0027).

In our evaluation presented in [Section 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0018), we assessed the effectiveness of our proposed method using a combination of three synthetic and three real‐world datasets. We compared its performance against three existing methods for numerical data and four methods for categorical data. Results demonstrated an approximate 20% reduction in noise.

Recently, several novel LDP methods have been developed, primarily focusing on estimating the distribution of user data and federated learning \[[22](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0022)–[25](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0025)\]. They employ techniques such as adding noise to data values or randomly changing category values to preserve privacy. The underlying objective is to mitigate the adverse effects of noise on statistical analysis. However, these methods do not explicitly account for the inherent sensing errors prevalent in IoT environments.

We address a scenario where data are collected on an untrusted server, which is one of the two main scenarios identified by Husnoo et al. [\[26\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0026) in their categorization of DP techniques in IoT environments. This scenario is particularly challenging due to the potential for considerable cumulative noise added to each data point, thereby compromising data utility. Considering measurement errors, the proposed method effectively reduces this cumulative noise, as evidenced by experimental results.

Further, although most existing security and privacy techniques in IoT overlook sensing noise issue, the proposed method explicitly addresses this factor in privacy preservation. This study aims to estimate personal data distributions in IoT environments and protect user data with DP while accounting for the inherent sensing noise. By doing so, we fill a critical gap in current methodologies that often introduce excessive privacy noise into sensor data due to neglecting sensing errors.

The proposed method, referred to as GDP, derives the probability distribution of the true values based on the known probability distribution of noise and noisy measurement. Noise is then added according to this derived distribution to achieve DP.

The major contributions of this study are summarized as follows:

*   We introduce GDP, a novel DP concept that explicitly incorporates sensing noise.
*   We develop anonymization algorithms for both numerical and categorical data within the GDP framework.
*   We provide rigorous proofs that our algorithms ensure GDP.
*   Through experiments with synthetic and real datasets, we showcase that the proposed method reduces DP noise.
*   We further demonstrate that the proposed method improves the accuracy of estimated personal data distributions when applied to the same datasets.

The remainder of this chapter is structured as follows. We discuss related methods in [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0002). [Section 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0007) outlines the application scenarios, underlying assumptions, and formal privacy definitions. [Section 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0014) details our design and mechanisms for achieving GDP. In [Section 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0018), we present simulation results obtained using synthetic real‐world datasets. We address design considerations specific to the proposed method in [Section 11.6](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0027). Finally, we conclude this study in [Section 11.7](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0043).

 

## 11.2 Related Research Work

This section provides an overview of related research in privacy‐preserving methods within the context of TinyML. It begins with [Section 11.2.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0003), which reviews various DP methods applied to TinyML, highlighting the key advancements and limitations. [Section 11.2.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0004) discusses anonymized data collection techniques, emphasizing their relevance to TinyML and the unique challenges they address. [Section 11.2.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0005) explores approaches that incorporate sensing noise into privacy‐preserving methods, examining how they handle errors in data collection. Finally, [Section 11.2.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0006) focuses on DP methods specifically designed for dirty data, showcasing their effectiveness in ensuring privacy while dealing with inconsistencies in large datasets. Collectively, these subsections illustrate the breadth of research in privacy preservation and its implications for TinyML offering a comprehensive understanding of the current landscape of this research area.

 

### 11.2.1 DP and TinyML

Numerous DP methods have been proposed to address privacy concerns in various contexts \[[27](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0027), [28](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0028)\]. Waheed et al. [\[29\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0029) designed a DP‐based system to safeguard data privacy in smart homes by applying LDP techniques, specifically using randomized response methods before data transmission to an aggregator. They further enhanced privacy protection by incorporating hidden Markov model technology at the aggregator level, achieving a dual‐layer privacy shield. Yang and Al‐Masri [\[30\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0030) proposed a user‐centric LDP optimization method that empowers users to manage their privacy preferences more effectively. This method uses multicriteria decision‐making to simplify the management of privacy preferences for users. Evaluation results indicate that this method successfully strikes an optimal balance between data accuracy and privacy protection. He et al. [\[31\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0031) proposed an adaptive LDP method to train clustered federated learning models on heterogeneous IoT data, aiming to reduce LDP noise and communication overhead while balancing between privacy and utility through utilizing adaptive clipping, weight compression, and parameter shuffling.

Additionally, several studies have explored ML techniques, including deep neural networks, for analyzing IoT sensing with DP. Shi et al. [\[32\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0032) introduced a reinforcement learning technique for transportation network companies using passenger data. Xu et al. [\[33\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0033) focused on mobile data analysis in edge computing. Guan et al. [\[34\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0034) applied ML to the Internet of Medical Things. However, these studies did not incorporate the proposed GDP. Incorporating GDP could enhance their accuracy while maintaining robust privacy preservation.

 

### 11.2.2 Anonymized Data Collection for TinyML

Many studies have explored anonymized data collection techniques. Wang et al. [\[35\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0035) proposed a method to identify the top‐![k](images/c11-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> most frequent new terms by collecting usage data under DP. Kim et al. [\[36\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0036) used DP to derive population statistics from indoor positioning data. Encryption‐based approaches for anonymized data collection have also been investigated \[[37](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0037), [38](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0038)\]. These approaches focus on aggregating data values and do not address individual data retrieval or consider value errors. In contrast, the proposed method aims to achieve high accuracy in individual data values, which is crucial for applications such as recommender systems that rely on detailed personal attributes.

 

### 11.2.3 Privacy‐Preserving Methods Accounting for Sensing Noises

Abul et al. [\[39\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0039) and Sei and Ohsuga [\[40\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0040) developed location anonymization methods that account for location errors, achieving ![k](images/c11-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐anonymity, a basic privacy metric. However, these methods are not applicable to ![epsilon](images/c11-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐DP.

 

### 11.2.4 DP Methods Considering Dirty Data

Ge et al. [\[41\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0041), Krishnan et al. [\[42\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0042), and Blass et al. [\[43\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0043) proposed methods for privately cleaning “dirty data” using DP as a privacy metric. These methods focused on resolving inconsistencies in large databases under the assumption that all database values were accurate and applying the Laplace mechanism without accounting for value errors.

[Table 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0001) shows a comparison of different methods.

## 11.3 Models

This section describes the application model of this study, including the assumptions, attack model, and privacy metric.

 

### 11.3.1 Application Model

IoT devices are capable of collecting and inferring various personal attributes, such as location, heart rate, health conditions, age, and movement patterns. This data can be used to provide personalized services, including recommender systems. The data collection entity can anonymize this information before transmitting it to the intended recipient.

The collected attribute data can be classified into two types: numerical attributes (e.g., heart rate in beats per minute) and categorical attributes (disease diagnosis like COVID‐19).

Notably, the collected attribute data often contains some degree of sensing errors due to the inherent difficulty associated with accurately sensing and estimating personal attributes. In extreme cases, some data may be entirely missing. While techniques like multiple imputations or regression‐based predictions can address missing data \[[45](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0045)–[47](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0047)\], the estimates may still carry notable errors. [Figure 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0002) illustrates the application model discussed in this chapter.

![Figure 11.2 Application model discussed in this chapter.](images/c11f002.png)

**Figure 11.2** Application model discussed in this chapter.

 

### 11.3.2 Assumptions

Anonymizers may not possess the exact true attribute values but can make estimations. However, these estimations are prone to errors. For numerical attributes, anonymizers can estimate the error distribution, often modeled as an ND due to the common occurrence of measurement errors following this pattern [\[48\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0048). This distribution is characterized by the standard deviation parameter (![sigma](images/c11-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>). Notably, the concept of GDP is adaptable to other error models as well.

For categorical attributes, the probability of misclassification, denoted as ![p Subscript i right-arrow j](images/c11-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math>, represents the likelihood that the true category ID is ![i](images/c11-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> while the anonymizer assumes it to be ![j](images/c11-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>.

In this study, the parameters ![sigma](images/c11-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> and ![p Subscript i right-arrow j](images/c11-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></math> for all ![i comma j](images/c11-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></math> are referred to as “error parameters.”

We consider the following three possible scenarios:

*   **Scenario 1:** The anonymizer has precise knowledge of the error parameters.
*   **Scenario 2:** The anonymizer lacks precise knowledge of the error parameters. The estimated parameters may deviate from the actual parameters, but the anonymizer is not overly optimistic about the degree of error. Formal mathematical definitions for numerical and categorical attributes are provided in [Sections 11.4.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0015) and [11.4.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0017), respectively.
*   **Scenario 3:** The anonymizer has no knowledge or estimation of the error parameters.

This chapter focuses on Scenario 2, as Scenario 1 is considered relatively impractical and Scenario 3 is not within the scope of this study.

 

### 11.3.3 Attack Model

In the privacy domain, especially concerning anonymized IoT data, a recipient of data is often treated as a potential adversary. This adversary is assumed to be semihonest, meaning that while one may adhere to established protocols for collecting anonymized IoT data, one might also attempt to infer personal information from that anonymized data. This assumption is crucial for understanding the potential privacy risks associated with data sharing.

An anonymized dataset is typically not an exact replica of the original data but is modified to mask the true values. This modification includes errors from two primary sources: original sensing errors and intentionally added noise. Sensing errors are inherent inaccuracies that occur during data collection due to limitations in sensor accuracy, environmental factors, or other technical constraints. In addition to these inherent inaccuracies, additional noise is intentionally introduced during the anonymization process to further obfuscate the data and protect individual privacy. This intentional noise addition is often guided by principles such as privacy, ensuring that the data cannot be easily traced back to an individual.

The concept of DP is fundamental in this context, as it involves adding calibrated noise to the data to obscure whether a specific individual's information is included in the dataset. This technique provides a mathematical guarantee of privacy. However, for IoT data, which already contains measurement errors, adding excessive noise can degrade the data utility, making it less useful for analytical purposes.

Given the presence of both sensor errors and intentionally added noise, even if an attacker adheres to the data collection protocols, the inaccuracies embedded in the anonymized data prevent them from accurately identifying individuals' true data values. Instead, the attacker can only estimate the probability distribution of these values that accounts for the errors and noise. This results in a range of possible values rather than a single precise value, adding a layer of security by masking the true data within a range of plausible values, thereby complicating the attacker's ability to determine the exact original data.

This approach aligns with advanced privacy‐preserving techniques, such as the GDP proposed in this chapter. GDP extends traditional DP by focusing on the “ground truth” – the true values that are often unknown to both the data owner and the anonymizer. By accounting for the inherent sensor data errors, GDP reduces the amount of additional noise needed, thereby preserving the data utility while still safeguarding privacy. This method ensures that the noise added for privacy preservation is optimized by considering existing inaccuracies, thereby improving the balance between data utility and privacy preservation. [Figure 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0003) shows the attack model discussed in this chapter.

![Figure 11.3 Attack model presented in this chapter.](images/c11f003.png)

**Figure 11.3** Attack model presented in this chapter.

In summary, treating the recipient of anonymized data as a semihonest adversary emphasizes the need for robust privacy‐preserving mechanisms. The dual errors – original sensor inherent inaccuracies and intentionally added noise – play a critical role in protecting the true data values. Advanced methods like GDP further refine this protection, ensuring that the data remains useful for analysis while protecting individual privacy against potential inference attacks.

 

### 11.3.4 Privacy Metric

In privacy‐preserving data mining, DP [\[13\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0013) serves as a crucial metric. Originally developed for query–response databases, DP has been applied in anonymized data collection.

Consider a scenario where an individual's attribute value is anonymized, either by the individual or by an anonymizer. Let ![epsilon](images/c11-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> be a positive real number. LDP is defined as follows:

It is assumed that the attribute value ![x](images/c11-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> may include sensing errors. Thus, the focus shifts to the ground truth of ![x](images/c11-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, which may be unknown even to the data owner or an anonymizer. To address this issue, GDP is proposed as a means of managing the privacy of these unknown values.

 

## 11.4 GDP

Previous studies have typically defined variables ![x](images/c11-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and ![x prime](images/c11-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></math> in [Definition 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fea-0002) as the values obtained directly from measurements. However, we deviate from this convention and redefine these variables as the underlying ground truths, devoid of any measurement errors. This shift in perspective necessitates the development of novel anonymization mechanisms for both numerical and categorical attributes, which are detailed in this chapter.

 

### 11.4.1 Numerical Value Anonymization

For numerical attributes, a well‐known method to add noise is the Laplace mechanism [\[13\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0013), which uses a Laplace distribution (LD). However, this mechanism does not inherently account for sensing errors. In the traditional approach, often referred to as the **baseline approach** for numerical attributes, noise following an ND is first added to the ground truth to simulate sensing errors. Subsequently, additional noise from the Laplace mechanism is introduced into this already noisy value. The proposed method invariably adds Laplace noise, regardless of the underlying data characteristics. The resulting probability density function (PDF), which describes the probability of the distance between the final noisy value and ground truth, can be obtained by convolving the ND and LD.

To express this mathematically, let ![script í’© left-parenthesis x semicolon sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> represent the PDF of the ND with standard deviation ![sigma](images/c11-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> and ![script upper L left-parenthesis x semicolon b right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#8466;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> represent the PDF of the LD with scale parameter ![b](images/c11-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. For simplicity and without loss of generality, we focus on centered distributions that peak at zero. As shown in [equation 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0004), ![upper R Subscript script í’© left-parenthesis x semicolon sigma squared right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> tends to infinity as ![x](images/c11-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> approaches negative infinity. This implies that even with a large ![sigma](images/c11-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>, additional noise must be introduced to satisfy the ![epsilon](images/c11-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐DP requirement.

In [Figure 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0004), ![upper R Subscript script upper L left-parenthesis x semicolon epsilon comma normal upper Delta right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#8466;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper R Subscript script í’° left-parenthesis x semicolon sigma squared comma epsilon comma normal upper Delta right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54448;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> represent the ratios of PDF values separated by ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> for the LD ![script upper L left-parenthesis x semicolon normal upper Delta slash epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#8466;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and convolution ![script í’° left-parenthesis x semicolon sigma squared comma normal upper Delta slash epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54448;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, respectively.

To adhere to the definition of ![epsilon](images/c11-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐DP, the ratio of PDF values separated by ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> should fall within the bounds of ![exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![1 slash exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. [Figure 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0004) demonstrates that both ![upper R Subscript script upper L left-parenthesis x semicolon epsilon comma normal upper Delta right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#8466;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper R Subscript script í’° left-parenthesis x semicolon sigma squared comma epsilon comma normal upper Delta right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54448;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> satisfy this condition, confirming that the mechanisms ![script upper L left-parenthesis x semicolon normal upper Delta slash epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#8466;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![script í’° left-parenthesis x semicolon sigma squared comma normal upper Delta slash epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="script">&#54448;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> achieve ![epsilon](images/c11-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐DP (where ![sigma equals normal upper Delta equals epsilon equals 1](images/c11-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> in the figure). However, although ![upper R Subscript script í’° left-parenthesis x semicolon sigma squared comma normal upper Delta slash epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54448;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math> approaches ![exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> (or ![1 slash exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>) as the absolute value of ![x](images/c11-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> increases, it does so slower than ![upper R Subscript script upper L left-parenthesis x semicolon normal upper Delta slash epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#8466;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></math>. This slower convergence leads to the addition of more noise than is strictly necessary for privacy preservation.

To address this issue, we propose a simple yet effective algorithm that selectively adds Laplace noise. Specifically, Laplace noise is only added when the magnitude of the generated noise exceeds a predefined threshold ![w](images/c11-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math>. This approach is expected to reduce the overall noise and allow the ratio of PDF values separated by ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> to converge more rapidly to ![exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![1 slash exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

Determining the optimal value for the threshold ![w](images/c11-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> is a complex task. Setting ![w](images/c11-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> too high would result in a failure to achieve either traditional ![epsilon](images/c11-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐DP or GDP. Conversely, setting ![w](images/c11-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> too low would lead to the inclusion of unnecessary noise in the output.

We can express the PDF that incorporates Laplace noise only when the noise magnitude ![StartAbsoluteValue x EndAbsoluteValue](images/c11-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></math> is greater than or equal to a predefined threshold ![w](images/c11-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> as follows (notably, this is technically a combination of a PDF and probability mass function):

Our goal is to determine an appropriate value for ![w](images/c11-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> such that ![upper R Subscript script í’±](images/c11-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54449;</mi></mrow></msub></math> closely approximates ![exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> without exceeding the bounds of ![exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> or ![1 slash exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>.

![Figure 11.5 Analysis of the metric upper R Subscript script í’± for different values of w. Results show that an excessively large w fails to meet the differential privacy (DP) requirement, while an excessively small w introduces more noise than necessary.](images/c11f005.png)

**Figure 11.5** Analysis of the metric ![upper R Subscript script í’±](images/c11-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54449;</mi></mrow></msub></math> for different values of ![w](images/c11-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math>. Results show that an excessively large ![w](images/c11-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> fails to meet the differential privacy (DP) requirement, while an excessively small ![w](images/c11-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> introduces more noise than necessary.

To achieve this, we propose the following theorem (illustrated in [Figure 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0005)):

In this study, we define the ratio of ![x plus normal upper Delta slash 2](images/c11-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math> to ![x minus normal upper Delta slash 2](images/c11-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. Therefore, we can examine the range ![negative w minus normal upper Delta slash 2 less-than x less-than 0](images/c11-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>w</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math> to determine whether the maximum ratio exceeds ![exp left-parenthesis epsilon right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>exp</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. Notably, owing to the symmetry of ![script í’±](images/c11-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">&#54449;</mi></mrow></math> with respect to the point ![left-parenthesis x comma y right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, where ![y](images/c11-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> denotes the ratio of PDF values separated by ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math>, it is sufficient to check for ![x less-than 0](images/c11-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></math>.

 

### 11.4.2 Categorical Attributes

First, consider Scenario I. Assume that an attacker obtains category ID ![gamma](images/c11-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> as the anonymized version of a categorical attribute. ## 11.5 Evaluation

In this section, we explain the parameter values used in the experiments in [Section 11.5.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0019) and the utility metric in [Section 11.5.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0023). Then, we present the results of the real datasets in [Section 11.5.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0024). Finally, we discuss the computation cost of the proposed method in [Section 11.5.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0025).

 

### 11.5.1 Parameter Settings

Realistic values need to be set for ![epsilon](images/c11-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>, ![sigma](images/c11-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>, and ![bold-italic p Subscript bold-italic i](images/c11-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">p</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi></msub></math> for all ![i](images/c11-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>.

 

#### 11.5.1.1 Value of ![epsilon](images/c11-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>

Apple's deployment ensures that ![epsilon](images/c11-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is set to either 1 or 2 per datum [\[49\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0049). In evaluations by Apple's DP team, ![epsilon](images/c11-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> values of 2, 4, and 8 were used [\[50\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0050). The paper proposing Randomized Aggregatable Privacy‐Preserving Ordinal Response (RAPPOR) by Google [\[51\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0051) used ![epsilon equals log left-parenthesis 3 right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>log</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> as a primary setting. Based on these references, ![epsilon](images/c11-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is chosen to be in the range of 1–10. For this range, if ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> is set to 100, the average noise added by the Laplace mechanism ranges from 5 to 50, indicating adequate privacy protection. Notably, if ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> is scaled by a factor of ![a](images/c11-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>, the average noise is also scaled by ![a](images/c11-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>. For categorical attributes with two categories (![upper M equals 2](images/c11-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>), the retention probability value ranges between 73.11% and 99.996% when ![epsilon](images/c11-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is between 1 and 10. An ![epsilon](images/c11-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> value of 10 suggests very low privacy protection when ![upper M](images/c11-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> is small, emphasizing the relevance of evaluating performance at small ![epsilon](images/c11-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> values for categorical attributes.

 

#### 11.5.1.2 Value of ![sigma](images/c11-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>

The average sensing error, ![upper A upper S upper E left-parenthesis sigma right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>, is defined as follows:

(11.11)![upper A upper S upper E left-parenthesis sigma right-parenthesis equals integral Subscript x equals negative infinity Superscript infinity Baseline StartAbsoluteValue x EndAbsoluteValue dot script í’© left-parenthesis x semicolon sigma squared right-parenthesis d x equals StartRoot StartFraction pi Over 2 EndFraction EndRoot sigma](images/c11-math-0011.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">&#54441;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>;</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mrow><mfrac><mi>&#960;</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow></msqrt><mi>&#963;</mi></math> 

If ![sigma](images/c11-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> is set to 1/40 of ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> (the range of possible values), ![upper A upper S upper E left-parenthesis sigma right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> will be 2.0% of ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math>, indicating high accuracy of the corresponding IoT device. Similarly, setting ![sigma](images/c11-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> to 1/10, 1/4, and 1/2 of ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> yields ![upper A upper S upper E left-parenthesis sigma right-parenthesis](images/c11-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>A</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> values of 8.0% (relatively high accuracy), 20% (relatively low accuracy), and 40% (low accuracy) of ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math>, respectively. Based on this, ![sigma](images/c11-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> is set between 1/40 and 1/2 of ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math>.

For all ![i](images/c11-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, ![p Subscript i right-arrow i](images/c11-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></math> is set to a common value ![tau](images/c11-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> within the range of 0.3–0.9. This reflects the probability that an IoT device correctly identifies an attribute category, from low (0.3) to high (0.9) accuracy. For numerical attributes, utility is defined as follows:

Higher utility values indicate better performance.

Some methods estimate statistical values or generate cross‐tabulations from collected data. For cross‐tabulations, the total loss comparing true and generated cross‐tabulations is used. However, this study focuses on personalized data applications in which analyzing each individual's attribute value is crucial, such as health monitoring, context‐aware recommendation, and navigation ([Figure 11.6](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0006)).

### 11.5.3 Real Dataset Results

Simulations were performed using the Adult dataset [\[55\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0055), a common benchmark in privacy‐preserving data mining, which includes six numerical and nine categorical attributes, with 30,162 records after removing unknown values.

Each value in the Adult dataset is assumed true, with IoT devices estimating age, sex, race, and nationality using various methods \[[56](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0056)–[58](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0058)\]. For numerical attributes, ![sigma](images/c11-i0173.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math> was set to 0.1 of ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0174.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> and ![epsilon](images/c11-i0175.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> was set to 8. For categorical attributes, ![tau](images/c11-i0176.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> was set to 0.6 and ![epsilon](images/c11-i0177.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> to 2. Simulation results, including attribute names with their respective ![normal upper Delta](images/c11-i0178.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> and ![upper M](images/c11-i0179.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>, are summarized in [Tables 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0002) and [11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0003). Compared with the baseline, the proposed mechanism increased ![upper U Subscript n](images/c11-i0180.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></math> to approximately 92% from 85% for all numerical attributes and increased ![upper U Subscript c](images/c11-i0181.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>U</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></math> by up to 20% for categorical attributes. These results demonstrate the proposed mechanism's ability to enhance utility (i.e., reduce total loss) on real datasets.

![Table 11.2 Results of numerical attributes of adult.](images/c11-i0182.png)

**Table 11.2** Results of numerical attributes of adult.

![Table 11.3 Results of categorical attributes of adult.](images/c11-i0183.png)

**Table 11.3** Results of categorical attributes of adult.

Additional simulations were performed using other real datasets using the same parameter settings.

The AReM dataset [\[59\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0059), containing 42,239 instances of six numerical attributes, was used for the numerical attributes.

For categorical attributes, the Activity Recognition Data (ADL) dataset [\[52\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0052), Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) dataset [\[53\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0053), and Localization dataset [\[54\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0054) with 741, 75,128, and 164,860 instances, respectively, were used. The simulation results are summarized in [Tables 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0004) and [11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0005), indicating that the proposed mechanism outperforms the baseline approach on all considered datasets.

![Table 11.4 Results of numerical attributes of AReM.](images/c11-i0184.png)

**Table 11.4** Results of numerical attributes of AReM.

### 11.5.4 Computation Cost

The proposed anonymizing algorithm is executed on local devices. We tested them on a laptop with 8 GB of memory and a Core i5 10210U central processing unit (CPU), where each dataset was processed in less than a second. User data distribution estimation was performed on a server with 128 GB memory and an Intel Xeon W‐2295 CPU, taking an average of 7.8 seconds for the AReM dataset with 42,239 values. The proposed method's computation time is proportional to the number of users and attributes; thus, it increases with more users. However, because data collection itself takes time, a few minutes of computation is practical for estimating data distribution, although the comparison methods have shorter computation times due to their simpler algorithms.

 

### 11.5.5 Overhead Cost

In [Section 11.5.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0025), we discussed computation costs. Here, we address the overhead cost, specifically the network cost between the server and the user. Our proposed method adds differential privacy noise to the IoT measurements, while accounting for the measurement errors of the IoT devices. The number of bits required to represent the IoT measurement remains the same before and after applying differential privacy noise. In addition, encryption of the communication channel between the server and the user is beyond the scope of this chapter. If encryption is necessary to prevent external attackers from eavesdropping on the communication channel, then encryption should be implemented. The encryption process, similar to conventional differential privacy techniques, does not affect our proposed scheme in any way. In summary, there is no additional overhead in implementing our proposed scheme.

 

## 11.6 Discussion

We discuss the relationships between TinyML and IoT data in [Section 11.6.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0028), followed by the connection between TinyML and DP in [Section 11.6.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0029). Our future research directions are outlined in [Section 11.6.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0042).

 

### 11.6.1 TinyML with Noisy IoT Data

Several studies have developed ML models from noisy IoT data, achieving high accuracy \[[60](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0060), [61](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0061)\]. However, DP studies \[[32](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0032)–[34](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0034)\] have shown that small privacy budgets, which correspond to high noise levels, can substantially degrade model accuracy.

This study demonstrates that accounting for observation noise in IoT data enables a reduction in the privacy preservation noise required. By integrating our method with existing DP techniques, we can enhance the accuracy of ML models while preserving privacy.

 

### 11.6.2 TinyML and DP

This section discusses the technical and applied aspects of integrating TinyML and DP, exploring how these technologies can synergistically enhance privacy‐preserving ML at edges.

 

#### 11.6.2.1 Implementing DP on Edge Devices

Implementing DP on resource‐constrained edge devices presents unique challenges due to their computational constraints and limited resources. Traditional DP algorithms, known for their computational intensity, must be optimized to match the capabilities of edge devices. This includes exploring efficient noise addition techniques and decentralized privacy‐preserving algorithms.

 

***Efficient Noise Addition Techniques*** Noise addition is a cornerstone of DP. On edge devices, it is critical to use computationally efficient noise generation algorithms. Techniques such as optimizing the Gaussian/Laplacian noise generation, or using precomputed noise values, can help achieve this efficiency.

 

***Decentralized Privacy‐Preserving Algorithms*** To ensure privacy across an entire network of edge devices, decentralized DP algorithms are employed. These algorithms allow each device to locally process data while collectively ensuring privacy. Integrating this approach with federated learning eliminates the need for centralized data collection, thereby further enhancing privacy.

 

#### 11.6.2.2 Use Cases and Applications

The integration of TinyML and DP opens up a wide range of applications, including real‐time medical data analysis, IoT device data processing, and smart home technologies. Each application presents unique benefits and challenges.

 

***Real‐Time Medical Data Analysis*** In the healthcare sector, there is a growing demand for real‐time data analysis while preserving patient privacy. TinyML enables the real‐time processing of data from wearable devices and medical equipment, while DP ensures that patient confidentiality is maintained. This combination supports more accurate and privacy‐conscious diagnostic processes.

 

***IoT Device Data Processing*** IoT devices, prevalent in smart homes and cities, generate massive data. Privacy concerns require careful handling of this data. By integrating TinyML with DP, data can be locally processed on these devices, enabling valuable insights without compromising user privacy.

 

***Smart Home Applications*** Smart homes collect data on user behaviors and habits, which are inherently personal and requires robust privacy protection. TinyML enables on‐device data processing, and when combined with DP, it ensures that users benefit from smart home technology while preserving their privacy.

 

#### 11.6.2.3 Technical Challenges and Solutions

The integration of TinyML and DP presents several technical challenges. Major challenges include resource limitations, privacy–utility trade‐offs, and data validation.

 

***Resource Constraints*** Implementing DP on edge devices with limited processing power and memory poses considerable challenges. To address this issue, researchers are actively developing lightweight algorithms and optimizing hardware.

 

***Privacy–Utility Trade‐Off*** Achieving an optimal balance between strong privacy preservation and data utility is critical. Excessive noise can render the data meaningless, making it essential to carefully calibrate the amount of noise added.

 

***Data Validation*** Ensuring data accuracy and consistency when applying DP is crucial. Establishing robust validation methods for edge devices is essential for reliable data processing.

 

#### 11.6.2.4 Future Directions

The convergence of TinyML and DP is poised to considerably influence the future of edge computing. Ongoing research and development efforts are expected to yield more efficient and secure algorithms, as well as practical implementations across diverse domains. The establishment of standards and guidelines will also be crucial in promoting widespread adoption and increasing the trustworthiness of these technologies.

This section provides a comprehensive overview of both the technical and applied aspects of integrating TinyML with DP. We have explored the implementation of DP on edge devices, highlighted real‐world use cases, addressed technical challenges, and provided a glimpse into the future prospects of this exciting field. The findings presented in this study aim to drive further advances in edge computing and privacy preservation, paving the way for more secure and effective technologies.

 

### 11.6.3 Future Work

There are various mechanisms for achieving DP beyond the Laplace and randomized response mechanisms. For instance, Geng and Viswanath [\[62\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0062) proposed the staircase mechanism for numerical values, which proves to be more effective when ![epsilon](images/c11-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is large. Additionally, Andrés et al. [\[63\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0063) introduced a geo‐indistinguishable mechanism for location information. We believe that GDP can be applied to other privacy metrics that manage attribute value probability distributions, such as ![p k](images/c11-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></math>‐anonymity \[[64](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0064), [65](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0065)\] and ![t](images/c11-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐closeness [\[66\]](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0066).

Future research should investigate the application of GDP to these and other privacy mechanisms. Although our focus has been on ND errors, exploring other error distributions could lead to the development of new algorithms.

Furthermore, our study has concentrated on individual anonymized data collection. Another crucial area of privacy research is privacy‐preserving data publishing, where a data holder anonymizes and publishes personal data. GDP could be applied to ![epsilon](images/c11-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐DP in this context as well, and we plan to address this aspect in future work.

 

## 11.7 Conclusions

DP is a key technique for protecting user privacy by adding noise to sensor values. However, in the context of IoT, where sensor data often contains inherent errors, existing solutions fail to account for this inherent sensing noise. Instead, they focus on protecting the already noisy detected noisy values rather than the ground truth. Our approach addresses this issue by modifying the added noise based on the sensor noise model, thereby reducing the DP noise by approximately 20%. We introduce GDP, a novel privacy metamodel that applies to DP and acknowledges that the ground truth might be unknown to both the data owner and the anonymizer. We validate our results with both synthetic and real datasets, marking the first application of GDP.

TinyML has revolutionized the deployment of ML models on resource‐constrained devices, remarkably advancing various domains, such as IoT, health care, and smart environments. With the rapid growth of IoT devices that generate massive data, ensuring data privacy while maintaining high accuracy is of paramount importance. Due to their inherent limitations in computational power, memory, and energy, TinyML necessitates innovative privacy‐preservation approaches that do not compromise performance.

The proposed GDP framework perfectly aligns with the objectives of TinyML by optimizing the balance between privacy and accuracy. By considering the inherent sensing errors in IoT data, GDP reduces the need for excessive noise addition, which is crucial for maintaining the utility of data processed on TinyML devices. This balance is particularly relevant in applications such as health monitoring, in which accurate real‐time data analysis can be life‐saving, and in smart homes, where user behavior data must be protected without degrading the service quality.

The integration of TinyML with DP opens several exciting avenues for future research and development.

These include further refining GDP and other privacy‐preserving algorithms to enhance their efficiency and effectiveness on TinyML platforms. This could involve exploring alternative noise mechanisms and error models that are better suited for the constraints of TinyML devices. Additionally, developing specialized hardware accelerators that can efficiently handle privacy‐preserving computations on TinyML devices, possibly through designing new microcontroller architectures optimized for differential privacy tasks, presents a great opportunity. Leveraging the synergy between TinyML and edge computing to create robust, privacy‐preserving systems that can process and analyze data locally while offloading more complex tasks to edge servers is another promising direction. This hybrid approach can remarkably enhance the scalability and flexibility of IoT deployments. Furthermore, tailoring privacy‐preserving techniques to specific TinyML applications such as environmental monitoring, industrial automation, and personalized health care, is essential. Each application has unique privacy and accuracy requirements that must be addressed through customized solutions. Collaboration with regulatory bodies and industry stakeholders will also be crucial for developing standardized guidelines and policies for implementing DP in TinyML applications. Ensuring that privacy‐preserving practices are consistently applied and trusted by users will help to foster confidence and broader adoption.

The integration of GDP with TinyML represents notable advancements in the field of privacy‐preserving data analysis on resource‐constrained devices. By addressing the inherent sensor errors in IoT data and optimizing the noise addition process, GDP enhances the utility of data processed on TinyML‐based devices while maintaining robust privacy protection. As TinyML continues to expand its influence across various industries, incorporating advanced privacy‐preserving techniques such as GDP will be crucial for building secure, efficient, and reliable IoT systems. Future research and development in this area will unlock new potentials and applications, driving the next wave of innovation in smart, connected devices.

# 12  
Security and Privacy of TinyML Devices

*Eftychia Mistillioglou, Evangelia Konstantopoulou, Nicolas Sklavos, and Andronikos Kyriakou*

*SCYTALE Group, Computer Engineering and Informatics Department, University of Patras, Patras, Greece*

 

## 12.1 Introduction

As tiny machine learning (TinyML) technology continues to advance and integrate into numerous applications, ranging from healthcare to industrial monitoring and smart cities, a critical issue that often goes unaddressed is security. TinyML models enable sophisticated machine learning (ML) directly on resource‐constrained devices, often deployed on microcontrollers and low‐power hardware. While this capability opens new opportunities, it also raises critical concerns regarding data integrity and device reliability in sensitive applications. Threats such as adversarial attacks, physical tampering, data exfiltration, and side‐channel attacks can severely compromise model functionality and data privacy. Ensuring robust security for TinyML within the limitations of small‐scale devices is essential to maintain trust and reliability across such applications.

The resource limitations of TinyML devices present unique challenges for implementing robust security measures. Unlike traditional Internet of Things (IoT) or edge devices, which often possess megabytes of random access memory (RAM) and processors running at gigahertz speeds, TinyML devices typically operate with kilobytes of memory and processors functioning at megahertz speeds [\[1\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0001). Because of these strict limitations, traditional security measures are not feasible. For example, deploying strong cryptographic protocols or sophisticated authentication methods is often infeasible. Given these issues, the proprietary nature of many TinyML models makes them attractive targets for theft or manipulation, further emphasizing the need for tailored security solutions.

The limitations of traditional ML methods and cloud‐based systems further complicate the security landscape for TinyML. While ML has proven effective in addressing certain cyberthreats, its computational complexity, high energy consumption, and reliance on extensive hardware resources make it unsuitable for TinyML's resource‐constrained environment [\[2\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0002). Similarly, cloud‐based ML systems face challenges such as high‐power usage, security vulnerabilities, privacy risks, and latency issues, which are incompatible with the real‐time, low‐power requirements of TinyML applications. Additionally, the deployment of TinyML on IoT devices raises sustainability concerns, as battery life becomes critical in scenarios where regular maintenance or replacement is not feasible [\[2\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0002). These factors highlight the urgency of developing security mechanisms that are lightweight, efficient, and adaptive to TinyML's specific constraints.

To meet these challenges, the development of lightweight, adaptive security strategies tailored to TinyML ecosystems is essential. Traditional security mechanisms, such as complex encryption schemes or advanced adversarial defenses, are often infeasible due to the computational and energy constraints inherent in TinyML devices. Instead, innovative approaches that balance security with operational efficiency must be prioritized. By addressing vulnerabilities through adaptive measures that consider the unique characteristics of TinyML, it becomes possible to ensure robust security and privacy without compromising the performance and functionality of these critical systems [\[1\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0001). The solutions addressed in this work encompass a combination of hardware‐based protections, federated learning (FL) frameworks, adversarial defenses, and real‐time anomaly detection methods that jointly address the multifaceted security requirements of TinyML.

 

### 12.1.1 Main Contributions

The key contributions of this chapter are as follows:

*   **Lightweight Security for TinyML Devices**: Development of security strategies tailored to the unique constraints of TinyML devices.
*   **Federated Learning Frameworks**: Privacy‐aware training methods, including federated meta‐learning for TinyML (TinyMetaFed) and distributed federated learning (D‐FedAvg), that ensure secure and decentralized model updates.
*   **Enhanced Adversarial Robustness**: Adoption of adversarial training techniques to defend against manipulated inputs.
*   **Hardware‐Based Security Solutions**: Implementation of physically unclonable functions (PUFs) for secure authentication and deployment of trusted execution environments (TEEs) to isolate sensitive computations.
*   **Real‐Time Threat Detection**: Integration of D‐score methodologies for low‐latency, real‐time detection of security breaches.

 

### 12.1.2 Chapter Organization

The organization of this chapter begins with an introduction to the security and privacy challenges faced in deploying TinyML models on constrained devices. Following this, [Section 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0004) reviews related work in TinyML security, identifying existing approaches and highlighting gaps in securing TinyML applications. [Section 12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0005), titled “Secure and Privacy‐Aware Training of TinyML Models,” delves into privacy‐preserving training methodologies, such as FL, intellectual property (IP) protection, and adversarial robustness strategies. [Section 12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0018), “Implementation of Novel Security Schemes for TinyML Applications,” discusses advanced security schemes, including hardware‐based protections like PUFs, TEEs, and anti‐tampering mechanisms, as well as techniques for anomaly detection and adaptive learning. [Section 12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0027) describes not only the lessons learned from this study but also the limitations of the presented methods. The chapter concludes with [Section 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0028), where a summary of key insights and implications for secure TinyML deployment in critical tiny applications is provided.

 

## 12.2 Related Work

As TinyML becomes an integral part of many ecosystems, addressing its security and privacy challenges has grown increasingly urgent. TinyML's limited computational resources, small memory, and constrained power capacities present unique obstacles that render conventional cybersecurity measures impractical. To mitigate these limitations, research in TinyML security has focused on several areas, including privacy‐preserving training, adversarial robustness, hardware‐based protections, and secure deployment frameworks. These approaches collectively represent significant strides toward securing TinyML applications, though critical gaps remain.

Privacy‐preserving training is essential for TinyML models, especially in applications where sensitive data is processed directly on the device, such as in healthcare or finance. FL has been widely adopted as a solution, allowing devices to collaboratively train models while retaining data locally. FedAvg, a foundational FL algorithm, has been adapted into frameworks like D‐FedAvg and TinyMetaFed, optimized for TinyML's constraints by reducing the communication load and computational demand. However, while FL enhances privacy by keeping raw data decentralized, studies indicate that it is still susceptible to model inversion and data reconstruction attacks, where attackers infer sensitive information from model updates. To mitigate these vulnerabilities, differential privacy (DP) has been explored as a supplement to FL; however, DP's computational demands limit its effectiveness for TinyML. Addressing this gap, the current study incorporates lightweight encryption techniques and proposes privacy‐enhanced FL algorithms that are customized for TinyML's constrained resources, reducing the risk of data inference attacks.

Another significant concern in TinyML security is adversarial robustness. Adversarial attacks, where inputs are manipulated to cause model misclassifications, pose substantial risks, particularly in sensitive applications like healthcare and industrial IoT. Conventional defenses, such as adversarial training, aim to expose models to perturbed data to increase resilience but are often computationally intensive. For TinyML, defensive distillation offers a lighter alternative by simplifying model outputs to obscure exploitable information, yet current defenses are limited in adaptability. Most adversarial defenses remain static, unable to counter dynamic attacks that adjust strategies based on model feedback. This study addresses this gap by implementing a multifaceted adversarial robustness framework that combines real‐time anomaly detection with adaptive model updates, equipping TinyML models to detect and respond to adaptive attacks more effectively.

Hardware‐based security measures have also been extensively explored to protect TinyML from both physical and logical threats. TEEs and PUFs are two widely studied solutions in this area. TEEs, such as ARM's TrustZone, create secure, isolated environments within microcontrollers, protecting critical model computations from tampering. PUFs, on the other hand, leverage device‐specific physical characteristics as a lightweight alternative to cryptographic keys, enabling secure device authentication. However, both TEEs and PUFs come with certain limitations. TEEs may impose a memory overhead and cannot fully prevent side‐channel attacks, such as power analysis, which can compromise data integrity. PUFs, while energy‐efficient, may produce inconsistent responses in different environmental conditions, affecting reliability. Recent literature addresses these challenges with additional protections, such as anti‐tampering sensors, signal obfuscation techniques, and fault‐resilient architectures, which help ensure that TinyML devices remain secure and operational even in volatile conditions. These approaches demonstrate the potential for multilayered hardware‐based security to enhance TinyML resilience against both physical and logical threats.

Secure deployment frameworks are another area of critical importance for TinyML applications, particularly when data must be transmitted across IoT networks. Frameworks such as TinyML as a Service (TMLaaS) have been proposed to support secure, scalable inference by enabling on‐device processing and reducing dependence on cloud infrastructure. TMLaaS leverages lightweight encryption algorithms, including Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) with reduced rounds and Diffie–Hellman key exchange, which provide essential data protection with minimal computational burden. Lightweight cryptography has been a well‐researched area in the past decade, with extremely low‐area hardware implementations proposed for resource‐constrained devices [\[3\]](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0003). However, many TinyML devices still face challenges in supporting even lightweight encryption schemes in real‐time applications. Moreover, current deployment frameworks often lack robust multi‐device coordination and network‐level anomaly detection, leaving TinyML applications susceptible to network‐based attacks. To address these limitations, various studies have explored solutions such as secure edge‐to‐cloud communication protocols and multi‐device coordination frameworks specifically tailored to TinyML's constrained computational resources, underscoring the ongoing need for advancements in data security and scalability to ensure dependable TinyML deployments.

Real‐time anomaly detection is essential for safeguarding TinyML systems operating in dynamic IoT environments, where data patterns can shift rapidly. TinyML online learning (TinyOL) is one approach that enables TinyML models to perform incremental learning directly on microcontrollers, helping models retain accuracy despite concept drift. This capability is especially important in applications like industrial IoT, where sudden changes in data may signal equipment malfunctions or security threats. However, TinyOL and similar anomaly detection frameworks are constrained by limited computational resources, which can restrict their ability to continuously adapt. To address these limitations, various studies have proposed efficient, resource‐aware anomaly detection algorithms that enable TinyML models to respond to emerging threats with minimal power consumption. These advancements contribute to TinyML's adaptability and security, making it more resilient across diverse applications.

The current study addresses several identified gaps in the general study of TinyML security and privacy. For privacy‐preserving training, vulnerabilities in model inversion and data interference attacks are addressed with the introduction of lightweight encryption and privacy‐enhanced FL, tailored to balance computational constraints and robust privacy protection. For adversarial defense, the limited adaptability of existing approaches to dynamic and adaptive adversarial attacks is mitigated through a multifaceted robustness framework incorporating real‐time anomaly detection, adaptive model updates, and preprocessing techniques. In hardware‐based security, challenges such as memory overhead in TEEs and the sensitivity of PUFs to environmental factors are resolved by implementing advanced solutions, including anti‐tampering sensors, signal obfuscation, and fault‐resilient architectures for consistent device functionality. Regarding deployment frameworks, the gaps in multi‐device coordination and the lack of network‐level anomaly detection are bridged by designing secure edge‐to‐cloud communication protocols and multi‐device coordination frameworks to ensure scalable and secure IoT deployments. Lastly, in anomaly detection, the energy constraints that limit continuous real‐time adaptation are addressed through resource‐efficient techniques enabling robust, real‐time anomaly detection in dynamic environments without excessive energy consumption. [Table 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-tbl-0001) outlines key approaches, identified gaps, and the contributions of the current study, highlighting how each of the identified challenges is addressed to advance TinyML security.

**Table 12.1** A summary of related works and contributions.

| Area || Key approaches || Identified gaps || Contributions of current study |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Privacy‐preserving training || Federated learning (FL), D‐FedAvg, TinyMetaFed || Vulnerability to model inversion and data inference attacks || Lightweight encryption and privacy‐enhanced FL tailored for TinyML |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
