### 14.4.2 Negative Impact

As indicated in [Section 14.3.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0006), poisoning attacks degrade the model accuracy by injecting harmful data into the training dataset. Therefore, when we search for and remove harmful data from a dataset, one of the criteria to consider is the “impact on the original model's accuracy.”

This method uses the RONI [\[16\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0016) concept to evaluate the effect of each device's training data on the accuracy of a model. The effect ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> on model accuracy is defined as the difference between the accuracy of the unfiltered model on the filtered validation set (![u n f i l t e r e d s c o r e](images/c14-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math>) and the accuracy of the filtered model on the filtered validation set ( ![f i l t e r e d s c o r e](images/c14-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math>).

(14.1)![upper I Subscript n e g Baseline equals f i l t e r e d s c o r e minus u n f i l t e r e d s c o r e](images/c14-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> 

The higher the value of ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math>, the more negatively it affects the model accuracy. Thus, with the proposed method, the higher the value of ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math>, the greater the likelihood that the data is harmful. To prevent the harmful data from having an effect on the validation, the filtered validation set is used to confirm ![u n f i l t e r e d s c o r e](images/c14-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> and ![f i l t e r e d s c o r e](images/c14-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math>.

If the value of [equation 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0001) is less than or equal to 0, the impact on the model accuracy is considered, at the least, not to be negative. In such cases, the device is judged to be normal by the proposed method regardless of the ![f i l t e r e d i m p a c t](images/c14-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>i</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>t</mi></math> ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> in [Section 14.4.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0012). The data obtained from devices that are judged not to be normal is not subject to removal; thus, no further steps are taken. Conversely, if ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> is greater than 0, then the data is considered to negatively affect the model accuracy, and the data becomes candidates for removal. The formula for the number of data points to be removed is described in [Section 14.4.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0013).

The function ![c a l c normal bar n e g](images/c14-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></math> for calculating ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> is shown in [Algorithm 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3002). This function requires the validation data ![v a l i d normal bar f Subscript i](images/c14-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>valid</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> that is used to calculate model accuracy and the models ![upper M Subscript u](images/c14-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></math> and ![upper M Subscript f](images/c14-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>. The algorithm simply calculates the accuracy of the two input models on the input validation data, and it stores the accuracy data in ![s c o r e Subscript u](images/c14-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></math> and ![s c o r e Subscript f](images/c14-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>, respectively. The process for calculating accuracy corresponds to the function ![s c o r e left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> in the algorithm. The result of [Equation 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0001) is then stored in ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> and returned as the output of the function ![c a l c normal bar n e g](images/c14-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></math>.

 

### 14.4.3 Adversarial Impact

Unlike existing methods, the proposed method defines an adversarial impact for each device. By executing a poisoning attack on the defense side and injecting harmful data into the filtered dataset, the method is able to virtually output the model accuracy if the data being validated is harmful data (referred to as ![a d v e r s a r i a l s c o r e](images/c14-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math>). The difference between ![a d v e r s a r i a l s c o r e](images/c14-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> and ![f i l t e r e d s c o r e](images/c14-i0070.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> is defined as the threshold, as shown in [equation 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0002):

(14.2)![upper I Subscript a d v Baseline equals f i l t e r e d s c o r e minus a d v e r s a r i a l s c o r e](images/c14-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> 

Here, it is assumed that even if an attack is executed by the use of harmful data, the harm caused to the model remains. This assumption is based on our preliminary experimental results. When a normal device is inspected, an executed attack on that device's data renders the data harmful data, which increases the proportion of total data that is harmful data. Conversely, when a harmful device is inspected, an attack on its data does not increase the total amount of harmful data according to the aforementioned assumption. Consequently, the value of ![a d v e r s a r i a l s c o r e](images/c14-i0071.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> is expected to be low for normal devices and high for harmful devices. Similarly, ![f i l t e r e d s c o r e](images/c14-i0072.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> is expected to be higher for harmful devices than for normal devices. Therefore, the value of ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0073.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> itself does not vary significantly between normal and harmful devices. However, compared with ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0074.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math>, which is a factor in normal/harmful judgments, the ![a d v e r s a r i a l s c o r e](images/c14-i0075.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> for normal devices is expected to be lower than the ![u n f i l t e r e d s c o r e](images/c14-i0076.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math>. As a result, ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0077.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> for normal devices does not fall below the value of ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0078.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math>, thereby preventing the false detection of normal devices. For harmful devices, the values of ![a d v e r s a r i a l s c o r e](images/c14-i0079.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> and ![u n f i l t e r e d s c o r e](images/c14-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> are expected to be similar, which makes harmful devices easier to detect than normal devices.

The function ![c a l c normal bar a d v](images/c14-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></math> for calculating ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> is shown in [Algorithm 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3003). The inputs required by the function are the data for the target device ![t r a i n normal bar s](images/c14-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>s</mi></math>, the filtered training and validation data ![t r a i n normal bar f Subscript i](images/c14-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![v a l i d normal bar f Subscript i](images/c14-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, the model trained on ![t r a i n normal bar f Subscript i](images/c14-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> ![upper M Subscript f](images/c14-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math>, and the model before training ![upper M Subscript a](images/c14-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></math>. Unlike the algorithm for calculating ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math>, the function ![c a l c normal bar a d v](images/c14-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></math> first needs to generate harmful data. Therefore, harmful data is generated using the function ![g e n e r a t e normal bar p o i s o n](images/c14-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></math> based on ![t r a i n normal bar s](images/c14-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>s</mi></math>. The algorithm specifically for ![g e n e r a t e normal bar p o i s o n](images/c14-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></math> depends on the attack method used, which is determined by the user of the defense system (the proposed method). In the experiments run for this study, the attack method proposed by Biggio et al. [\[17\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0017) was used. The generated harmful data is stored in ![upper D Superscript p](images/c14-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math>, and then ![t r a i n normal bar f Subscript i](images/c14-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is concatenated with ![upper D Superscript p](images/c14-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></math> and stored in ![a d v e r s a r i a l normal bar d a t a](images/c14-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></math>. This way, ![a d v e r s a r i a l normal bar d a t a](images/c14-i0098.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></math> virtually recreates the unfiltered data while assuming device ![i](images/c14-i0099.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is a harmful device. Subsequently, the accuracy values ![s c o r e Subscript f](images/c14-i0100.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></math> and ![a d v e r s a r i a l normal bar s c o r e](images/c14-i0101.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi></math> are calculated using the function ![s c o r e left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0102.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>s</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math>. The calculated accuracies are then used to compute the value of ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0103.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> according to [equation 14.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0002), and the result is stored in ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0104.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>, which is returned as the output of function ![c a l c normal bar a d v](images/c14-i0105.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>c</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></math>.

 

### 14.4.4 Data Removal

Finally, the proportion of data to be removed is calculated by using the relationship between the impact on model accuracy ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0106.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> defined in [Section 14.4.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0011) and ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0107.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> defined in [Section 14.4.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0012). The equation for the data removal rate is shown as [equation 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0003):

(14.3)![r e m o v a l r a t e equals StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column 0.0 2nd Column i f 3rd Column upper I Subscript n e g Baseline less-than-or-equal-to 0 2nd Row 1st Column StartFraction upper I Subscript n e g Baseline Over upper I Subscript a d v Baseline EndFraction 2nd Column i f 3rd Column 0 less-than upper I Subscript n e g Baseline less-than upper I Subscript a d v Baseline 3rd Row 1st Column 1.0 2nd Column Blank 3rd Column e l s e EndLayout](images/c14-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>removal</mi><mspace width="0.15em"/><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>rate</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mrow><mtable><mtr><mtd><mn>0.0</mn></mtd><mtd><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>if</mi></mtd><mtd><mspace width="-2.7em"/><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>neg</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>neg</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>adv</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfrac></mtd><mtd><mspace width="0.15em"/><mi>if</mi></mtd><mtd><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>neg</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>adv</mi></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mn>1.0</mn></mtd><mtd></mtd><mtd><mspace width="-4em"/><mi>else</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced></math> 

In the proposed method, if the value of the negative impact ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0108.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> is less than or equal to 0, the device is judged to be normal, and the corresponding data is not removed. This policy is based on the definition of negative impact, where data from a device with a value less than or equal to 0 does not adversely affect (degrade) the accuracy of the other data. When ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0109.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> is greater than 0 but less than ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0110.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>, the removal rate is defined as the ratio of ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0111.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> to ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0112.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>. If ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0113.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> exceeds 0, it adversely affects the model accuracy and thus becomes a candidate for data removal. However, in this study, we calculate an independent removal rate and apply it to each device instead of removing all the data from a device marked for removal. The value of ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0114.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> represents the ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0115.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> value that assumes that all data from the target device is harmful. The closer ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0116.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> is to ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0117.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>, the higher the likelihood that the data from the device is harmful. Therefore, the removal rate is determined from the proximity of ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0118.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> to ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0119.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>. If ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0120.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> exceeds ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0121.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>, it is considered to be worse than the value that would be assumed if all the data were harmful, and the removal rate is set to 1.0, which indicates that all the data from the target device will be removed.

After the data removal process, the removed data is excluded from all subsequent data that is used for validating the next device. That is, no data that is deemed harmful exists in the data used after the judgment. Therefore, the data judged as harmful does not affect the judgment of subsequent devices.

The algorithm that is used to calculate the data removal rate is presented as [Algorithm 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3004). The function ![r e m o v e normal bar d a t a](images/c14-i0122.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>e</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></math> takes the training and validation data ![upper D Subscript t r](images/c14-i0123.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper D Subscript v a l](images/c14-i0124.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></math>, the filtered data ![t r a i n normal bar f Subscript i](images/c14-i0125.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![v a l i d normal bar f Subscript i](images/c14-i0126.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, and the negative impact ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0127.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> and adversarial impact ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0128.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> used for calculating the removal rate, as well as the number of data points from the target device ![n normal bar d a t a](images/c14-i0129.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></math> as inputs.

This function processes the conditions according to [Equation 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0003) to determine the removal rate within those conditions. The first conditional branch of the algorithm checks whether ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0130.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> exceeds the value of ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0131.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>, which corresponds to the last case in [equation 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0003). If this condition is met, the data removal rate is 100%, and the training and validation data is set to the filtered data, which effectively removes the data from the target device. The second conditional branch checks whether ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0132.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> is greater than 0 but does not exceed ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0133.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>, which corresponds to the middle case in [equation 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0003). If this condition is met, the removal rate is calculated by dividing ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0134.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> by ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0135.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>. After the removal rate is calculated, the number of data points to be removed is determined using ![n normal bar d a t a](images/c14-i0136.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi></math> on both training and validation data. Then, the function for determining the removal priority is called to store the priority lists in ![p r i normal bar t r a i n](images/c14-i0137.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></math> and ![p r i normal bar v a l i d](images/c14-i0138.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></math>. Finally, the function ![d e l e t e left-parenthesis right-parenthesis](images/c14-i0139.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> is called with the original data to be removed, the number of data points to be removed, and the priority lists to perform data removal according to the priority. After data removal is carried out, the training and validation data ![upper D Subscript t r](images/c14-i0140.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper D Subscript v a l](images/c14-i0141.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></math> are returned. If neither condition is met, then ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0142.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> is less than or equal to 0, and no data is removed as the device is judged to be normal.

 

### 14.4.5 Removal Priority

Harmful devices can be classified into two types: those that provide only harmful data (all data is harmful) and those that provide both harmful and non‐harmful data (some data is harmful). This section describes the scenario where only some of the provided data is harmful.

This functionality is called only when the algorithm in [Section 14.4.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0013) determines that part of the data should be removed. The priority for removing data is set highest for data whose features are furthest away from the opposite side of the Support Vector Machine (SVM) decision boundary. In other words, data that deviates significantly from the SVM prediction is preferentially removed. First, the data from the target device is compressed into two dimensions using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, the distance between the SVM and the mapped data is calculated in the two‐dimensional space. The data whose SVM prediction is incorrect is prioritized for removal according to the calculated distance, starting from the largest. If the number of data points that are removed by this method is less than the number of data points to be removed as determined by the removal rate, the data points whose SVM prediction is correct but that are close to the SVM boundary are prioritized for removal.

The algorithm for this functionality is shown in [Algorithm 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3005). The function ![d e t normal bar p r i o r i t y](images/c14-i0143.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi></math> takes as inputs the training and validation data ![upper D Subscript t r](images/c14-i0144.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></math> and ![upper D Subscript v a l](images/c14-i0145.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></math>, the device identifier ![i](images/c14-i0146.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, the data from the target device ![t r a i n normal bar s Subscript i](images/c14-i0147.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![v a l i d normal bar s Subscript i](images/c14-i0148.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, and the filtered data ![t r a i n normal bar f](images/c14-i0149.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>f</mi></math> and ![v a l i d normal bar f](images/c14-i0150.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>f</mi></math>. Because the removal priority is determined within a two‐dimensional plane, dimensionality reduction is needed for data whose dimensionality exceeds two. In this study, PCA is used to reduce the dimensionality of ![t r a i n normal bar s Subscript i](images/c14-i0151.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, ![v a l i d normal bar s Subscript i](images/c14-i0152.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, and ![upper D Subscript t r](images/c14-i0153.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub></math>. Next, to determine whether the data is on the opposite side of the SVM decision boundary, an array mesh grid is generated to represent the two‐dimensional plane. The model boundary can be understood by predicting the components of this mesh grid. The prediction results are stored in ![upper Z](images/c14-i0154.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math>. Then, for each data point, the following are calculated:

1.  Distance from the decision boundary.
2.  Whether it is located on the opposite side of the boundary.

These values are stored in ![d i s t a n c e](images/c14-i0155.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>e</mi></math> and ![l o c a t i o n](images/c14-i0156.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></math>, respectively. After all data points are processed, ![p r i o r i t y normal bar a r r a y](images/c14-i0157.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>y</mi></math> is split into training and validation and stored in ![p r i normal bar t r a i n](images/c14-i0158.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></math> and ![p r i normal bar v a l i d](images/c14-i0159.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi></math>, respectively. These two lists are returned as the output of the function ![d e t normal bar p r i o r i t y](images/c14-i0160.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>d</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi></math>.

Although this algorithm assumes a binary classification, in the case of multi‐class classification, a single data label value can be assumed to be binary against other labels. By generating a linear SVM as in [Algorithm 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-3005) and calculating the distance to the target data, the priority can be determined in the same manner as in binary classification.

 

## 14.5 Evaluation Experiment

This section presents the evaluation results.

 

### 14.5.1 Overview

We conducted experiments to verify the effectiveness of the proposed defense method against the poisoning attacks presented in this paper. The accuracies of the following four models were compared in the experiments:

*   Model trained with data containing no harmful data (Perfect defense)
*   Model trained with data containing harmful data (No defense)
*   Model defended by the proposed method (Proposal)
*   Model defended by the existing method (Existing)

The accuracies of these models were evaluated using test data independent of the experimental environment.

Furthermore, the attack method and existing method used in this study were implemented according to the open‐source code provided in Nicolae et al. [\[46\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0046). To shorten the duration of the experiment, the harmful data generated by the attack method was prepared and used in advance. We varied the number of malicious devices and compared the accuracy of each defended model against the proportion of harmful data. Additionally, the threshold for determining harmful devices in the existing method was set to values of 0.0 and 0.2 (the default value set in the open‐source code by Nicolae et al. [\[46\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0046)) for comparison. The experimental results reported in the present study are the values averaged over 10 runs.

The following datasets were used for experiments:

*   Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology (MNIST)
*   Synthetic data
*   Environmental sensor telemetry data

The experimental settings and the results obtained on each dataset are described in [Sections 14.5.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0017)–[14.5.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0025).

 

### 14.5.2 MNIST

 

#### 14.5.2.1 Experimental Setting

In this experiment, the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits was used. Although the original dataset has 10 classes labeled from 0 to 9, we set up a binary classification task for digits 0 and 4, similar to the experiment settings by Biggio et al. Harmful data was generated using the attack method proposed by Biggio et al. [\[17\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0017). Their attack method is an algorithm that generates harmful data in a poisoning attack that targets SVM. The experiment was conducted in two ways: with and without determining the removal priority. For the case with the removal priority determination, the proportion of harmful data in malicious devices was also used as a parameter to verify the effectiveness of the removal priority described in [Section 14.4.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0014). For the case without the removal priority determination, the proportion of harmful data in each malicious device was set to 100%, and the experiment was conducted in an environment in which all the data provided by the malicious devices was harmful.

 

#### 14.5.2.2 Results

The graph depicting the accuracy of the defended models is shown in [Figure 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0008)a. The results in this figure do not represent the case that used the removal priority described in [Section 14.4.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0014). As shown in [Figure 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0008)a, both the existing method and the proposed method significantly outperform the model with no defense up to a proportion of harmful data of 40%. However, when the proportion of harmful data exceeds this level, the accuracy deteriorates even compared with the model without defense. This is likely because an increase in the proportion of harmful data in the training data causes the ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0161.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> values for both the existing method and the proposed method to be high for normal data, which indicates that normal data is judged to have a negative impact on model accuracy.

Furthermore, the F1 score and accuracy for the harmful data detection rate of the existing method and the proposed method are shown in [Figures 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0008)b and c, respectively. The proposed method with a threshold of 0.2 significantly outperforms the existing method on the F1 score. However, the existing method, with a threshold of 0.0, has nearly the same values as the proposed method. These results suggest that the definition of the removal rate in the proposed method ([equation 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0003)) causes it to produce results similar to the existing method with a threshold of 0.0.

[Figures 14.9](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0009)a and b show the precision and recall results for harmful data detection in the above experiment. From the results in (a), it is evident that the proposed method outperforms the existing methods on both threshold values of 0.0 and 0.2 up to a proportion of harmful data of 40%. In (b), however, at a threshold of 0.0, the results for the existing method generally surpass those of the proposed method. These results indicate that the proposed method suppresses false positives with its removal rate formula, but that it also has difficulty detecting a large amount of harmful data.

[Figure 14.10](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0010) shows, using a box plot, the distribution of F1 score values from the detection accuracy of the experiment in [Figure 14.8](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0008). As can be seen, both the existing and proposed methods exhibit similar shapes, which indicates that neither has superiority in detection stability.

![Figure 14.8 Results of model accuracy and harmful data detection accuracy (without removal priority). (a) Model accuracy, (b) detection accuracy F1 score, and (c) detection accuracy.](images/c14f008.png)

**Figure 14.8** Results of model accuracy and harmful data detection accuracy (without removal priority). (a) Model accuracy, (b) detection accuracy F1 score, and (c) detection accuracy.

![Figure 14.9 Detection accuracy results of each defense method (without removal priority) (a) Detection accuracy precision and (b) detection accuracy recall.](images/c14f009.png)

**Figure 14.9** Detection accuracy results of each defense method (without removal priority) (a) Detection accuracy precision and (b) detection accuracy recall.

![Figure 14.10 Box plot of detection accuracy (F1 score) results for each defense method (without removal priority).](images/c14f010.png)

**Figure 14.10** Box plot of detection accuracy (F1 score) results for each defense method (without removal priority).

[Figures 14.11](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0011) and [14.12](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0012) show the experimental results for the case when removal priority is determined. As mentioned in the previous section, the proportion of harmful data in each malicious device was set to 50%. Therefore, even if all of the 10 devices were malicious, the proportion of harmful data in the entire dataset would be only 50%.

Because the MNIST data is used for a binary classification task in this experiment, the task is relatively simple. Therefore, as shown in [Figure 14.11](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0011)a, the accuracies of the models are generally high after each of the defense methods is used. However, it can be observed that the accuracies of “Existing\_0.0” and the proposed method are higher than that of “No defense” up to a proportion of harmful data of 25%. This indicates that the proposed method's defense effectively reduces the degradation in the model's accuracy for a proportion of harmful data of up to 25%. [Figures 14.11](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0011)b and c show the detection accuracy of harmful data in terms of F1 score and accuracy, respectively. These results show that the proposed method generally shows higher detection accuracy than the existing method.

[Figures 14.12](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0012)a and b show the precision and recall results for the detection of harmful data in the above experiment. For precision, the proposed method generally shows higher accuracy. Particularly, the difference is dramatic when the proportion of harmful data is in the range from 5% to 35%. In contrast, the results for recall show that, at a threshold of 0.0, the existing method generally outperforms the proposed method. These results suggest that although the proposed method suppresses false positives, it has greater difficulty detecting harmful data than the existing method.

To summarize these results, there is no significant difference in model accuracy between the proposed method and the existing method; however, the proposed method demonstrates a much higher detection accuracy for harmful data. This indicates that the proposed method's model accuracy would improve in complex tasks in which the detection and removal of harmful data have a significant impact on model performance ([Figure 14.13](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0013)).

### 14.5.3 Synthetic Data

 

#### 14.5.3.1 Experimental Setting

The dataset and harmful data generation method that are used for the poisoning attack in this experiment are based on the method used in Zhou et al. [\[47\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0047). [Figure 14.14](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0014) shows a sample of the synthetic data. This attack algorithm specifies a parameter (![a t t a c k normal bar p a r a m e t e r](images/c14-i0162.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi></math>) that represents the strength of the attack, with values ranging from 0 to 1. The strength of the attack indicates how much the generated harmful data deviates from the original distribution, where data that is farther from the original distribution shows greater deviation. As can be seen from [Figure 14.14](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0014), the light gray and dark gray plots represent normal data, whereas the medium gray represents harmful data. With the attack parameter set to 0.5, the harmful data is distributed around the midpoint between the ight gray and dark gray normal data. An attack parameter value set close to 0 represents a weaker setting, whereas a value close to 1 represents more harmful data.

![Figure 14.14 Synthetic data (a t t a c k normal bar p a r a m e t e r equals 0.5).](images/c14f014.png)

**Figure 14.14** Synthetic data (![a t t a c k normal bar p a r a m e t e r equals 0.5](images/c14-i0163.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></math>).

We conducted experiments with three different values for the attack parameter (0.3, 0.5, 0.7). As was done in the experiments in [Section 14.5.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0017), the total number of devices was set to 10, where each device provided 100 data points. The thresholds for the existing method were set the same values as in [Section 14.5.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0017).

 

#### 14.5.3.2 Results

The results for the accuracy of each model after the defense methods were implemented are shown in [Figures 14.15](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0015)a, [14.16](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0016)a, and [14.17](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0017)a. The accuracy of the models that were trained without any defense decreases as the proportion of harmful data increases, whereas the existing and proposed methods maintain their accuracy relatively well. Additionally, with higher values of the attack parameter, the accuracy of the models for each defense method decreases.

![Figure 14.15 Results of model accuracy and harmful data detection rate (a t t a c k normal bar p a r a m e t e r equals 0.3) (a) Model accuracy, (b) detection accuracy F1 score, and (c) detection accuracy.](images/c14f015.png)

**Figure 14.15** Results of model accuracy and harmful data detection rate (![a t t a c k normal bar p a r a m e t e r equals 0.3](images/c14-i0164.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></math>) (a) Model accuracy, (b) detection accuracy F1 score, and (c) detection accuracy.

The rate of detection of harmful data when the attack parameter value is set to 0.5 is shown in [Figures 14.16](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0016)b and c. These results indicate that the proposed method is slightly better at detecting harmful data than the existing method. Regarding the F1 score, it can be seen that the detection rate increases as the proportion of harmful data increases up to a proportion of 60%. This may be because the degree of influence of false positives decreases with an increase in the number of harmful data. However, the detection rate drops sharply when the proportion of harmful data reaches 70%. When the proportion of harmful data is 70%, the ratio of harmful data to the total data exceeds 50% for both the existing and proposed methods. Therefore, it is thought that the reason for this is the difficulty in judging whether harmful data has an adverse effect on the model. [Figure 14.18](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0018) shows the negative impact values for a given ratio of harmful data to total data. As can be seen from this figure, the difference in negative impact between normal and harmful devices is small, which indicates that the lower detection rate may be due to the above reason.

**Figure 14.16** Results of model accuracy and harmful data detection rate (![a t t a c k normal bar p a r a m e t e r equals 0.5](images/c14-i0165.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">\_</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>r</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></math>) (a) Model accuracy, (b) detection accuracy F1 score, and (c) detection accuracy.

Similar to the accuracy results for each model, the rate of detecting harmful data decreases for higher values of the attack parameter. This result is likely due to the following two factors:

*   The stronger effect of harmful data makes it easier to detect the proportion of harmful data up to a certain value.
*   The stronger effect of harmful data makes it more difficult to detect a smaller amount of harmful data compared with weaker parameters.

### 14.5.4 Environmental Sensor Telemetry Data

 

#### 14.5.4.1 Experimental Setting

The dataset used in this experiment was obtained from the data analysis platform Kaggle [\[48\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0048). This sensing data was generated by an environmental sensor array [\[49\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0049). The breadboard‐based sensor array is connected to a Raspberry Pi single‐board computer. These IoT devices are intentionally placed in physical locations under various environmental conditions, such as temperature and humidity conditions, to collect data. The attributes of these data are shown in [Table 14.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0003).

In this experiment, we aim to predict the “light” attribute value using other sensed data except for “motion.” The reason for excluding “motion” from the explanatory variables is to avoid making the task overly simple, as “motion” is a Boolean value.

**Table 14.3** Environmental sensor telemetry data.

| Notation || Description || Units |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ts || Timestamp of event || epoch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| device || Unique device name || string |
| co || Carbon monoxide || ppm (%) |
| humidity || Humidity || percentage |
| light || Light detected? || Boolean |
| lpg || Liquid petroleum gas || ppm (%) |
| motion || Motion detected? || Boolean |
| smoke || Smoke || ppm (%) |
| temp || Temperature || Fahrenheit |

The experimental settings are similar to those of the experiments in [Sections 14.5.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0017) and [14.5.3](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0021), with the total number of devices set to 10. The number of data points for each device is set to 20 and 100, and we conduct experiments for both settings. The proportion of harmful data in the malicious devices is set to 50% and 100%, as was done in [Section 14.5.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0017). When the proportion is set to 50%, the algorithm for determining the removal priority is used, and it is not used when the proportion is set to 100%.

 

#### 14.5.4.2 Results

The results obtained when the number of data points per device is 20 and the proportion of harmful data in the malicious devices is 100% are shown in [Figures 14.20](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0020) and [14.21](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0021). Both the existing method and the proposed method can detect harmful data up to a proportion of harmful data of 40%. However, when the proportion exceeds 40%, neither method detects harmful data effectively. Correspondingly, the model accuracy shown in [Figure 14.20](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0020)a is almost the same as that for the no defense for this proportion ([Figure 14.22](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0022)).

[Table 14.4](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0004) shows the ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0169.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> values for each device in the experiment with three to five malicious devices. The results, which are averaged over 10 runs, show that as soon as the number of malicious devices reaches four (i.e., 40% harmful data), the ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0170.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> values for all malicious devices become 0. As was defined in [equation 14.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-disp-0001) of [Section 14.4.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0011), ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0171.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> is the difference between the accuracy of the filtered model and that of the unfiltered model. A value of 0 indicates that both models have either endpoint accuracy values (0 or 1) or the same accuracy value. Because the accuracy values are not extreme, as is shown in [Figure 14.20](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0020)a, the accuracy of the filtered and unfiltered models is taken to be the same. This means that including or excluding the data from a single malicious device does not affect the model accuracy.

This means that the increase in the number of harmful devices has a greater negative impact on the accuracy of the model than does the proportion of harmful data within those devices.

Furthermore, [Figure 14.25](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0025) shows the box plot of the F1 score values for the detection accuracy in the experimental setting shown in [Figure 14.23](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0023). The results in [Figure 14.24](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0024) indicate that in a setting where the proportion of harmful data is set to 5%, the existing method consistently detects the harmful data with high accuracy. However, the proposed method sometimes achieves higher detection rates than the existing method, but it generally has lower average detection rates. When the proportion of harmful data is set to 10% and 15%, the median values indicate that the proposed method obtains higher detection rates than the existing method. When the proportion of harmful data is set to 20% or higher, there is no significant difference in detection stability between the existing method and the proposed method. These results suggest that in the experimental settings for this section, when the proportion of harmful data in malicious devices is 50%, there is little difference in detection stability between the existing and proposed methods.

[Figures 14.26](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0026) and [14.27](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0027) show the results of experiments conducted with the number of data points per device set to 20, the proportion of harmful data in malicious devices set to 100%, and the attack method changed to “label flip.” “Label flip” is an attack in which the labels of the attack data are simply flipped in the binary data.

As shown in [Figure 14.26](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0026)a, the accuracy of the models after each defense method is applied drops to almost zero, except for the “perfect defense” model. Additionally, the accuracy of the models tends to rapidly decrease when the proportion of harmful data reaches 50%, and the accuracy takes values that are opposite to those for the settings where the proportion of harmful data is 0% to 40%. These results suggest that the increase in reversed data due to the label flip caused significant learning interference in the training data, which resulted in reversed prediction outcomes. This means that for the settings where the proportion of harmful data was 60% or higher, the normal data became a minority and was treated as harmful data.

The results for the accuracy in detecting harmful data are shown in [Figures 14.26](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0026)b and c and [14.27](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0027). These results show there is almost no difference in detection accuracy between the existing and proposed methods.

[Figure 14.28](#c14.xhtml#c14-fig-0028) shows the distribution of F1 score values from the detection accuracy of the experimental setting described above using a box plot. In the results for proportions of harmful data of 70% or higher, both the existing and proposed methods detected almost no harmful data, and this is consistent with the results for model accuracy. For the settings where the proportion of harmful data is set to 10%–60%, both methods detect some harmful data, but the box plots cover a wide vertical margin, which indicates instability in detection.

## 14.6 Discussion

We discuss several issues related to our proposed method in this section.

 

### 14.6.1 Attack Methods Utilized

The method proposed in this study is a defense mechanism against poisoning attacks that leverages the harmful data generated by the attack algorithms. In the evaluation experiments presented in [Section 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0015), both the attack and defense sides use the same poisoning attack method as in the setting. However, in real‐world scenarios, it is unlikely that the defense would be able to use the same methods as the attackers. The proposed method takes advantage of the characteristic that harmful data does not revert to normal data, even when the attack algorithm is rerun. Therefore, it is necessary to verify in the future whether this premise holds when different attack algorithms are combined.

 

### 14.6.2 Adversarial Impact of Each Device

Baracaldo et al. [\[32\]](#c14.xhtml#c14-bib-0032) used a fixed threshold to determine the harmful or benign status of each device. In contrast, the method proposed in this study defines a unique threshold, ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0186.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>, for each device. [Table 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0005) shows the values of ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0187.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> for the normal and harmful devices according to the proposed method. From these results, it can be seen that normal devices have values of ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0188.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> that are relatively more likely to be judged as harmful. Intuitively, smaller values of ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0189.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> for the harmful devices would be expected to improve detection accuracy. The results presented in [Section 14.5](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0015) suggest that the accuracy of the proposed method is not inferior to that of the existing method for two reasons: Normal devices with an ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0190.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> less than or equal to zero are judged as benign, regardless of ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0191.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math>, and harmful devices having ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0192.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> values close to ![upper I Subscript a d v](images/c14-i0193.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> undergo higher data removal rates ([Table 14.6](#c14.xhtml#c14-tbl-0006)).

**Table 14.5** Values of ![equation](images/c14-i0194.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub></math> in the proposed method.

| --- | --- | --- |
| 8% || 0.064 || 0.115 |

**Table 14.6** Values of ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0195.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> in the proposed method.

 

### 14.6.3 When Harmful Data Constitutes the Majority

As described in [Section 14.4.2](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0011), the proposed method adopts the strategy of judging all devices with a value of ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0200.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> less than or equal to zero as normal and not removing the corresponding data. However, when more than half of the dataset under protection consists of harmful data, it is conceivable that “normal data have an adverse effect on harmful data.” In other words, the roles of normal and harmful data are essentially reversed. In such a case, the defense algorithm proposed in this paper may detect a greater number of normal devices than harmful devices because the ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0201.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> of normal data would have a relatively high value.

 

### 14.6.4 Against Attackers Aware of the Defense Method's Internal Structure

As described in [Section 14.2.1](#c14.xhtml#c14-sec-0003), this study assumes an environment in which data is collected from multiple devices in an IoT setting. However, the proposed method could be applied to many sources of data outside such environments. For instance, consider the scenario in which the annotation of training data is outsourced. In this case, data providers may be divided by company or employee. If an attacker is among these providers, the attacker can execute a poisoning attack. This scenario assumes that modifications to the data before and after the annotation are not detected by comparing hash values.

Additionally, it is conceivable that attackers could possess partial or complete knowledge about the algorithms of proposed method. In such cases, attackers may attempt to minimize ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0202.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> to evade detection. Because the proposed method uses the impact on the accuracy of the model as a criterion for identifying harmful data, reducing ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0203.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> would make detecting harmful data more challenging. However, reducing ![upper I Subscript n e g](images/c14-i0204.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>g</mi></mrow></msub></math> also reduces the effectiveness of an attack. Therefore, this method could potentially serve as a deterrent to attacks.

 

### 14.6.5 Limitations

Our proposed method determines whether the received data has been subject to a poisoning attack by applying known poisoning attacks to the data and then checking if the accuracy of the machine learning model subsequently decreases. If the server receives data that has been subject to an unknown poisoning attack, our proposed method may not correctly detect the attack. Existing defense methods for detecting poisoning attacks, other than our proposed method, may also be vulnerable to unknown attacks. Therefore, this drawback is not unique to our method. However, it is necessary to further evaluate how robust our method is against unknown attacks.

Additionally, the proposed method requires that the machine learning model be repeatedly trained, which results in significant computational cost. It will become necessary to explore ways to reduce this computational burden in the future.

 

## 14.7 Conclusion

The advent of TinyML, which focuses on deploying machine learning models on resource‐constrained devices, introduces additional layers of complexity and potential vulnerabilities to the security landscape. As TinyML systems become integral to various applications, from smart home devices to wearable health monitors, ensuring the security and robustness of these systems becomes paramount. TinyML systems, by design, operate under extreme constraints in terms of computational power, memory, and energy consumption. These constraints necessitate highly optimized and often simplified machine learning models, which may inadvertently introduce new attack surfaces. For example, the reduced complexity of models in TinyML systems could make them more susceptible to certain types of poisoning attacks that exploit these simplifications.

Furthermore, the environments in which TinyML systems are deployed are often less controlled than those of traditional machine learning systems, as these devices are widely distributed and interact directly with the physical world. This increases the number of potential attack vectors and the ease with which malicious actors can introduce poisonous data. Therefore, the security strategies employed must be lightweight yet effective to balance the need for robust defenses with the limited resources available.

In this context, our study focuses on developing efficient detection and mitigation strategies for poisoning attacks. The proposed defense method, which is intended to minimize model degradation and accurately identify harmful data, is particularly suited to the TinyML paradigm. By ensuring that the defensive mechanisms are computationally efficient and do not overburden the limited resources of TinyML devices, we can enhance the security of these systems without compromising their performance or functionality.

Additionally, the practical implications of securing TinyML systems are considerable. As TinyML devices are often embedded in critical infrastructure and personal environments, any successful attack may have far‐reaching consequences and impact not only individual users but also entire communities. Hence, our efforts to improve the resilience of machine learning systems against poisoning attacks are crucial for the broader adoption of and trust in TinyML technologies.

In conclusion, the integration of robust, lightweight security measures into TinyML systems is essential to safeguarding the next generation of smart devices. Our proposed method contributes to this goal by addressing the unique challenges posed by the resource constraints and deployment scenarios of TinyML, and it ensures that these innovative systems are both powerful and secure.

# 15  
TinyML for Real‐Time Medical Image Classification and Diagnosis

*Jelil O. Agbo‐Ajala^([1](#c15.xhtml#c15-aff-0001)), Lateef A. Akinyemi^([1](#c15.xhtml#c15-aff-0001),[2](#c15.xhtml#c15-aff-0002)), Olufisayo S. Ekundayo^([1](#c15.xhtml#c15-aff-0001)), and Ernest Mnkandla^([1](#c15.xhtml#c15-aff-0001))*

*¹Centre for Augmented Intelligence and Data Science, School of Computing, University of South Africa, Johannesburg, South Africa*

*²Department of Electrical and Smart Systems Engineering, School of Computing, University of South Africa, Johannesburg, South Africa*

 

## 15.1 Introduction

Medical image classification and diagnosis involve the analysis and interpretation of medical images, such as X‐ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound images, to detect and classify various diseases, medical conditions, and abnormalities \[[1](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0001), [2](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0002)\]. This process classifies medical images into different conditions using their visual features and patterns. The diagnosis of medical images goes a step further by using classified images to make a diagnosis, identify the type and stage of the conditions, and detect the location and severity of injuries \[[3](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0003), [4](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0004)\].

Real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis are critical in health care, with accurate and timely information to make reliable decisions and appropriate patient care [\[5\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0005). Conventional methods like machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have limitations, including requiring large amounts of training images, being computationally expensive and resource‐intensive, and susceptibility to overfitting, especially with small data. However, these limitations led to delayed diagnoses and encouraged ongoing research in deep learning and real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis, as well as alternative techniques to address these limitations \[[6](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006), [7](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0007)\].

Recently, TinyML (Tiny Machine Learning) has proven to be a promising technology in medical image analysis, supporting real‐time classification and diagnosis in resource‐constrained devices. TinyML focuses on developing tiny and lightweight models that can run efficiently and effectively on devices with limited computational resources, such as edge devices, smartphones, and embedded systems. These benefits make TinyML suitable for real‐time analysis and interpretation of medical images. TinyML empowers healthcare professionals to make more accurate and timely diagnoses that reduce healthcare costs, improve patient outcomes, and increase accessibility in remote and resource‐constrained areas \[[8](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0008), [9](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0009)\]. This research aims to explore TinyML models for real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis ([Figure 15.1](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0001)), achieving the following objectives:

![Figure 15.1 A typical TinyML architecture; the architecture consists of four major stages: input, pre‐processing, model training and testing, and output. The input stage utilizes medical images from sources such as CT, X‐ray, MRI, or PET scans. The pre‐processing stage encompasses image denoising, resizing, augmentation, and other data preparation techniques. Next, the model training and testing phase. Finally, the output stage that produces the disease detection, classification, or segmentation results.](images/c15f001.png)

**Figure 15.1** A typical TinyML architecture; the architecture consists of four major stages: input, pre‐processing, model training and testing, and output. The input stage utilizes medical images from sources such as CT, X‐ray, MRI, or PET scans. The pre‐processing stage encompasses image denoising, resizing, augmentation, and other data preparation techniques. Next, the model training and testing phase. Finally, the output stage that produces the disease detection, classification, or segmentation results.

1.  We present a comprehensive review and detailed analysis of various methods used in medical image classification and diagnosis.
2.  We conducted a comparative study between TinyML models and other machine learning methods, including traditional machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL).
3.  We also explore the advantages and benefits of TinyML models over other approaches, particularly in real‐time classification and diagnosis performance across different datasets, and their potential to improve the field.
4.  We also present a description of popular datasets and evaluation metrics used in medical image classification, especially breast cancer, brain tumor, and COVID‐19.
5.  We then examine future research and development directions for TinyML, in medical image classification and diagnosis.

This work serves as a comprehensive guide for researchers interested in employing TinyML for medical image classification and presents new and advanced methods utilized in this area that provide important insight into the current and existing works.

The rest of this work is arranged as follows: [Section 15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0002) presents a comprehensive review and analysis of medical image classification and diagnosis methods, with a thorough examination of various methods/models used for medical image classification and diagnosis. [Section 15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0006) presents the performance of conventional methods, including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), as well as novel TinyML models. In [Section 15.4](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0010), we present the results of our findings, highlighting the benefits of TinyML models while stating the limitations of other mechanisms. Finally, we summarize our contributions and highlight future research directions, which provide a conclusion to our work in [Section 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0016).

 

## 15.2 Literature Review

This section presents a comprehensive review of existing work, including research focusing on machine learning and deep learning techniques for medical image analysis. Despite varying degrees of success, these studies have collectively advanced the field, highlighting key methodologies, achievements, and challenges.

 

### 15.2.1 Methods Employed in Medical Image Classification and Diagnosis

Medical imaging is a significant area of computer vision research, with many publications published over the last few decades [\[10\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0010). Machine learning algorithms, particularly deep neural networks, have become popular in this field of image analysis. Therefore, this section presents a comprehensive and detailed analysis of the most recent and relevant work (see [Tables 15.1](#c15.xhtml#c15-tbl-0001) and [15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-tbl-0002)), including TinyML, on the classification and diagnosis of three popular diseases: breast cancer, brain tumor, and COVID‐19. We aim to present an overview of the current and recent methods, understand the complexities of the field, identify application areas for novel TinyML, and highlight areas that require further exploration.
