*   **Breast Cancer**: In [\[11\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0011), the authors presented a novel channel attention model that employed “multiscale grid average pooling,” for the segmentation of breast cancer on ultrasound images. This module incorporated both local and global spatial information, to enhance the segmentation task. The proposed network was trained and validated on popular dataset of breast cancer ultrasound images. The experimental results demonstrated the ability of the proposed model to perform the segmentation task. In [\[12\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0012), the authors introduced a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture for automatic breast cancer segmentation. The model was trained on a diverse, large, and evenly distributed dataset and evaluated on popular benchmark datasets. Robust training on these datasets enabled the model to achieve excellent generalization that demonstrated its capacity to accurately segment breast cancer. In [\[10\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0010), the authors presented a novel method for breast cancer segmentation in ultrasonography images that addressed the challenges posed by complex noise and artifacts. They introduced an integrated architecture that combined ultrasonography image pre‐processing, “linear iterative clustering,” and a U‐Net model. This approach enhanced the accuracy of breast cancer diagnosis and provided medical professionals with a valuable tool for improved patient outcomes. Also, the authors in [\[13\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0013) developed an effective and intelligent method for breast cancer diagnosis and segmentation of breast cancer images. They proposed a novel pre‐processing technique for pathological images and an image recognition technology for breast cancer. This intelligent architecture for breast cancer employed digital image processing technology and filtering techniques to improve the clarity of the image data. Moreau et al. [\[14\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0014) proposed a model that automated the segmentation of metastatic breast cancer lesions on positron emission tomography (PET) and CT images. The novel model was evaluated on benchmark datasets. The results showed that the proposed model can accurately segment lesions in images with metastatic breast cancer. Similarly, in [\[15\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0015), the authors developed an automatic method for evaluating histopathological cancer sections. Using the whole images of breast cancer collected from Norway, they proposed a convolutional but cascaded neural network model, H2G‐Net, to segment the regions with breast cancer from histopathological images. The design also employed a patch‐wise technique and a convolution autoencoder. To validate the proposed model, they investigated ablation study to analyze the importance of the chosen regions on cancer segmentation. In [\[16\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0016), the authors investigated a novel model that combined a multiscale CNN with a joint transformer, for segmenting breast cancer in “Dynamic Contrast‐Enhanced MRI (DCE‐MRI).” This two‐stage segmentation method first employed a U‐Net network model to delineate the breast area in MRI images. The model was then evaluated using standard evaluation metrics, where it achieved excellent results in the segmenting and classifying of breast cancer lesions. In [\[17\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0017), the authors proposed a breast cancer model that detected and classified cancer at its early stage. They developed a diagnosis and segmentation method for breast cancer using both deep neural networks and transfer learning that is validated on a publicly available dataset. The results showed that the proposed method achieved a high accuracy for both binary and multi‐class classification of cancer cases. In [\[18\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0018), the authors presented a model for automatic diagnosis of high‐resolution breast cancer of pathological images. The proposed model is based on a “dual‐path feature extraction network” for breast pathology, which utilized dilated convolution networks to encode rich contextual information. Additionally, they introduced a “channel attention mechanism” and a feature attention and fusion module to selectively filter and combine features. This fused approach achieved excellent performance on the image data while reducing the computational complexity associated with existing models. Patra et al. [\[19\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0019) presented a novel approach for automatic breast cancer segmentation using “DCE‐MRI.” Their framework employed a multiple‐level thresholding technique, with an optimization algorithm, to segment breast lesions in the DCE‐MRI images. Additionally, they utilized an enhanced “simple metaheuristic algorithm (SMA)” with a “quasi‐opposition‐based learning mechanism,” to determine the optimal threshold values. This approach showed superior performance compared to existing methods. In [\[20\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0020), Xianjun et al. employed an attention‐learning approach for breast cancer segmentation of mammography images. The proposed model comprised a novel architecture, an attention‐based scheme, and a method for learning image labels. This multi‐task approach integrated multiscale feature fusion and an enhanced U‐Net architecture that improves the segmentation capability. The model achieved significant success when evaluated on benchmark datasets. In [\[21\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0021), Liping et al. presented a novel breast cancer segmentation method that comprises a hybrid “AttendSeg architecture” and “gravitational clustering optimization” method. The proposed hybrid method was employed to segment breast cancer images into various regions such as normal, malignant, and benign. The model demonstrated great performance when evaluated using some evaluating metrics, such as recall, precision, Dice coefficient, and Jaccard index. Ahmed et al. [\[22\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0022) introduced a deep learning‐based model for classifying, detecting, and segmenting cancerous regions in mammogram images. They introduced a pre‐processing mechanism to remove noise, artifacts, and muscle regions, followed by converting the pre‐processed image into 512 ![times](images/c15-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math> 512 patches. The model was trained on two benchmark breast cancer datasets and evaluated on popular metrics where it achieved excellent performance in terms of area under the receiver operating curve (AUC‐ROC), average precision, and accuracy. These results demonstrated the proposed model's potential to assist medical practitioners in breast cancer classification and segmentation. Balaha et al. [\[23\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0023) proposed a novel approach for diagnosing breast cancer at its early stage. They suggested a hybrid framework for breast cancer classification and segmentation, consisting of two phases: classification and segmentation. The classification phase employed five different CNN models, with the Aquila optimizer used to calculate the optimal hyperparameters for the transfer learning architectures. The framework was trained on common datasets, and the results demonstrated good performance in binary and multiclass classification, as well as in the segmentation task. Also, Raza et al. [\[24\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0024) proposed an efficient and robust deep‐learning model, “DeepBreastCancerNet,” for breast cancer detection and classification. The novel architecture employed “clipped rectified linear unit (ReLU) and leaky ReLU activation functions,” cross‐channel normalization, and batch normalization. Experimental results showed that the proposed model achieved comparable performance with other state‐of‐the‐art models on classification accuracy.
*   **Brain Tumor**: In [\[25\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025), Bag et al. proposed an advanced CNN technique for detecting abnormalities in MRI scans, aimed at supporting prompt decision‐making by radiologists. The technique comprises three stages including pre‐processing of brain MRI images, application of machine learning feature extraction methods to identify significant features from these images, and utilization of CNN models to classify the detected regions in the MRI images. The results showed the effectiveness of the automated abnormal brain growth detection model in real‐world scenarios, showcasing its potential to save medical practitioners time and facilitate early diagnosis. In [\[26\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0026), Vaiyapuri et al. introduced an ensemble learning‐driven diagnosis model that employed deep learning techniques and CNNs on MRI scans. The model featured a Gabor filter to enhance image quality and utilized popular CNNs like EfficientNet, MobileNet, and DenseNet for feature extraction. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using the “social spider optimization algorithm.” The proposed model achieved significant success compared to other methods. Similarly, Dhakshnamurthy et al. [\[27\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0027) explored a algorithms for detecting and classifying brain tumors using transfer learning models, for medical imaging. They employed three CNN‐based models: VGG16, AlexNet, and ResNet‐50. The ensemble of VGG16 and ResNet‐50 models showed exceptional performance on benchmark datasets, with remarkable results in specificity, sensitivity, accuracy, and F1 score. Also in [\[28\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0028), the authors proposed a deep transfer learning architecture for brain tumor diagnosis. They applied four different transfer learning architectures of DenseNet121, VGG19, InceptionV3, and MobileNet. They also employed images from three benchmark datasets of Br35H, Figshare, and SARTAJ, to validate the models. The experimental results showed that the MobileNet outperformed other existing models achieving great accuracy. Similarly, in [\[29\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0029), Noreen et al. proposed a method utilizing pre‐trained models, where features are extracted from down layers. They employed a multilevel feature extraction and concatenation technique for early detection and diagnosis of brain tumors. They specifically used the pre‐trained DenseNet201 to extract features from different DenseNet layers, which were then concatenated and transferred to a softmax classifier. The two models achieved excellent performance in detecting brain tumors when evaluated on a three‐class brain tumor dataset. Güler and Namlı [\[30\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0030) presented a novel deep‐learning model for detecting brain tumors on MRI images. Their automatic brain tumor diagnosis and classification system aim to assist radiologists by eliminating the need for manual diagnosis. The authors trained and evaluated their proposed model on a large dataset of 7022 brain MR images. Initially, they employed machine learning methods to classify the extracted features, followed by an ensemble learning approach. The model demonstrated outstanding results, confirming the effectiveness of the employed techniques and methods. In [\[31\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0031), Mohammed and Hilai developed a hybrid model that integrated CNN and support vector machine (SVM) kernels for brain tumor classification. They utilized a CNN‐based model to identify regional variations and classify brain tumors, using already pre‐trained CNN models, including VGG19, EfficientNetB0, and NASNetLarge. The extracted features were then classified using an SVM classifier, which demonstrated comparable performance to existing models. Rasool et al. [\[32\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0032) proposed a novel approach that combined SqueezeNet with SVM for brain tumor classification. The hybrid deep learning method utilized a pre‐trained CNN for feature extraction phase and an SVM for pattern classification, where it achieved high accuracy on MRI scans. Parveen et al. [\[33\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0033) developed an automated brain tumor diagnosis and classification model using an equilibrium optimization method and deep learning. Their model employed a Wiener filtering technique to remove noise from images and a ShuffleNet model for feature extraction. The model was validated on the benchmark Br35H dataset, comprising 1500 tumor and 1500 non‐tumor images, and demonstrated significant success over existing techniques.
*   **COVID‐19**: In [\[34\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0034), Jin et al. proposed a hybrid model that included a feature extractor, feature selector, and classifier. They primarily pre‐trained AlexNet CNN for the feature extraction phase before employing ReliefF algorithm for feature sorting and selected important features using a trial‐and‐error technique. The proposed model showed great performance compared to other state‐of‐the‐art models. Sufian et al. [\[35\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0035) introduced a novel image processing technique for grayscale medical images where it employed “histogram equalization and contrast‐limited adaptive histogram equalization,” to produce a “three‐channel image representation.” The proposed representation technique improved the classification performance when evaluated on six popular pre‐trained models. Al et al. [\[36\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0036) developed a deep transfer learning (VGG16) model for the diagnosis of COVID‐19 infection in chest X‐ray images. They developed six different classifiers for different chest X‐ray image data before combining them into a final classifier, and this demonstrated an encouraging capability of the model in COVID‐19 detection. Zazzaro et al. [\[37\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0037) proposed a deep learning and ensemble technique for automated COVID‐19 detection on chest CT images. They employed transfer learning techniques of a CNN originally pre‐trained on popular ImageNet dataset, to allow for feature extraction from CT images. Babukarthik et al. [\[38\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0038) also proposed a genetic deep learning and CNN model, for COVID‐19 prediction. The model was trained from scratch, to extract features needed for the classification task. The model achieved a good performance on precision, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, in COVID‐19 diagnosis. Ozyurt et al. [\[39\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0039) proposed an automatic COVID‐19 detection method using transfer learning of a lightweight deep learning approach. They used a lightweight (ShuffleNet) architecture and a multilevel activation visualization layer, to detect COVID‐19 pneumonia from large‐scale chest radiographic images. Owais et al. [\[40\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0040) proposed a method for analyzing and diagnosing COVID‐19 infection from large‐scale radiographic image datasets. They used a lightweight network with an ensemble design of ShuffleNet, MobileNet, and FCNet, for the diagnosis of COVID‐19, and it achieved good performance when compared to existing and conventional procedures. In [\[41\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0041), Polsinelli et al. developed a lightweight CNN‐based model that used SqueezeNet architecture for the diagnosis of COVID‐19 in CT images. The model achieved good accuracy and competitive results. Ullah et al. [\[42\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0042) employed a holistic approach using ShuffleNet CNN architecture, to detect and classify COVID‐19 from CT scans, chest radiographs, and electrocardiogram (ECG) images. The extensive classification experiments demonstrated the ability of the proposed method on the classification task. Alghamdi et al. [\[43\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0043) introduced an enhanced deep learning approach for the multiclass classification of COVID‐19 infection of chest X‐rays. They utilized various deep CNN models, data normalization and augmentation, and approaches, to improve performance. The model successfully classified the images into five different cases, including normal, COVID‐19, and other lung infections. Akpinar et al. [\[44\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0044) developed a CNN‐based model using SqueezeNet for detecting abnormalities in chest X‐ray images, and this achieved great success after experimental evaluations. Mehmood et al. [\[45\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0045) proposed an automated system (CP\_DeepNet) for detecting COVID‐19 infections in lung X‐ray images. They utilized a pre‐trained SqueezeNet model and convolution layers and employed data augmentation, to avoid overfitting.

In general, despite the significant advances in medical image classification and diagnosis presented in the literature, TinyML still outperforms state‐of‐the‐art methods in classification and diagnosis of medical images, particularly in real‐time applications.

 

### 15.2.2 TinyML Models and Architecture Used in Real‐Time Medical Image Classification and Diagnosis

Medical image classification and diagnosis involve developing models and architectures to analyze and process medical images, such as computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), X‐rays, and ultrasound images, to support disease classification and diagnosis. These models and architectures are typically optimized for accuracy, memory constraints, and computational efficiency, making them suitable for deployment on resource‐constrained devices, including smartphones, tablets, and embedded systems. In this section, we therefore present some popular TinyML models and architectures used in real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis.

*   **MobileNet**: MobileNet is a renowned lightweight neural network model developed by Google researchers, specifically designed for embedded devices and devices that are memory‐constrained. Its efficient design has made it a popular choice among computer vision researchers, who adapt it for various applications, including medical image classification, detection, and segmentation. MobileNet excels in managing computational resources and memory usage, making it an ideal choice for mobile devices, smartphones, and other resource‐constrained devices. The architecture employs “depthwise separable convolutions” that significantly reduce the number of parameters and computational requirements. The MobileNet family includes several variants, such as MobileNet‐v1, MobileNet‐v2, MobileNet‐v3, and MobileNet‐v3‐Small, which are commonly used to classify medical images, classify magnetic resonance scans, and detect breast cancer. These variants offer developers a variety of options to choose from, depending on their specific requirements and constraints [\[46\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0046).
*   **ShuffleNet**: ShuffleNet is a lightweight CNN architecture that has demonstrated exceptional performance in various medical image classification tasks, including breast cancer and lung nodule. The model was designed for mobile devices with limited computing power, and ShuffleNet was introduced in 2018 by researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China. Its architecture combines “depthwise separable convolutions,” pointwise convolutions, and channel shuffle operations, to achieve efficient computation and memory usage. The network has several variants: ShuffleNet‐v1, ShuffleNet‐v2, and ShuffleNet‐v3, which hold great promise for various real‐world computer vision applications, such as detecting brain tumors, classifying MRI scans, diagnosing Alzheimer's diseases. ShuffleNet's efficiency and accuracy make it an attractive solution for resource‐constrained devices and real‐time applications [\[47\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0047).
*   **SqueezeNet**: SqueezeNet is a compact and lightweight neural network architecture widely used in medical image classification tasks, including cardiovascular disease detection, diabetic retinopathy detection, chest radiograph classification, and skin lesions. SqueezeNet was developed by DeepScale, specifically for deployment on resource‐constrained mobile and embedded devices. Its unique architecture enables reduced parameters and computations while still maintaining accuracy. This is achieved through a combination of techniques, including fire modules, depthwise separable convolution, squeeze layers, and expand layers [\[48\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0048).
*   **Tiny CNN**: Tiny CNN is one of the common lightweight CNN architectures that have been used in medical image classification and the diagnosis of breast cancer and prostate cancer. The CNN architecture was specifically designed to be used on resource‐constrained devices (smartphones, embedded systems, and other mobile devices). It is commonly used for detecting cardiovascular diseases, classifying ultrasound images, and classifying mammography images. Tiny CNN has several key benefits including low memory usage, fast inference times, power efficiency, and its ability to work on resource‐constrained devices including mobile and embedded systems. It also has its usability in medical devices, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and autonomous vehicles [\[49\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0049).
*   **NASNet**: NASNet (neural architecture search network) is a search‐based CNN architecture that has shown promising applications in medical image classification, diagnosis, and segmentation. NASNet was designed to be highly efficient and has achieved state‐of‐the‐art accuracy on the popular ImageNet dataset, with exceptional performance. With neural architecture search techniques, NASNet can automatically learn optimal network architectures, making it a powerful tool for various computer vision tasks, including medical image analysis [\[50\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0050).
*   **ESPNet**: ESPNet is another lightweight CNN architecture, designed for medical image classification and segmentation. It is particularly useful in classifying MRI, classifying CT imaging, and detecting prostate cancer. The model employed spatial pyramid architecture, channel shuffle operations, “depthwise separable convolutions,” hierarchical feature fusion, and spatial attention techniques to reduce memory usage and computational complexity and achieve high accuracy and fast inference for efficient feature extraction [\[51\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0051).
*   **EfficientNet**: EfficientNet is a family of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) proposed by Mingxing Tan and Quoc VL. The model is renowned for achieving state‐of‐the‐art accuracy in medical image classification with reduced computations and parameters when compared to other models. The EfficientNet model is specifically designed for classifying medical images, including CT scans, and detecting diabetic retinopathy. The EfficientNet family comprises various variants, such as EfficientNet‐B0 and EfficientNet‐B1, each offering a unique trade‐off between model size and accuracy for deployment in different applications [\[52\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0052).
*   **PeleeNet**: PeleeNet is also a lightweight neural network architecture optimized for the efficient classification of medical images. The model was introduced by Robert Cheng et al. in their paper “Pelee: A Real‐Time Object Detection System on Mobile Devices,” and PeleeNet is a streamlined variant of the singleshot detector (SSD) network, specifically designed for mobile and embedded devices. It uses a simple architecture with reduced computation requirements and parameters that enable real‐time medical image detection on resource‐constrained devices, making it an ideal solution for applications where computational resources are limited [\[53\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0053).

In summary, TinyML models and architectures, such as MobileNet, ShuffleNet, SqueezeNet, and Tiny CNN, have demonstrated exceptional promise in medical image classification and diagnosis, achieving outstanding accuracy and efficiency. These models are particularly valuable in resource‐constrained devices, including mobile devices and embedded systems, where computational resources and memory are limited. With techniques like model compression, quantization, and pruning, TinyML models can attain high accuracy with significantly reduced computational requirements, making them ideal for real‐time classification and diagnosis of medical images. As medical imaging continues to advance, TinyML models and architectures are poised to play a vital role in enabling accurate and efficient image classification, ultimately improving patient care and outcomes.

 

### 15.2.3 Application Areas of TinyML in Medical Image Classification and Diagnosis

The rapid advancement of medical imaging technologies has led to an increase in the number of medical images generated daily [\[54\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0054). However, a timely and accurate interpretation of these images was a challenge, particularly in real‐time scenarios [\[55\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0055). Recently, with the advent of TinyML, a solution has been provided for classification and diagnosis tasks. TinyML can run on resource‐constrained devices while still maintaining its high accuracy and real‐time processing abilities, making it a promising solution for timely diagnostics and remote healthcare services \[[6](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006), [8](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0008), [56](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0056)\]. In this section, we therefore study a comprehensive overview of TinyML applications in medical image classification and diagnosis, exploring their applicability in various medical imaging modalities, including CT, MRI, X‐rays, and ultrasound images. Some of those application areas include the following.

*   **Detection of Diseases**: TinyML can be used to detect several diseases, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, brain tumor, cardiovascular disease, diabetic retinopathy, pneumonia, skin, and lung, among others types. The model is utilized to analyze images to detect signs of infections in MRI, CT, X‐rays, and ultrasound images \[[57](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0057), [58](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0058)\].
*   **Classification of Medical Images**: TinyML can also be used to classify medical images into different categories, such as normal or abnormal, tumor or non‐tumor, and benign or malignant. TinyML has numerous applications in medical image classification, including skin disease classification, tumor disease classification, orthopedic disorder classification, and lung disease classification \[[57](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0057), [59](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0059)\].
*   **Segmentation of Medical Images**: TinyML is also used in segmenting medical images to identify specific structures or features such as organs, tumors, or tissues. The model has its applications in lesion segmentation, tissue segmentation, organ segmentation, and tumor segmentation. It can also segment different tissues such as muscle, bone, and fat \[[60](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0060), [61](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0061)\].
*   **Denoising of Medical Images**: TinyML can also be employed to remove noise from medical images, to improve their quality and diagnostic ability. It can be used to reduce noise in medical images, including CT, MRI, X‐ray, ultrasound, mammography, and fluoroscopy [\[62\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0062).

TinyML therefore has varying and vast applications in medical imaging including medical image classification, segmentation, disease detection, diagnosis, and image denoising, and it therefore has the potential to improve medical imaging by enabling efficient, accurate, and personalized diagnosis and treatment. It helps to improve accuracy and efficiency that enhances patient care and outcomes, reducing computational resources and energy consumption, among others.

 

## 15.3 Methodology

In this section, we present a description of three state‐of‐the‐art approaches in medical image classification and diagnosis. These methods include the following.

 

### 15.3.1 Machine Learning (ML)

Machine learning (ML) is an aspect of artificial intelligence (AI) technology that allows machines to learn from data, identify the patterns, and automatically make decisions without human intervention [\[76\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0076). In medical image classification and diagnosis, ML models play a vital role because they can learn from medical images and adapt to them, identify the patterns in those images, and produce reliable results on new image data, among other key characteristics. ML is also useful in medical imaging to interpret medical images employing computer‐aided design (CAD) and algorithms where it applies ML techniques, to CT scans, X‐ray scans, MRI scans, etc. The conventional ML models rely on structured datasets with predefined techniques for each step. However, new algorithms can adapt to missing data, ensuring robustness in disease classification and diagnosis [\[77\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0077).

 

### 15.3.2 Deep Learning (DL)

Deep learning (DL) is also a branch of machine learning that has been widely applied in computer vision and image processing. It utilizes multiple processing layers or multiple layers of complex structures that included multiple nonlinear transformations. Recently, various medical image processing and image recognition tasks have adopted deep learning methods on CT images, MRI images, ultrasound images, X‐ray images, pathological images, etc. Deep learning technology has applications in medical imaging to detect, classify, and segment infections. The key benefits of deep learning techniques lie in their ability to replace manual feature learning with unsupervised or semi‐supervised feature learning and hierarchical feature extraction efficiency. Some of the popular deep learning models used in classification tasks include GoogLeNet, VGGNet, and ResNet. In medical imaging, deep learning has demonstrated exceptional capabilities in segmenting diseases, discriminating between diseases, and classifying diseases [\[64\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0064).

 

### 15.3.3 TinyML

TinyML utilizes intelligence on edge layers and mobile devices, such as smartphones and tablets. TinyML techniques are designed to perform effectively on mobile devices with limited computational resources and battery restrictions. This technique focuses on deploying compressed and optimized machine learning models on low‐powered, tiny devices like micro‐controllers and embedded systems. TinyML was inspired by mobile machine learning features, including resource constraints, low latency, and moderate cost. The model emerged from technical breakthroughs in the IoT field and can be applied in various areas, particularly in medical image classification. TinyML technology addresses the need to apply intelligence in a wide range of applications previously hindered by the high power and computing requirements of standard machine learning models [\[78\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0078).

 

## 15.4 Results and Discussion

This section contains information on the medical imaging data used for this study, the popular evaluation metrics used to evaluate TinyML models, comparative analysis, and presentation of the results of our findings.

 

### 15.4.1 Description of Datasets Employed in this Work

Medical image classification and diagnosis play an important role in the healthcare industry. To develop and evaluate accurate classification models, researchers rely on various datasets. These datasets consist of labeled medical images, annotated with essential information such as the presence of severity and other relevant features of the disease. This section reviews popular datasets used in medical image classification research, focusing on three popular applications: breast cancer, brain tumor, and COVID‐19 diagnosis.

*   **BreakHis (Breast Cancer on Histopathology Images)**: BreakHis dataset was collected to be used in medical image classification, for binary and multiclass problems. The dataset consists of 7,909 microscopic images of breast tumor samples collected from 82 patients with different magnification factors, including 10![times](images/c15-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math>, 100![times](images/c15-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math>, 200![times](images/c15-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math>, and 400![times](images/c15-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math> of histopathological images of BC. The dataset is divided into 5,429 malignant image samples and 2,480 benign image samples. Those image samples were pre‐processed and resized to 224 ![times](images/c15-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math> 224 pixels [\[79\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0079).
*   **Brain Tumor MRI**: Brain tumor MRI dataset consists of medical images of human brain MRI scans, consisting of information about the location, presence, and characteristics of the brain tumor. Those MRI images are classified into 4 classes, namely, pituitary, glioma, meningioma, and no tumor. This dataset is essential for training computer vision algorithms to automate brain tumor detection, to help with early diagnosis and treatment planning [\[80\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0080).
*   **COVID‐19 CXR Dataset**: This dataset comprises COVID‐19 positive and negative chest X‐ray (CXR) images obtained from various sources, including the BIMCV‐COVID19+ database, a German medical school, Eurorad, SIRM, Kaggle, GitHub, and other COVID‐19 repositories. The images, representing both male and female subjects, were curated to facilitate detection of lung damage caused by COVID‐19 pneumonia. Specifically, subjects with confirmed cases and clinical symptoms are likely to exhibit abnormal lung X‐ray patterns, allowing researchers to develop accurate diagnostic models for early detection and treatment planning [\[81\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0081). Some of the sample images are presented in [Figures 15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0002)–[15.4\[\[dot\]\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0004).

 

### 15.4.2 Model Evaluation Metrics

Evaluation metrics are essential in medical image classification where they help to evaluate the performance of machine learning models. In this work, we focus on common and benchmark evaluation metrics comprising true positive (TP), false positive (FP), false negative (FN), and true negative (TN). TP refers to correctly classified positive images, FP refers to incorrectly classified positive images, FN represents incorrectly classified negative images, and TN refers to correctly predicted negative images. We analyze our findings using five performance evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision, sensitivity (recall), specificity, and F1 score. This can be defined and calculated as follows.

**Figure 15.2** Sample images of breast cancer data.

![Figure 15.3 Sample images of brain tumor data.](images/c15f003.png)

**Figure 15.3** Sample images of brain tumor data.

*   **Accuracy**: Accuracy is a fundamental evaluation metric in medical imaging tasks, where it measures the percentage of correctly classified images by the proposed model. The metric provides an overall assessment of the model performance. However, accuracy can be influenced by class imbalance in the datasets, potentially masking underlying issues. However, the higher the accuracy, the better the performance of the model [\[82\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0082). Accuracy is therefore calculated as in equation ([15.1](#c15.xhtml#c15-disp-0001)):

*   **Precision**: Precision is a vital evaluation metric in medical imaging, calculating the proportion of true positives among all possible positive classifications made by the model. This metric is particularly sensitive to false positives, making it invaluable in applications where incorrect detections have significant consequences, such as cancer diagnosis or disease monitoring. A higher precision value indicates fewer false positives, ensuring that positive predictions are reliable [\[83\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0083). Precision is calculated as in equation ([15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-disp-0002)): (15.2)![upper P r e c i s i o n equals StartFraction upper T upper P Over upper T upper P plus upper F upper P EndFraction](images/c15-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> 
*   **Sensitivity (Recall)**: Sensitivity, also known as recall, measures the proportion of actual positive possibilities that are correctly evaluated by the developed model. This metric is particularly useful in applications where missing true positives has significant effects, like in medical diagnosis or disease detection [\[84\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0084). We can calculate sensitivity as in equation ([15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-disp-0003)): (15.3)![upper S e n s i t i v i t y left-parenthesis upper R e c a l l right-parenthesis equals StartFraction upper T upper P Over upper T upper P plus upper F upper N EndFraction](images/c15-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>S</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>t</mi><mi>y</mi><mspace width="2.77695pt"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>N</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> 
*   **Specificity**: Specificity measures the value of actual negative occurrences that are correctly classified by the model, which provided insight into its ability to avoid false positives. This metric is crucial in situations where false positives can lead to unnecessary treatment, costly interventions, or adverse consequences. High specificity indicates that more actual negative instances are accurately identified, reducing the risk of unnecessary actions [\[85\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0085). Specificity is calculated as in equation ([15.4](#c15.xhtml#c15-disp-0004)):

    .
    
*   **F1 Score**: F1 score metric is a widely used measure of performance in computer vision, providing a balanced evaluation of recall and precision through its harmonic mean. A higher F1 score indicates a better balance between recall and precision that makes it a valuable metric in applications where both false positives and false negatives are important. Specifically, the F1 score is extensively utilized in medical image classification, detection, and segmentation [\[86\]](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0086). ### 15.4.3 Results of Key Findings

In this section, we present the performance evaluation results ([Figures 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0005)–[15.7](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0007)) of existing and recent state‐of‐the‐art methods used in the classification and diagnosis tasks for breast cancer, brain tumors, and COVID‐19 diseases.

*   **Results of Breast Cancer Models**: From [Table 15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-tbl-0003), the accuracy results of the latest models are as follows: 99.87% on ResNet50, 99.86% on lightweight CNN, 99.28% on DenseNet, 99.15% on SVM and 98.95% on VGG19. The ResNet50 model was observed to achieve the best result; however, the lightweight and TinyML models achieved comparable results despite having lighter models with lower resources. Regarding precision metrics, custom and lightweight CNN achieved a perfect score of 100%, outperforming machine learning models like SVM (99%) and deep learning models like VGG19 (98.95%), ResNet50 (98.77%), and DenseNet (97%). For sensitivity, the SVM machine learning model achieved the best result (99.0%), while the DenseNet, VGG19, and ResNet50 deep learning models achieved comparable results but used more resources and were not suitable on devices limited in resources. The specificity results were 98.95% for VGG19, 89.69% for VGG, and 84% for deep belief networks. Furthermore, DenseNet achieved the best F1 score result (99.48%). In particular, TinyML achieved comparable results with significantly lower memory usage, making it suitable for real‐time applications.

### 15.4.4 Discussion

This section presents a discussion of the significance and interpretation of key findings within the context of classification of medical imaging in real‐time scenarios. Furthermore, we evaluate the results of the study highlighting areas for improvement by exploring the advantages and disadvantages of TinyML models compared to other approaches including the following:

**Traditional Machine Learning (ML) Approaches**: From our findings, we observed the following key differences between TinyML and traditional ML:

*   TinyML is designed for resource‐constrained devices, while traditional ML was designed for powerful hardware.
*   TinyML models are compact, efficient, and optimized for inference, while traditional ML models are complex, large, and optimized for training.
*   TinyML typically uses pre‐processing techniques like pruning, while traditional ML typically uses techniques like deep learning and ensemble methods.
*   TinyML focuses on real‐time inference and low latency, while traditional ML focuses on high accuracy and large datasets.
*   TinyML is used for edge AI applications, while traditional ML is often used for cloud‐based applications.

**Deep Learning (DL) Approaches**: The following are some of the comparisons and key differences between TinyML and other deep learning approaches:

*   TinyML employs lightweight models such as MobileNet, SqueezeNet, etc., while DL uses large, complex models like CNNs, recurrent neural networks (RNNs), etc.
*   TinyML uses shallow model architectures, while DL uses deep model architectures with many layers.
*   TinyML focuses on efficiency, interpretability, and generalization, while DL focuses on high accuracy, often at the cost of interpretability.
*   TinyML requires a small amount of training data, while DL requires a large amount of training data.
*   TinyML typically uses techniques like feature engineering, regularization, and early stopping, while DL typically uses techniques like batch normalization, dropout, and transfer learning.
*   TinyML is designed for resource‐constrained devices, while DL requires powerful hardware and large datasets.

We can therefore deduce that in medical image classification, TinyML offers several advantages over other approaches, including

*   TinyML approach enables real‐time medical image diagnosis, which allows for timely and accurate diagnoses, improved patient outcomes, and enhanced healthcare delivery.
*   TinyML is also suitable for battery‐powered devices and remote applications, which has led to significant reductions in power consumption and enables the development of efficient, portable, and wearable medical devices that can perform image classification tasks in real time.
*   TinyML allows for efficient storage and transmission. The models are designed to be compact and efficient, with small model sizes that offer several advantages in reduced memory usage, and faster inference.
*   TinyML models can achieve comparable accuracy when compared with larger models. They are designed to achieve comparable accuracy to larger models despite their smaller size and computational requirements.
*   TinyML enables analysis on edge devices, which offers several benefits including reducing latency and dependence on cloud systems.
*   TinyML enables medical image analysis in resource‐constrained areas, achieving faster diagnosis and treatment, a cost‐effective solution, that offers scalable and sustainable medical image analysis benefits.
*   TinyML can update and refine models with new data, and this ensures the medical image analysis remains accurate and effective.
*   TinyML enables autonomous medical devices, such as robots and drones, to perform remote healthcare tasks that expand access to medical care.

**Limitations of the Study**: Although the study on TinyML for real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis showed significant potential, it also has several limitations, including the following:

*   The compact nature and limited model size of typical TinyML models may compromise their ability to capture complex patterns in medical images.
*   The limitation in terms of dataset size may not provide a comprehensive representation of all medical image diagnosis scenarios and may affect model training and performance.
*   The memory and computational limitations of most mobile and edge devices reduce the processing power, which may affect the model's performance.
*   Issues with a class imbalance in most medical imaging datasets result in the under‐representation of certain diseases, which impacts the model's performance.

Future research in developing TinyML models should provide solutions to these challenges in order to further improve their accuracy and suitability of the model in medical image analysis.

Future research in developing TinyML models should focus on addressing these challenges to further enhance their accuracy, robustness, and suitability for medical image analysis applications.

 

### 15.4.5 Lessons Learned and Future Research Direction

Some of the key lessons learned from the study on TinyML for real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis include the following:

*   The novel TinyML models can achieve high accuracy in medical image classification and diagnosis despite computational resource constraints.
*   Class imbalance issues must be considered when preparing and pre‐processing datasets.
*   The size and diversity of the dataset can affect the generalization of TinyML model.
*   Using appropriate model optimization techniques can enhance model performance.
*   Real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis improve speed and diagnostic accuracy.
*   TinyML‐based models enable point‐of‐care and real‐time diagnostics.
*   Transfer learning techniques applied to pre‐trained models can improve performance.
*   Hyperparameter tuning is very important for optimal model performance.
*   Combining models through ensemble methods improves model robustness.

Despite the existing challenges, the future research directions of TinyML in medical image classification and diagnosis are promising. More research in areas such as transfer learning, distributed learning, and the collection of larger and diverse datasets will continue to advance the field to achieve robust, faster, more accurate, and accessible diagnosis and treatment of various medical conditions.

 

## 15.5 Conclusion

In conclusion, TinyML has the potential to improve the diagnosis and classification of medical images in real‐time scenarios, particularly on devices limited by resources, while maintaining an accurate and accessible diagnosis and treatment of various medical conditions. The model has various applications in the diagnosis of medical images, including tumor detection and classification, disease diagnosis, image segmentation, and denoising. Among these numerous benefits, its efficiency and effectiveness make it an invaluable tool in medical imaging.

Biometric Authentication in TinyML: Opportunities and Challenges
