## 16.1 Introduction

In the era of ubiquitous computing and the Internet of Things (IoT), securing access to devices and protecting sensitive information has become a paramount concern \[[1](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0001), [2](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0002)\]. Traditional authentication methods, such as passwords and personal identification numbers (PINs), often fall short in providing the necessary level of security and user convenience required by the diverse range of IoT applications. Biometric authentication, which relies on the unique physiological or behavioral characteristics of individuals, has emerged as a promising solution to address these challenges [\[3\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003).

The integration of biometric authentication techniques into tiny machine learning (TinyML) systems has gained significant attention in recent years [\[4\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0004). TinyML refers to the deployment of machine learning algorithms on resource‐constrained devices, such as microcontrollers and low‐power IoT nodes \[[5](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0005), [6](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0006)\]. By combining the power of biometric authentication with the efficiency and scalability of TinyML, it becomes possible to develop secure and user‐friendly authentication mechanisms for a wide range of IoT applications.

This chapter explores the opportunities and challenges associated with the integration of biometric authentication techniques into TinyML systems. It provides a comprehensive overview of various biometric modalities, including fingerprint recognition, facial recognition, iris scanning, voice recognition, gait recognition, and ear recognition [\[7\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0007). The chapter delves into the fundamental concepts, algorithms, and performance metrics associated with each modality, highlighting their strengths and limitations in the context of resource‐constrained environments.

One of the key challenges addressed in this chapter is the adaptation of biometric techniques for TinyML systems. The limited computational power, memory capacity, and energy budget of microcontrollers pose significant constraints on the implementation of biometric algorithms. The chapter discusses various strategies for developing resource‐efficient biometric algorithms, such as lightweight feature extraction, template compression, efficient matching, and hardware acceleration. It also explores the hardware considerations for integrating biometric sensors into IoT devices, focusing on factors such as sensor selection, form factor, power consumption, and interface requirements.

The chapter presents a comparative analysis of different biometric authentication methods, evaluating their performance based on metrics such as accuracy, efficiency, and user acceptance. The analysis provides valuable insights into the trade‐offs and suitability of each modality for specific TinyML applications. It also highlights the potential of multimodal biometric authentication, where multiple biometric traits are combined to enhance the overall security and reliability of the system.

Furthermore, the chapter discusses the privacy and ethical considerations associated with the deployment of biometric authentication in IoT devices. It emphasizes the importance of establishing clear privacy policies, implementing robust data protection measures, and adhering to relevant regulations and standards. The chapter also explores future research directions in the field of biometric authentication for TinyML systems, including the development of novel biometric modalities, optimization techniques for energy efficiency and real‐time performance, and the integration of biometric authentication with other security mechanisms.

The key points covered in this chapter are

*   Overview of biometric authentication techniques and their relevance to TinyML systems
*   Comparative analysis of different biometric modalities, including fingerprint, facial, iris, voice, gait, and ear recognition
*   Adaptation of biometric techniques for resource‐constrained environments, focusing on resource‐efficient algorithms and hardware considerations
*   Future research directions and opportunities in the field of biometric authentication for TinyML systems

The chapter is organized as follows: [Section 16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0002) presents the related work. [Section 16.3](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0003) provides an overview of various biometric authentication techniques, discussing their fundamental concepts, algorithms, and performance metrics. [Section 16.4](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0011) presents a comparative analysis of these techniques, evaluating their strengths and limitations in the context of TinyML systems. [Section 16.5](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0021) focuses on the adaptation of biometric techniques for resource‐constrained environments, exploring resource‐efficient algorithms and hardware considerations. Finally, [Sections 16.6](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0025) and [16.7](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0026) conclude the chapter by summarizing the key insights and emphasizing the potential of biometric authentication in enhancing the security and user experience of TinyML systems.

 

## 16.2 Related Work

The integration of biometric authentication techniques into TinyML systems has garnered significant attention from the research community in recent years. This section provides an overview of the relevant literature, highlighting the key contributions and advancements in this field.

Agarwal and Joshi [\[8\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0008) proposed a secure and effective self‐error‐correctable physical unclonable function (PUF) for tiny IoT nodes. They employed systematic Golay code and decoding algorithms to improve the reliability of PUF‐based authentication in IoT applications. Using an efficient error correction mechanism, their hardware implementation on an field‐programmable gate array (FPGA) board demonstrated good performance with 45% uniqueness and 97% reliability.

Awad et al. [\[9\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0009) conducted a comprehensive review of artificial intelligence (AI)‐powered biometrics for IoT security. They analyzed the interdependencies between AI, biometrics, and IoT domains, covering the applications of AI and biometrics in the context of IoT. The authors highlighted the current challenges and future research directions for the deployment of intelligent biometrics in various IoT application domains.

Coelho et al. [\[10\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0010) presented a security management approach for authentication that combines two convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for the biometric identification of users. Their approach relies on federated learning (FL) to support data management and privacy by training decentralized models collaboratively without effective data exchange. The authors combined photoplethysmography (PPG) and electrocardiogram signals to improve identification accuracy and establish multimodal authentication.

Cremonezi et al. [\[11\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0011) provided a comprehensive state‐of‐the‐art review of identity management (IdM) systems, presenting the fundamental concepts and challenges when developing an IdM for IoT applications. They explored existing works that propose solutions to address at least one component of IdMs in response to the current challenges, including the scalability of identity provisioning, authentication for IoT devices, and concerns regarding the performance and management of the authorization processes.

Ding et al. [\[12\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0012) introduced a fuzzy‐based temporal convolutional autoencoder (FTCAE) framework for gait recognition from inertial gait time series. They incorporated an interval type‐2 fuzzy set (IT2FS) dense layer to handle uncertainties, imprecision, and noise of feature maps, enabling the learning of curious representations in fuzzy latent space. Their experimentation on public gait sensory datasets validated the efficiency of the proposed FTCAE with accuracies of 98.48% and 95.11% for authentication and identification, respectively.

Galasso et al. [\[13\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0013) focused on classifying subjects' physical activity levels using kinematic features provided by wearable wireless inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors. They employed the neighborhood component analysis (NCA) algorithm to process the statistical feature space and select the most significant ones. Their approach resulted in a significant increase in accuracy for various classifiers, with an improvement of approximately 20%.

Kamruzzaman and Alruwaili [\[14\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0014) proposed a new methodology named optimizing computer vision with AI‐enabled technology (OCV‐AI) for solving image classification, object classification, and facial recognition problems in 6G wireless networks. They introduced deep learning 6G proposed frameworks (Dl‐6G) to recognize pattern recognition and intelligent management systems and provide a driven methodology planned to be provisioned automatically.

Khalid et al. [\[15\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0015) summarized the state‐of‐the‐art approaches for preserving privacy in AI‐based healthcare applications. They elaborated on prominent privacy‐preserving techniques such as FL and hybrid techniques, along with potential privacy attacks, security challenges, and future directions.

Oliveira et al. [\[4\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0004) comprehensively reviewed the emerging concept of the Internet of Intelligent Things (IoIT), adopting an integrated perspective centered on the areas of embedded systems, edge computing, and machine learning. They performed an extensive state‐of‐the‐art survey to identify recent works that have implemented TinyML models on different off‐the‐shelf embedded devices, analyzing the development of practical solutions and discussing recent research trends and future perspectives.

Praveen Kumar and Priyanka [\[16\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0016) provided a comprehensive overview of the security issues related to various hardware‐level attacks, memory attacks, hardware Trojans, and their countermeasures in different domains. They investigated the use of primitive hardware techniques, such as physically unclonable functions (PUFs), to generate unique keys for devices by preventing unauthorized access to the hardware during authentication for different domains.

Sodhro et al. [\[17\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0017) conducted a survey on intelligent authentication for securing IoT‐5G devices deployed in the healthcare domain. They reviewed IoT‐5G device authentication, radio‐frequency fingerprinting, and mutual authentication and envisioned the use of AI to integrate the attributes of the physical layer and 5G networks to empower intelligent healthcare devices.

Wan et al. [\[18\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0018) proposed a novel approach for biometric authentication using PPG signals and deep learning techniques. They designed and trained a multiscale feature fusion deep learning (MFFD) model that takes the relevant features extracted from PPG signals as input and learns to differentiate between individuals based on their unique PPG patterns. Their evaluation demonstrated the effectiveness of the PPG‐based biometric authentication system, achieving high accuracy while addressing key security concerns.

These studies collectively contribute to the growing body of knowledge on biometric authentication techniques for TinyML systems. They encompass various aspects, including the development of resource‐efficient algorithms, the integration of AI and deep learning techniques, the exploration of novel biometric modalities, and the consideration of privacy and security challenges. The insights gained from these works provide a solid foundation for further research and development in this field, paving the way for the widespread adoption of biometric authentication in IoT and TinyML applications.

Despite the significant advancements in biometric authentication techniques for TinyML systems, there is still a need for a comprehensive and systematic approach that addresses the unique challenges posed by resource‐constrained environments. Our work aims to fill this gap by providing a holistic framework that encompasses the adaptation of biometric techniques, the development of resource‐efficient algorithms, and the consideration of privacy and security aspects, enabling the effective deployment of biometric authentication in a wide range of TinyML applications.

 

## 16.3 Overview of Biometric Authentication Techniques

Biometric authentication has emerged as a robust and reliable means of verifying user identity in various domains, including access control, financial transactions, and personal device security \[[19](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0019), [20](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0020)\]. This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of the most prevalent biometric modalities, focusing on their fundamental principles, algorithmic foundations, and suitability for integration into TinyML systems. By examining the strengths and limitations of each technique, we aim to guide researchers and practitioners in selecting the most appropriate biometric solution for their specific TinyML application.

 

### 16.3.1 Fingerprint Recognition

Fingerprint recognition stands as one of the most widely adopted biometric authentication techniques, owing to its long‐standing use in forensic investigations and its high accuracy in identifying individuals \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [21](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0021)\]. The unique patterns of ridges and valleys on the surface of a finger, formed during embryonic development, provide a distinctive and permanent signature that can be captured and analyzed for authentication purposes [\[21\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0021).

The flowchart in [Figure 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0001) delineates the comprehensive process of fingerprint recognition, highlighting each critical stage from acquisition to matching. Initially, a high‐resolution fingerprint image is obtained through dedicated sensors, followed by preprocessing techniques to enhance image quality. Subsequently, feature extraction algorithms identify unique characteristics such as minutiae points and additional features like ridge orientation and texture descriptors. The matching phase involves comparing the query template with stored database templates using sophisticated algorithms. This process is underscored by the inherent properties of fingerprints, including their unique patterns, permanence, and high reliability in identification.

![Figure 16.1 Fingerprint recognition process.](images/c16f001.png)

**Figure 16.1** Fingerprint recognition process.

At the core of fingerprint recognition lie two fundamental concepts: feature extraction and matching [\[22\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0022). The first step involves acquiring a high‐resolution image of the fingerprint using a dedicated sensor, such as an optical, capacitive, or ultrasonic scanner \[[9](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0009), [17](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0017)\]. Preprocessing techniques, including image enhancement, segmentation, and normalization, are then applied to improve the quality and consistency of the captured image.

Feature extraction algorithms subsequently analyze the preprocessed image to identify and encode the discriminative characteristics of the fingerprint. The most common features employed in fingerprint recognition are minutiae points, which represent the local discontinuities in the ridge patterns, such as ridge endings and bifurcations [\[22\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0022). Minutiae‐based methods, such as the widely used crossing number (CN) algorithm, detect and map these points, recording their spatial coordinates and orientation \[[9](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0009), [21](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0021)\].

In addition to minutiae, other feature sets, such as ridge orientation maps, frequency maps, and texture descriptors, can be extracted to complement the minutiae‐based representation \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [17](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0017)\]. These additional features capture the global and local structural properties of the fingerprint, enhancing the discriminative power of the biometric template.

Once the features are extracted, the matching process compares the query fingerprint template with the enrolled templates stored in a database. Matching algorithms, such as the minutia cylinder code (MCC) and the iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm, assess the similarity between two templates by aligning their feature sets and computing a matching score. The comparison can be performed in a one‐to‐one (verification) or one‐to‐many (identification) manner, depending on the application requirements.

Despite its widespread adoption and proven accuracy, fingerprint recognition faces challenges when applied to TinyML systems. The limited computational resources and memory constraints of microcontrollers necessitate the development of lightweight and efficient algorithms for feature extraction and matching. Furthermore, the form factor and power consumption of fingerprint sensors must be optimized to ensure seamless integration into IoT devices.

Ongoing research efforts in fingerprint recognition for TinyML focus on developing compact and energy‐efficient sensing technologies, such as thin‐film transistor (TFT) and microelectromechanical system (MEMS) sensors \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [21](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0021)\]. Additionally, researchers are exploring the use of deep learning techniques, such as CNNs, to enhance the robustness and accuracy of fingerprint recognition algorithms in resource‐constrained environments.

The flowchart in [Figure 16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0002) illustrates the challenges and research directions in fingerprint recognition for TinyML systems. It identifies the primary challenges, such as limited computational resources, the need for lightweight algorithms, and sensor optimization. Research directions focus on developing compact sensors, optimizing algorithms, applying deep learning techniques, and ensuring integration with IoT devices. These efforts aim to overcome TinyML system limitations and enhance performance in resource‐constrained applications.

![Figure 16.2 Challenges and research directions in fingerprint recognition for TinyML.](images/c16f002.png)

**Figure 16.2** Challenges and research directions in fingerprint recognition for TinyML.

As the demand for secure and convenient authentication in IoT devices continues to grow, fingerprint recognition remains a promising biometric modality for TinyML systems. By addressing the challenges of resource efficiency and sensor miniaturization, researchers can unlock the full potential of fingerprint‐based authentication in a wide range of TinyML applications, from smart homes and wearables to industrial IoT and beyond.

 

### 16.3.2 Facial Recognition

Facial recognition has gained significant attention as a biometric authentication technique due to its non‐intrusive nature and the ubiquity of cameras in modern devices \[[9](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0009), [14](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0014)\]. Leveraging the unique features and geometry of an individual's face, this modality offers a natural and intuitive means of verifying identity in various applications, including access control, surveillance, and user authentication on mobile devices \[[23](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0023), [24](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0024)\].

The process of facial recognition involves several key stages: face detection, preprocessing, feature extraction, and matching \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [25](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0025)\]. Face detection algorithms, such as the Viola–Jones framework, and deep learning‐based methods, like Single Shot MultiBox Detector (SSD) and You Only Look Once (YOLO), localize and isolate the facial region from the input image or video frame. These algorithms exploit the distinctive characteristics of facial features, such as eyes, nose, and mouth, to rapidly identify faces in real time \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [25](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0025)\].

Once the facial region is detected, preprocessing techniques are applied to normalize the image and mitigate the impact of variations in illumination, pose, and expression. Common preprocessing steps include face alignment, which involves rotating and scaling the face to a canonical pose, and illumination normalization, which compensates for uneven lighting conditions using techniques like histogram equalization and homomorphic filtering.

Feature extraction is a critical step in facial recognition, as it aims to capture the discriminative information that distinguishes one individual from another. Traditional approaches, such as principal component analysis (PCA) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA), project the high‐dimensional facial data onto a lower‐dimensional subspace, retaining the most salient features. These methods, often referred to as holistic or appearance‐based techniques, treat the entire face as a single entity and learn a compact representation of facial variations \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [25](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0025)\].

In recent years, deep learning techniques have revolutionized facial recognition by enabling the learning of hierarchical and abstract features directly from raw pixel data. CNNs, such as DeepFace, FaceNet, and ArcFace, have achieved remarkable performance in face verification and identification tasks \[[26](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0026)–[28](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0028)\]. These networks employ a series of convolutional and pooling layers to extract local and global facial features, followed by fully connected layers that learn a compact face embedding \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [25](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0025)\].

The derived facial features, whether obtained through traditional methods or deep learning, are then compared during the matching stage to determine the identity of an individual \[[29](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0029), [30](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0030)\]. Matching algorithms compute the similarity between the query face and the enrolled face templates stored in a database. Common similarity measures include Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, and learned similarity metrics optimized by the deep learning models.

The flowchart in [Figure 16.3](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0003) illustrates the key stages and methodologies in the facial recognition process. It begins with face detection using algorithms like Viola–Jones, SSD, and YOLO, followed by preprocessing to normalize the image and adjust for illumination and pose variations. Feature extraction employs both traditional methods like PCA and LDA and modern CNN‐based approaches, including DeepFace, FaceNet, and ArcFace. The final stage, matching, compares the extracted features with database templates using similarity measures such as Euclidean distance and cosine similarity. This structured approach highlights the integration of advanced techniques to enhance the accuracy and reliability of facial recognition systems.

![Figure 16.3 Facial recognition process.](images/c16f003.png)

**Figure 16.3** Facial recognition process.

Facial recognition systems face several challenges, particularly when deployed on resource‐constrained TinyML platforms. The high dimensionality of facial data and the complexity of deep learning models pose significant computational and memory requirements. To address these challenges, researchers have explored techniques such as model compression, quantization, and pruning to reduce the size and computational cost of facial recognition models without compromising accuracy.

Another critical aspect of facial recognition in TinyML is the acquisition of high‐quality face images under varying environmental conditions. Low‐resolution cameras, limited processing power, and constrained energy budgets of IoT devices necessitate the development of efficient face detection and preprocessing algorithms that can operate in real time with minimal overhead.

Privacy concerns surrounding the collection and use of facial data have also spurred research into privacy‐preserving facial recognition techniques. Approaches such as FL, homomorphic encryption, and differential privacy enable the training and deployment of facial recognition models without the need for centralized storage of sensitive biometric data.

 

### 16.3.3 Iris Scanning

Iris scanning has emerged as a highly accurate and reliable biometric authentication technique, leveraging the intricate patterns of the human iris for identity verification [\[3\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003). The iris, the colorful ring surrounding the pupil, contains a complex arrangement of features, including furrows, ridges, and crypts, which remain stable throughout an individual's lifetime \[[7](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0007), [31](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0031)\]. These unique characteristics, along with the iris's protected location behind the cornea, make it an ideal candidate for biometric authentication in various domains, including high‐security access control and border control systems.

The process of iris recognition begins with image acquisition, where a specialized camera captures a high‐resolution image of the eye under near‐infrared (NIR) illumination. NIR light is preferred due to its ability to penetrate the surface of the iris and reveal the underlying texture details, while minimizing reflections and artifacts caused by ambient light \[[32](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0032), [33](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0033)\].

Preprocessing techniques are then applied to the captured image to isolate the iris region from surrounding structures, such as the pupil, sclera, and eyelids \[[32](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0032), [34](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0034)\]. This segmentation step typically involves a combination of edge detection, Hough transform, and active contour models to precisely localize the iris boundaries. Once segmented, the iris region undergoes normalization, which unwraps the circular iris into a rectangular block of fixed dimensions, accounting for variations in pupil size and image orientation.

Feature extraction is a crucial step in iris recognition, aiming to capture the discriminative information within the normalized iris texture. The most widely adopted approach is Daugman's algorithm, which applies 2D Gabor wavelets to the iris image to extract a binary feature vector known as the IrisCode. The Gabor wavelets, with their ability to capture both spatial and frequency information, effectively encode the local and global iris patterns into a compact representation \[[29](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0029), [35](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0035)\].

Other feature extraction techniques have also been explored, including the use of discrete cosine transform (DCT), wavelet packets, and deep learning‐based methods. These approaches aim to capture complementary iris features and enhance the discriminative power of the extracted representation.

During the matching stage, the extracted iris features are compared against a database of enrolled iris templates to determine the identity of an individual. The comparison is typically performed using the Hamming distance, which measures the dissimilarity between two binary IrisCodes. A decision threshold is applied to the Hamming distance to classify the comparison as a match or a non‐match.

[Figure 16.4](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0004) illustrates the process of iris recognition, highlighting the sequential stages from image acquisition to matching. The process begins with capturing a high‐resolution image of the eye under NIR illumination. Preprocessing techniques then isolate the iris, segment the image, and normalize it. Feature extraction is performed using methods such as Daugman's algorithm and other techniques, followed by the matching stage, which compares the extracted features with database templates using similarity measures like the Hamming distance.

![Figure 16.4 Iris recognition process.](images/c16f004.png)

**Figure 16.4** Iris recognition process.

Deploying iris recognition on TinyML platforms presents several challenges due to the resource constraints of microcontrollers. The high‐resolution imaging requirements and the computational complexity of iris segmentation and feature extraction algorithms demand efficient implementations that can operate within the limited memory and processing power of TinyML devices.

Researchers have explored various techniques to optimize iris recognition for resource‐constrained environments. These include the use of lightweight segmentation algorithms, such as the integro‐differential operator and the Hough transform, which reduce the computational burden while maintaining accurate iris localization. Feature extraction methods based on compressed sensing and sparse representations have also been investigated to minimize the storage and processing requirements of iris templates.

[Figure 16.5](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0005) outlines the properties, challenges, and research directions for iris recognition, particularly in the context of TinyML platforms. It underscores the high accuracy and reliability of iris patterns, their security advantages, and key applications. The challenges include limited resources and computational complexity, while research directions focus on algorithm optimization, compact sensors, and robust preprocessing techniques to handle varying conditions.

![Figure 16.5 Iris recognition: properties, challenges, and research directions.](images/c16f005.png)

**Figure 16.5** Iris recognition: properties, challenges, and research directions.

In addition to computational efficiency, the integration of iris scanning into TinyML systems must address the challenges of image acquisition in uncontrolled environments. The development of compact and low‐power NIR cameras, along with robust preprocessing algorithms that can handle variations in lighting, distance, and user cooperation, is crucial for the practical deployment of iris recognition in IoT devices.

 

### 16.3.4 Other Emerging Biometric Modalities

While fingerprint recognition, facial recognition, and iris scanning have established themselves as the most widely adopted biometric authentication techniques, researchers continue to explore novel and emerging modalities to address the limitations of traditional approaches and cater to the diverse requirements of TinyML applications. This subsection delves into three promising biometric modalities: voice recognition, gait recognition, and ear recognition, discussing their principles, advantages, and challenges in the context of TinyML systems.

 

#### 16.3.4.1 Voice Recognition

Voice recognition, also known as speaker recognition, leverages the unique acoustic characteristics of an individual's voice for biometric authentication [\[36\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0036). The human voice contains a wealth of information, including the fundamental frequency, pitch, and timbre, which are determined by the physical structure of the vocal tract and learned speaking habits. Voice recognition systems aim to capture and analyze these distinctive features to verify or identify speakers.

The process of voice recognition typically involves two main stages: feature extraction and matching \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [37](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0037)\]. During feature extraction, the speech signal is segmented into short frames, and various acoustic features are computed from each frame. Common feature extraction techniques include Mel‐frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), linear predictive coding (LPC), and perceptual linear prediction (PLP). These features capture the spectral and temporal characteristics of the speech signal, providing a compact representation of the speaker's voice.

Matching algorithms then compare the extracted features against a database of enrolled speaker templates to determine the identity of the speaker. Techniques such as Gaussian mixture models (GMMs), hidden Markov models (HMMs), and deep learning‐based approaches like CNNs and long short‐term memory (LSTM) networks have been successfully applied to voice recognition tasks \[[37](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0037), [38](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0038)\].

[Figure 16.6](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0006) illustrates the voice recognition process, detailing the sequential stages from feature extraction to matching. Initially, the speech signal is segmented into short frames, and acoustic features such as MFCCs, LPC, and PLP are computed. These features capture the spectral and temporal characteristics of the voice. The extracted features are then compared with speaker templates in a database using techniques like GMMs, HMMs, CNNs, and LSTM networks \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [37](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0037), [38](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0038)\].

![Figure 16.6 Voice recognition process.](images/c16f006.png)

**Figure 16.6** Voice recognition process.

The integration of voice recognition into TinyML systems offers several advantages. Voice‐based authentication provides a hands‐free and natural user experience, making it suitable for applications where physical contact with the device is inconvenient or impractical. Moreover, the ubiquity of microphones in IoT devices enables the seamless acquisition of speech data for biometric processing.

However, voice recognition in TinyML faces challenges related to resource constraints and environmental factors. The limited computational power and memory of microcontrollers necessitate the development of lightweight feature extraction and matching algorithms that can operate efficiently on TinyML platforms. Additionally, the presence of background noise, variations in recording conditions, and the impact of emotions and health conditions on an individual's voice can affect the accuracy and robustness of voice recognition systems.

Researchers have explored techniques to address these challenges, such as noise reduction algorithms, feature normalization methods, and domain adaptation techniques to improve the performance of voice recognition in diverse acoustic environments. The use of deep learning models, particularly those optimized for resource‐constrained devices, has shown promise in enhancing the accuracy and generalization ability of voice recognition systems in TinyML applications.

 

#### 16.3.4.2 Gait Recognition

Gait recognition is an emerging biometric modality that utilizes an individual's walking pattern for authentication \[[39](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0039), [40](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0040)\]. The human gait is a complex and idiosyncratic motion that involves the coordination of various body parts, including the legs, arms, and torso. Gait recognition systems capture and analyze the spatiotemporal characteristics of an individual's gait to extract unique features for biometric identification [\[41\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0041).

The process of gait recognition typically involves the following steps: data acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, and matching. Data acquisition is performed using various sensors, such as cameras, pressure sensors, or IMUs, which capture the motion dynamics of the individual. Preprocessing techniques, including background subtraction, silhouette extraction, and gait cycle detection, are applied to isolate the relevant gait information from the raw sensor data \[[13](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0013), [42](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0042)\].

Feature extraction methods aim to capture the discriminative characteristics of the gait pattern. Approaches like the gait energy image (GEI) and the gait entropy image (GEnI) generate compact 2D representations of the gait by averaging the silhouettes over a complete gait cycle. Other techniques, such as the use of spatial‐temporal motion descriptors, kinematic features, and deep learning‐based feature learning, have also been explored to capture the dynamics and variability of gait patterns \[[12](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0012), [42](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0042)\].

Matching algorithms compare the extracted gait features against a database of enrolled templates to determine the identity of an individual. Distance metrics, such as Euclidean distance and dynamic time warping (DTW), are commonly used to measure the similarity between gait features. Machine learning classifiers, including support vector machines (SVMs) and neural networks, have also been employed for gait recognition \[[13](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0013), [39](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0039)\].

[Figure 16.7](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0007) illustrates the gait recognition process, detailing the key stages from data acquisition to matching. Data are acquired using various sensors, followed by preprocessing steps such as background subtraction, silhouette extraction, and gait cycle detection. Feature extraction methods like GEI, GEnI, spatial‐temporal motion descriptors, and deep learning‐based methods are used to capture the unique gait characteristics. The extracted features are then matched with database templates using distance metrics and classifiers.

![Figure 16.7 Gait recognition process.](images/c16f007.png)

**Figure 16.7** Gait recognition process.

Gait recognition offers several advantages for TinyML systems. It enables unobtrusive and continuous authentication, as gait data can be collected passively without requiring explicit user interaction. Gait recognition can be particularly useful in applications like activity monitoring, access control, and user identification in smart environments.

However, gait recognition in TinyML faces challenges related to sensor limitations, environmental factors, and individual variations. Factors such as walking speed, surface conditions, footwear, and physical changes due to aging or injuries can affect its accuracy. The resource constraints of TinyML platforms also require the development of computationally efficient gait recognition algorithms that can operate with limited memory and processing power.

[Figure 16.8](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0008) outlines the properties, challenges, and research directions for gait recognition, particularly in the context of TinyML. The properties emphasize the unique gait pattern and its advantages for unobtrusive and continuous authentication. Challenges include sensor limitations, environmental factors, individual variations, and resource constraints. Research directions focus on multimodal sensors, feature selection and dimensionality reduction, and domain adaptation techniques to enhance gait recognition performance.

![Figure 16.8 Gait recognition: properties, challenges, and research directions.](images/c16f008.png)

**Figure 16.8** Gait recognition: properties, challenges, and research directions.

Researchers have investigated techniques to improve the robustness and efficiency of gait recognition in TinyML systems. These include the use of multimodal sensors to capture complementary gait information, feature selection and dimensionality reduction methods to optimize the gait representation, and domain adaptation techniques to handle variations across different walking conditions and individuals.

 

#### 16.3.4.3 Ear Recognition

Ear recognition is a relatively new biometric modality that exploits the unique shape and structure of the human ear for authentication. The external ear, or pinna, exhibits a complex and stable pattern of curves, ridges, and valleys that remain relatively unchanged throughout an individual's lifetime. These distinctive characteristics make the ear a promising biometric trait for personal identification \[[3](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003), [21](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0021), [43](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0043)\].

Ear recognition systems typically involve the following stages: image acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, and matching. Image acquisition is performed using cameras or specialized ear scanners that capture high‐resolution images of the ear. Preprocessing techniques, such as ear detection, alignment, and normalization, are applied to isolate the ear region from the captured image and compensate for variations in pose and scale.

Feature extraction methods aim to capture the discriminative information present in the ear structure. Approaches like the use of geometric features, such as the shape and size of the ear, and the analysis of the ear's morphological characteristics, including the helix, antihelix, and tragus, have been explored for ear recognition. Other techniques, such as the use of wavelet transforms, local binary patterns (LBPs), and deep learning‐based feature learning, have also been investigated to capture the intricate details of the ear structure \[[44](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0044), [45](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0045)\].

Matching algorithms compare the extracted ear features against a database of enrolled templates to determine the identity of an individual. Similarity measures, such as Euclidean distance and cosine similarity, are commonly used to assess the resemblance between ear features. Machine learning classifiers, including SVMs and neural networks, have also been employed for ear recognition [\[43\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0043).

[Figure 16.9](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0009) illustrates the ear recognition process, detailing the stages from data acquisition to matching. High‐resolution images of the ear are captured using cameras or specialized scanners. Preprocessing steps include ear detection, alignment, and normalization to isolate the ear region and compensate for pose and scale variations. Feature extraction methods, such as geometric features, morphological characteristics, wavelet transforms, LBPs, and deep learning‐based techniques, capture the unique ear structure. The extracted features are then matched with database templates using similarity measures and classifiers like SVMs and neural networks.

![Figure 16.9 Ear recognition process.](images/c16f009.png)

**Figure 16.9** Ear recognition process.

[Figure 16.10](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0010) outlines the properties, challenges, and research directions for ear recognition, particularly in the context of TinyML. The properties emphasize the stability of ear features, convenience, and compact size, making ear recognition suitable for wearable devices and IoT applications. Challenges include image quality issues due to occlusion, resource constraints, and variations in ear appearance. Research directions focus on multi‐view ear recognition, occlusion‐resistant methods, algorithm optimization for resource‐constrained environments, and integration with other biometric modalities to enhance accuracy and robustness.

![Figure 16.10 Ear recognition: properties, challenges, and research directions.](images/c16f010.png)

**Figure 16.10** Ear recognition: properties, challenges, and research directions.

Ear recognition offers several advantages for TinyML systems. The ear is a relatively stable biometric trait that is less affected by aging and facial expressions compared to other modalities like face recognition. Ear‐based authentication can be performed unobtrusively, as the ear is often visible even when the face is partially occluded. Moreover, the compact size of the ear makes it suitable for integration into wearable devices and IoT applications.

However, ear recognition in TinyML faces challenges related to image quality, occlusion, and variations in ear appearance. The accuracy of ear recognition can be affected by factors such as earrings, hair, and head coverings that obscure the ear structure. The limited resolution and computational resources of TinyML platforms also require the development of efficient ear recognition algorithms that can operate with constrained memory and processing capabilities.

Researchers have explored techniques to address these challenges, such as the use of multi‐view ear recognition to handle variations in pose and occlusion, the development of occlusion‐resistant feature extraction methods, and the optimization of ear recognition algorithms for resource‐constrained environments. The integration of ear recognition with other biometric modalities, such as face or voice recognition, has also been investigated to enhance the overall authentication accuracy and robustness.

 

## 16.4 Comparative Analysis of Biometric Authentication Methods

The selection of an appropriate biometric authentication method for TinyML systems depends on various factors, including the application requirements, resource constraints, user acceptability, and performance characteristics. To facilitate informed decision‐making, this section presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of the biometric modalities discussed in [Section 16.3](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0003). We begin by introducing a set of performance metrics that quantify the accuracy, efficiency, and usability of biometric systems. Subsequently, we evaluate and compare the strengths and limitations of each modality based on these metrics, considering the unique challenges posed by TinyML environments.

 

### 16.4.1 Performance Metrics for Biometric Authentication

To objectively assess and compare the performance of biometric authentication methods, we employ a set of widely adopted metrics that capture different aspects of system accuracy, efficiency, and user experience. These metrics provide a standardized framework for evaluating the suitability of each modality for TinyML applications. In this subsection, we introduce seven key performance metrics, presenting their definitions, mathematical formulations, and interpretations in the context of biometric authentication.

 

#### 16.4.1.1 False Acceptance Rate (FAR)

The false acceptance rate (FAR) measures the probability of a biometric system incorrectly accepting an unauthorized individual as a genuine user. It quantifies the system's susceptibility to security breaches caused by imposter attacks. The FAR is calculated as the ratio of the number of false acceptances to the total number of imposter attempts:

![italic upper F upper A upper R equals StartFraction italic Number italic of italic False italic Acceptances Over italic Total italic Number italic of italic Imposter italic Attempts EndFraction](images/c16-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">FAR</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Number</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">False</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Acceptances</mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Total</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Number</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Imposter</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Attempts</mtext></mrow></mfrac></math> 

A lower FAR indicates a more secure biometric system, as it minimizes the chances of unauthorized access. However, achieving a low FAR often comes at the cost of increased user inconvenience, as the system becomes more stringent in rejecting potential imposters.

 

#### 16.4.1.2 False Rejection Rate (FRR)

The false rejection rate (FRR) measures the probability of a biometric system incorrectly rejecting a genuine user as an imposter. It quantifies the system's tendency to deny access to legitimate users, causing frustration and inconvenience. The FRR is calculated as the ratio of the number of false rejections to the total number of genuine attempts:

![italic upper F upper R upper R equals StartFraction italic Number italic of italic False italic Rejections Over italic Total italic Number italic of italic Genuine italic Attempts EndFraction](images/c16-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">FRR</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Number</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">False</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Rejections</mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Total</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Number</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Genuine</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Attempts</mtext></mrow></mfrac></math> 

A lower FRR indicates a more user‐friendly biometric system, as it minimizes the chances of genuine users being denied access. However, achieving a low FRR often requires a more lenient decision threshold, which may compromise the system's security by increasing the FAR.

 

#### 16.4.1.3 Equal Error Rate (EER)

The equal error rate (EER) is the point at which the FAR and FRR are equal. It represents a balanced trade‐off between security and usability, where the system's acceptance and rejection errors are minimized simultaneously. The EER is determined by finding the intersection point of the FAR and FRR curves as the decision threshold is varied:

![italic upper E upper E upper R equals italic upper F upper A upper R equals italic upper F upper R upper R italic a t italic the italic point italic of italic intersection](images/c16-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">EER</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">FAR</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">FRR</mi><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi mathvariant="italic">at</mi><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">the</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">point</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">intersection</mtext></math> 

A lower EER indicates a more accurate and reliable biometric system, as it achieves a better balance between security and user convenience. The EER serves as a single‐number metric for comparing the overall performance of different biometric modalities.

 

#### 16.4.1.4 Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) Curve

The ROC curve is a graphical representation of the trade‐off between the FAR and the true‐positive rate (TPR) as the decision threshold is varied. The TPR, also known as the genuine acceptance rate (GAR), measures the probability of correctly accepting a genuine user.

A biometric system with a higher ROC curve, closer to the top‐left corner of the graph, indicates better performance, as it achieves higher TPRs at lower FARs. The area under the ROC curve (AUC) serves as a scalar metric for comparing the performance of different biometric systems, with a higher AUC indicating better overall accuracy.

 

#### 16.4.1.5 Failure to Enroll (FTE) Rate

The failure to enroll (FTE) rate measures the proportion of individuals who are unable to provide a usable biometric sample during the enrollment process. It quantifies the system's ability to accommodate a wide range of user characteristics and capture high‐quality biometric data. The FTE rate is calculated as the ratio of the number of failed enrollments to the total number of enrollment attempts:

![italic upper F upper T upper E italic Rate equals StartFraction italic Number italic of italic Failed italic Enrollments Over italic Total italic Number italic of italic Enrollment italic Attempts EndFraction](images/c16-math-0004.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="italic">FTE</mi><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Rate</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Number</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Failed</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Enrollments</mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Total</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Number</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Enrollment</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Attempts</mtext></mrow></mfrac></math> 

A lower FTE rate indicates a more inclusive and user‐friendly biometric system, as it minimizes the chances of users being unable to enroll due to factors such as poor biometric quality, sensor limitations, or user inexperience.

 

#### 16.4.1.6 Throughput Rate

The throughput rate measures the number of biometric comparisons or identifications that a system can perform within a given time period. It quantifies the system's efficiency and scalability in handling a large volume of authentication requests. The throughput rate is expressed as the number of comparisons or identifications per unit time:

![italic Throughput italic Rate equals StartFraction italic Number italic of italic Comparisons italic or italic Identifications Over italic Unit italic Time EndFraction](images/c16-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="italic">Throughput</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Rate</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Number</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Comparisons</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">or</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Identifications</mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Unit</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Time</mtext></mrow></mfrac></math> 

A higher throughput rate indicates a more efficient and responsive biometric system, capable of handling a greater number of authentication requests within a shorter time frame. This metric is particularly relevant for TinyML applications that require real‐time or near‐real‐time authentication.

 

#### 16.4.1.7 User Acceptance Rate

The user acceptance rate measures the proportion of users who are willing to use and trust a biometric authentication system. It captures the subjective aspects of user experience, such as perceived ease of use, comfort level, and privacy concerns. The user acceptance rate is typically determined through user surveys or feedback, and it is expressed as a percentage:

![italic User italic Acceptance italic Rate equals StartFraction italic Number italic of italic Users italic upper W h o italic Accept italic the italic System Over italic Total italic Number italic of italic Users italic Surveyed EndFraction times 100 percent-sign](images/c16-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtext mathvariant="italic">User</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Acceptance</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Rate</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Number</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Users</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mi mathvariant="italic">Who</mi><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Accept</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">the</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">System</mtext></mrow><mrow><mtext mathvariant="italic">Total</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Number</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">of</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Users</mtext><mspace width="0.5em"/><mtext mathvariant="italic">Surveyed</mtext></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></math> 

A higher user acceptance rate indicates a more user‐friendly and socially acceptable biometric system, which is crucial for the successful adoption and deployment of TinyML applications in real‐world scenarios.

These performance metrics provide a comprehensive framework for evaluating and comparing biometric authentication methods in TinyML systems. By considering these metrics in conjunction with the specific requirements and constraints of the target application, developers and researchers can make informed decisions when selecting the most suitable biometric modality for their TinyML implementation.

In [Section 16.4.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0020), we will apply these performance metrics to compare and contrast the biometric authentication methods discussed earlier, highlighting their strengths, limitations, and suitability for various TinyML scenarios.

We evaluate these methods based on the performance metrics introduced in [Section 16.4.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0012), considering their accuracy, efficiency, and user acceptance in the context of TinyML systems.

Fingerprint recognition exhibits the second‐best accuracy metrics, with low FAR and FRR values and a high AUC. It also achieves the highest throughput rate among the compared modalities, making it a favorable choice for TinyML systems that require fast and efficient authentication. Furthermore, fingerprint recognition has the highest user acceptance rate ([Figure 16.12](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0012)), indicating its widespread familiarity and ease of use.

![Figure 16.12 Throughput (comparison \[s\]) and user acceptance rate (%) values for different biometric modalities.](images/c16f012.png)

Facial recognition offers a balance between accuracy and user acceptance, with moderate FAR, FRR, and EER values and a high AUC. Its throughput rate is lower than fingerprint recognition but higher than the other modalities, making it suitable for TinyML applications that prioritize user convenience and non‐intrusive authentication.

Voice recognition, gait recognition, and ear recognition demonstrate lower accuracy compared to the other modalities, with higher FAR, FRR, and EER values and lower AUC scores. These methods also have lower throughput rates and user acceptance rates, indicating potential challenges in their implementation and adoption in TinyML systems. However, they offer unique advantages, such as the ability to perform continuous and unobtrusive authentication, which may be valuable in specific TinyML scenarios.

It is important to note that the performance values presented in [Table 16.1](#c16.xhtml#c16-tbl-0001) are based on average results reported in the literature. The actual performance of each biometric modality may vary depending on factors such as the sensor quality, environmental conditions, user diversity, and the specific algorithms employed. Therefore, the selection of a biometric authentication method for a TinyML system should consider not only these general performance metrics but also the specific requirements, constraints, and trade‐offs of the target application.

Furthermore, the comparative analysis highlights the potential for multimodal biometric authentication, where multiple biometric traits are combined to enhance accuracy and security. By fusing complementary modalities, such as fingerprint and facial recognition, or iris scanning and voice recognition, TinyML systems can achieve higher performance and robustness compared to single‐modality approaches.

In conclusion, the comparative analysis of biometric authentication methods for TinyML systems reveals the strengths and limitations of each modality based on various performance metrics. Iris scanning and fingerprint recognition demonstrate the highest accuracy, while facial recognition offers a balance between accuracy and user acceptance. Voice recognition, gait recognition, and ear recognition, although less accurate, provide unique opportunities for continuous and unobtrusive authentication in specific TinyML scenarios. The selection of an appropriate biometric modality should align with the specific requirements and constraints of the target application, considering factors such as security, user experience, and resource efficiency.

 

## 16.5 Adapting Biometric Techniques for TinyML Systems

The integration of biometric authentication methods into TinyML systems presents a unique set of challenges and opportunities. While biometric techniques offer enhanced security and user convenience, their implementation on resource‐constrained microcontroller‐based systems requires careful consideration of computational efficiency, memory footprint, and power consumption. This section explores the constraints and challenges associated with deploying biometric authentication on TinyML platforms and discusses strategies for developing resource‐efficient biometric algorithms and hardware considerations for biometric sensors in IoT devices.

 

### 16.5.1 Constraints and Challenges of Microcontroller‐Based Systems

Microcontroller‐based systems, which form the backbone of TinyML applications, impose several constraints on the implementation of biometric authentication techniques [\[6\]](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0006). These constraints arise from the limited computational resources, memory capacity, and power budget of microcontrollers, which are designed to be compact, low cost, and energy‐efficient.

One of the primary challenges is the limited processing power of microcontrollers. Unlike high‐performance computing systems, microcontrollers typically feature low‐frequency processors with reduced instruction sets and limited parallelism. This constrains the complexity and speed of biometric algorithms that can be executed on these devices. Biometric techniques that rely on computationally intensive operations, such as high‐dimensional feature extraction or deep learning models, may not be feasible or may require significant optimization to run efficiently on microcontrollers.

Memory constraints pose another significant challenge for biometric authentication in TinyML systems \[[5](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0005), [6](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0006)\]. Microcontrollers have limited on‐chip memory, typically in the range of a few kilobytes to a few megabytes, which must be shared among the operating system, application code, and data storage. Biometric algorithms often require storing large amounts of enrollment data, templates, and intermediate results, which can quickly exhaust the available memory resources. Techniques such as template compression, feature selection, and efficient data structures must be employed to minimize the memory footprint of biometric methods.

Power consumption is a critical consideration for battery‐powered IoT devices, which are expected to operate for extended periods without frequent battery replacements. Biometric authentication processes, particularly those involving high‐resolution sensors or intensive computations, can significantly impact the power budget of TinyML systems. Strategies such as low‐power sensing, duty cycling, and hardware acceleration must be explored to optimize the energy efficiency of biometric methods.

[Figure 16.13](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0013) illustrates the constraints and challenges of microcontroller‐based systems used in TinyML applications. The main challenges include limited processing power, memory constraints, power consumption, data security and privacy, and environmental robustness. Each category details specific issues, such as the impact of low‐frequency processors on algorithm complexity, the need for efficient memory usage, strategies to optimize power efficiency, the importance of lightweight security measures, and techniques to improve robustness under diverse conditions.

![Figure 16.13 Constraints and challenges of microcontroller‐based systems.](images/c16f013.png)

**Figure 16.13** Constraints and challenges of microcontroller‐based systems.

In addition to these resource constraints, TinyML systems also face challenges related to data security and privacy. Biometric data are highly sensitive and must be protected against unauthorized access, tampering, and leakage. Implementing robust security mechanisms, such as secure storage, encryption, and secure communication protocols, is essential to ensure the confidentiality and integrity of biometric information. However, these security measures must be lightweight and efficient to avoid overburdening the limited resources of microcontrollers.

Another challenge arises from the diverse range of IoT devices and their operating conditions. TinyML systems may be deployed in various environments, ranging from controlled indoor settings to harsh outdoor conditions. Biometric sensors and algorithms must be robust to variations in lighting, temperature, humidity, and other environmental factors that can affect the quality and consistency of biometric data. Techniques such as sensor fusion, data preprocessing, and adaptive thresholding can help mitigate the impact of environmental variations on biometric performance.

[Figure 16.14](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0014) outlines approaches to address the constraints and challenges faced by microcontroller‐based systems in TinyML. These approaches include the development of resource‐efficient algorithms, hardware optimization, and system‐level considerations. By integrating these strategies, the overall efficiency and effectiveness of biometric systems can be significantly enhanced.

![Figure 16.14 Approaches to address constraints and challenges.](images/c16f014.png)

**Figure 16.14** Approaches to address constraints and challenges.

Addressing these constraints and challenges requires a holistic approach that encompasses algorithm design, hardware optimization, and system‐level considerations. [Sections 16.5.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0023) and [16.5.3](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0024) delve into resource‐efficient biometric algorithms and hardware considerations for biometric sensors, which are crucial for adapting biometric techniques to the unique requirements of TinyML systems.

 

### 16.5.2 Resource‐Efficient Biometric Algorithms for TinyML

Developing resource‐efficient biometric algorithms is crucial for enabling biometric authentication on TinyML platforms \[[6](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0006), [17](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0017)\]. These algorithms must strike a balance between accuracy, computational efficiency, and memory footprint to operate effectively within the constraints of microcontroller‐based systems.

One approach to achieving resource efficiency is through the use of lightweight feature extraction methods. Traditional biometric algorithms often rely on high‐dimensional feature representations, such as minutiae points for fingerprints or dense facial landmarks, which can be computationally expensive to extract and store. Lightweight alternatives, such as binary descriptors, local pattern operators, and compact feature representations, can significantly reduce the computational complexity and memory requirements of biometric algorithms. For example, binary fingerprint descriptors, such as the fingerprint minutia descriptor (FMD) and the LBP, encode fingerprint patterns using compact binary strings, enabling efficient matching and storage on resource‐constrained devices \[[6](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0006), [16](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0016)\].

Another strategy for resource optimization is the use of template compression techniques. Biometric templates, which represent the enrolled biometric data of users, can occupy significant memory space, especially when dealing with large user populations. Template compression methods, such as quantization, subsampling, and feature selection, can reduce the size of biometric templates without significantly compromising recognition accuracy. For instance, the use of vector quantization or PCA can effectively compress facial templates while preserving the discriminative information necessary for authentication.

Efficient matching algorithms are also essential for resource‐constrained TinyML systems. Traditional biometric matching methods, such as the ICP algorithm for fingerprint matching or the Euclidean distance for facial comparison, can be computationally intensive and memory hungry. Alternatively, lightweight matching techniques, such as the use of binary string comparisons, Hamming distance calculations, or locality‐sensitive hashing (LSH), can significantly reduce the computational overhead and memory requirements of biometric matching. These methods exploit the compact and binary nature of lightweight feature representations to enable fast and memory‐efficient matching operations.

The use of domain‐specific hardware acceleration can further optimize the performance and energy efficiency of biometric algorithms on TinyML platforms. Microcontrollers often incorporate hardware accelerators, such as digital signal processors (DSPs), floating‐point units (FPUs), or cryptographic engines, which can be leveraged to speed up specific biometric operations. For example, DSPs can efficiently perform signal processing tasks, such as filtering or frequency‐domain analysis, while FPUs can accelerate floating‐point computations common in biometric algorithms. By carefully mapping biometric algorithms to the available hardware resources and utilizing hardware acceleration, significant performance improvements and energy savings can be achieved.

Adaptive algorithms and dynamic resource management techniques can also help optimize the resource utilization of biometric methods in TinyML systems. These approaches involve dynamically adjusting the algorithmic parameters, such as the feature extraction resolution or the matching threshold, based on the available system resources and the current operating conditions. For instance, in low‐power scenarios, the biometric algorithm can switch to a lower‐resolution feature extraction mode or employ a more lenient matching threshold to conserve energy. Conversely, when more resources are available, the algorithm can adapt to a higher accuracy mode to improve recognition performance. Adaptive algorithms enable a flexible trade‐off between accuracy and resource consumption, allowing biometric methods to operate optimally within the constraints of TinyML systems.

Collaborative and distributed biometric processing is another promising approach for resource‐efficient biometric authentication in IoT environments. In this paradigm, the biometric processing workload is distributed among multiple IoT devices or offloaded to edge servers, leveraging the collective computational resources of the network. For example, a lightweight IoT device can perform the initial feature extraction and send the compressed features to a more powerful edge server for matching and decision‐making. This distributed approach allows for the efficient utilization of resources across the IoT ecosystem while reducing the computational burden on individual devices.

Specialized software frameworks and libraries have emerged to facilitate the development and deployment of resource‐efficient biometric algorithms. These frameworks provide optimized implementations of biometric algorithms, along with tools for performance profiling, resource estimation, and hardware abstraction. Examples include the OpenMV framework for computer vision on microcontrollers, the Embedded Learning Library (ELL) for machine learning on resource‐constrained devices, and the TinyML framework for deploying deep learning models on microcontrollers. These frameworks abstract the low‐level details of hardware‐specific optimizations and provide high‐level application programming interfaces (APIs) for biometric algorithm development, enabling researchers and developers to focus on algorithmic innovations rather than low‐level system intricacies.

These include the OpenMV framework for computer vision on microcontrollers, the ELL for machine learning on resource‐constrained devices, and the TinyML framework for deploying deep learning models on microcontrollers. These frameworks provide optimized implementations and tools, facilitating the development of efficient biometric solutions.
