# 18  
TinyML for Environmental Applications

*Duy Nam Khanh Vu^([1](#c18.xhtml#c18-aff-0001)) and Anh Khoa Dang^([2](#c18.xhtml#c18-aff-0002))*

*¹Lê Quý Đôn High School, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam*

*²Perkiomen School, Pennsburg, PA, USA*

 

## 18.1 Introduction

At first, much research and many inventions that contribute to the growth of many environmental aspects are correlated to a great technological term in the Internet of Things (IoT) industry: machine learning (ML). Specifically, IoT plays a crucial role and is the resource for many fields such as residential systems and manufacturers [\[1\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0001). In order to truly make the potential of IoT available to life, scientists, researchers, and engineers have created and used ML for IoT application and development, especially for environmental applications.

ML has advanced significantly, leading to the development of many sophisticated algorithms, techniques, and libraries. One notable advancement is tiny ML (TinyML), which focuses on deploying machine learning models on resource‐constrained devices, enabling efficient and fast processing. Generally, TinyML enables faster local decision‐making progress, reduces the cost to deploy, enhances accuracy, minimizes power consumption, is portable, and is easy to integrate \[[2](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0002)–[4](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0004)\]. Thus, there have been and will be a lot of substantial inventions related to TinyML, a new future for ML.

TinyML has contributed significantly to industries, science fields, etc., and is promised to continually participate in the development of larger aspects of life. According to \[[1](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0001), [5](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0005)\] and \[[6](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0006), [7](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007)\], there are several fields that can benefit from TinyML. [Figure 18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0001) shows some benefits of the application \[[8](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0008)–[17](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0017)\].

So what actually is TinyML? The answer is that TinyML is a type of “approach” within ML that does not need to process and train data on cloud or within Internet connections. In contrast, TinyML enables microcontrollers to train and make use of data to make predictions locally [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). Therefore, TinyML's “circle of processing” represents a much simpler process diagram than the traditional ML approach. [Figure 18.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0002) describes the difference between TinyML and ML's “circle of processing.”

![Figure 18.1 Examples of some benefited TinyML applications.](images/c18f001.png)

**Figure 18.1** Examples of some benefited TinyML applications.

![Figure 18.2 Difference in processing between TinyML and ML approach.](images/c18f002.png)

**Figure 18.2** Difference in processing between TinyML and ML approach.

Over this survey, there will be some points demonstrated in order to fulfill the author's research purpose and also the key point of this chapter:

*   TinyML applications in smart agriculture.
*   TinyML applications in healthcare systems.
*   TinyML applications in military systems.
*   TinyML applications in wireless systems.

Moreover, the paper will be presented in the following order: [Section 18.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0002) presents related work, [Section 18.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0003) presents methodology, [Section 18.4](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0016) presents a case study related to a study in the survey, [Section 18.5](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0023) presents results and discussions, and [Section 18.6](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0028) presents conclusion and future scope.

 

## 18.2 Related Work

TinyML is an interesting field and needs to be investigated in more depth to explore its potential usefulness. One of such fields that TinyML can be applied in and researched on is environment, and there have been numerous surveys mentioning these applications.

Firstly, smart agriculture, also known as precision agriculture, makes use of technologies, such as ML, to improve crop quality, farming practices, and enhance resource sustainability. This aspect also applies to multi‐form sensors, including drones and satellite imagery, to collect data, record soil conditions, weather patterns, and crop health [\[19\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0019).

Secondly, healthcare systems are complex networks that encompass various organizations, such as hospitals or medical centers, working together with technologies to provide medical services to patients. With the addition of TinyML in medical fields, including surgery, disease detection, and bacterial analysis, doctors and researchers can further delve into collecting medical information and streamline many operations in medical procedures [\[20\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0020).

Thirdly, military systems encompass ML and artificial intelligence (AI) with various embedded systems to enhance military operations; some possible examples will be combat drones, self‐driven airplanes, etc. Integrated with ML and AI, military operations will be improved, allowing strategic and economic implications of modern systems [\[21\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0021).

Lastly, wireless systems are crucial in modern communication; within a second, many messages can be delivered everywhere in the world, and with the support of TinyML, researchers are helped in exploring and developing wireless technologies such as 5G, Wi‐Fi ‐6, and IoT. Moreover, TinyML in wireless systems ensures to improve data transmission, network efficiency, etc. \[[22](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0022), [23](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0023)\].

The study presented in Bamoumen et al. [\[19\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0019) highlights various applications of TinyML in addressing environmental challenges across diverse domains, such as the atmosphere, hydrosphere, and their respective subcategories. For instance, in the atmospheric domain, the authors examine the monitoring of carbon dioxide (![CO Subscript 2](images/c18-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>CO</mtext><mn>2</mn></msub></math>) emissions and the prediction of temperature. They employ microcontrollers such as TEDA, Arduino Nano 33 BLE, and STM32, paired with ML techniques such as unsupervised learning and neural networks (NNs). In the hydrosphere, the focus shifts to monitoring water quality, identifying water misuse, and detecting diseases in water bodies. The technological framework here relies on devices like Raspberry Pi and ML algorithms such as support vector machines (SVMs) and artificial neural networks (ANNs). In the lithosphere, the discussion is limited to smart agriculture, which utilizes the ATMega32Sp microcontroller along with TensorFlow Lite, Naive Bayes, ANN, and other tools. This system aims to help farmers manage climate conditions and improve crop quality. Lastly, the biosphere is associated with wildlife conservation and bioactivity monitoring, which involve the use of multiple microcontrollers, echo boxes, ANNs, and Python libraries like scikit‐learn. Overall [\[19\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0019), outlines the potential applications of TinyML in environmental sectors, including water management, agriculture, air quality, and temperature control, while also providing a consolidated view of the research projects covered in the survey.

The study in Qi et al. [\[20\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0020) highlights several significant research contributions in which machine learning, particularly TinyML, is integrated into healthcare systems, with a particular focus on personalized and mobile health care (PHS). An important mark of this survey is the use of IoT technologies to improve PHS, using wearable devices, mobile apps, and sensors. The report discusses technologies such as global positioning system (GPS), radio frequency identification (RFID), accelerometers, gyroscopes, altimeters, electroencephalogram (EEG), and electrocardiogram (ECG) sensors. These tools support healthcare solutions by collecting and processing diverse forms of health data based on references in the survey. Many of the studies referenced in this survey incorporate a variety of machine learning techniques, including decision trees (DTs), hidden Markov models (HMMs), SVM, as well as supervised and unsupervised learning approaches. The primary target for these studies tends to be patients and individuals aged between 16 and 40. In addition to the reviews, the survey discusses crucial features of several studies, such as sensor types, monitored parameters, and data processing techniques. It also introduces mobile applications that implement machine learning in health care, such as Self‐Management with Assistive Rehabilitation and Telecare Technologies (SMART), mHealthDroid, and Emergency Monitoring and Prevention (EMERGE).

Military systems include a wide range of applications, such as rescue operations and intelligent transportation. One of the most prominent areas in this domain is unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). UAVs are technologies that include flying vehicles capable of operating without direct human control and are ubiquitous in the research field of the IoT. Common detection methods in this field involve radar, RFreq, and acoustic surveillance systems [\[21\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0021). The survey in Yan et al. [\[21\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0021) examines successful reports of the above technologies along with other paradigms and algorithms being used such as SVM and regions with convolutional neural network (CNN) features (RCNN). Moreover, TinyML can be integrated with IoT in the field of military network. In a related field survey, there are challenges related to computational and networking resources, such as Agile computing hardware (ACM) or Sieve, Process, and Forward (SPF).

The work in Sharma et al. [\[22\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0022) surveys ML applications within wireless systems, particularly focusing on smart cities. It explores various ML approaches aimed at enhancing the efficiency of wireless sensor network (WSN)‐IoT networks, addressing key challenges such as network coverage, connectivity, energy efficiency, bandwidth optimization, and infrastructure demands. The paper also highlights a number of ML approaches, including reinforcement learning (RL), DT, random forests (RFs), and ANN, alongside popular algorithms like ![upper Q](images/c18-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐learning, SVM, and ![upper K](images/c18-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐nearest neighbors (KNN), all of which are reviewed for their potential to enhance WSN‐IoT systems.

The study in Jagannath et al. [\[23\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0023) explores the applications of ML within wireless communication systems, with a specific focus on expanding the understanding of various ML techniques. The authors of this survey also evaluate existing ML implementations in IoT‐related projects, particularly projects that focus on network performance. Additionally, the paper points out the process of integrating ML into network‐related hardware, ensuring the availability of applying ML techniques to different network elements. Ultimately, the survey offers a deeper understanding of the impact of ML and IoT, particularly referring to wireless ad hoc networks (WANETs) [\[23\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0023).

## 18.3 Methodology

In this section, the survey reviews the ML techniques, paradigms, algorithms, reference methods, practical testing of some references, etc. There will be figures, equations, formulas, etc., and they will be explained in detail. As mentioned in the Introduction section of this survey, the following four topics are covered and reviewed:

*   Smart agriculture
*   Healthcare systems
*   Military systems
*   Wireless systems

 

### 18.3.1 Smart Agriculture

Agricultural products encompass a wide range of goods derived from plants, animals, and microorganisms. These products can be broadly categorized into four main groups:

*   **Foods:** This includes cereals (wheat, rice, and corn), fruits (apples, oranges, and bananas), vegetables (potatoes, tomatoes, and lettuce), and animal products (meat, milk, and eggs).
*   **Fibers:** These are materials used for textiles and clothing, such as cotton, wool, and silk.
*   **Fuels:** Agricultural products can also be used to produce biofuels, such as ethanol made from corn or biodiesel from soybeans.
*   **Raw Materials:** This category includes products like rubber, timber, and other materials used in manufacturing and construction.

From this, agricultural products play a crucial role in supplying essential resources for human life, and with the erosion of global warming, TinyML will be an effective method to guarantee the quality of the products and safeguard consumer health.

One of the current challenges in the industry is the short shelf life of fresh fruits, and TinyML can be used to tackle this issue. Fresh fruits are known to be perishable and prone to quick spoilage. Thus, finding a reliable solution is crucial, and predicting the freshness period of these fruits is a promising strategy. Previously, non‐ML solutions like modified atmosphere packaging (MAP) have been used for this purpose. By slowing the ripening process, MAP extends the shelf life of fruits, allowing for longer storage. The study mentioned in Srinivasagan et al. [\[24\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0024) applies ML techniques with MAP to predict the shelf life of fruits under various controlled conditions. This approach is crucial in determining the optimal consumption time and ensuring that consumers enjoy the nutrients in fruits. [Figure 18.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0003) shows steps in making a shelf life estimator.

The study also involves the use of an Arduino BLE 33 Sense microcontroller, which includes various sensors such as those for temperature, humidity, and light. The architecture is designed by edge impulse (EI), a cloud‐based platform for training and deploying the model. The microcontroller performs real‐time inference, while the AS7256x sensor measures incident and reflected light, reducing the calculation of reflectance ratios. Besides fruit freshness, monitoring weather conditions is also crucial in agriculture. Weather data collection involves tracking various atmospheric factors, such as temperature, humidity, and solar radiation, using tools such as IoT sensors, satellites, and weather stations. Accurate weather records and ML predictions are pivotal for agricultural productivity, as unpredictable weather patterns can negatively impact crops. For example, the ongoing drought in the U.S. Southwest since 2020 has caused a significant downfall in rainfall and elevated temperatures, severely destroying crop yields.

![Figure 18.3 Shelf life estimator process.](images/c18f003.png)

**Figure 18.3** Shelf life estimator process.

In other cases, increased humidity can promote fungal diseases, warm temperature can boost pest populations, or smoke from wildfires can affect air quality and plant health. Therefore, it is essential to prevent them before they actually occur. Centuries ago, farmers could only learn to prevent agricultural problems using their senses. Today, technologies have advanced, and the application of TinyML in weather has been feasible in recent decades. Some benefits of TinyML in weather measurement are listed:

*   Real‐time data processing
*   Cost‐effective
*   Data privacy
*   Scalability

Many reports employing TinyML for weather measurement collect data such as temperature, rainfall, wind speed and direction, and sunlight to ML datasets. These studies primarily aim to improve crop management, control pests and plant diseases, and mitigate risks such as floods and storms. In one particular study, TinyML is integrated for weather measurement with IoT technology to create a cheap, lightweight AI‐based weather station, which includes wind turbine energy generators (WTEGs) in urban settings. The study uses parameters including wind direction (WD), wind velocity (WV), temperature, pressure, sea level, and humidity for prediction, focusing mainly on WD and WV. The research achieved 95% accuracy for WV predictions and 92% for WD predictions. [Figure 18.4](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0004) reveals the process of making an ML model as a weather measurement system.

![Figure 18.4 Procedures in building a TinyML weather station. ¶ Source: Adapted from \[25\].](images/c18f004.png)

**Figure 18.4** Procedures in building a TinyML weather station. ¶ *Source:* Adapted from [\[25\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0025).

Referring to the hardware being used, the study employs the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense from the Harvard TinyML kit for WV measurements. For WD measurement, a custom 3D‐printed panel houses eight piezoelectric pressure sensors, each matched with one of the eight cardinal and intercardinal directions (north, northeast, east, southeast, south, southwest, west, and northwest) [\[25\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0025).

| Srinivasagan et al. [\[24\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0024) || Estimating shelf life of fresh fruits || CNNs, RNNs, EI platform, backpropagation learning algorithm || Average MAPE = 94.11, average RMSE = 0.43 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Albuali et al. [\[25\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0025) || Low‐cost weather station || DT, EI platform, computer vision (spectrogram), 1D‐CNN || Average overall accuracy = 0.94, average F1 score = 0.92 |

 

#### 18.3.1.1 Machine Learning Methods

In previous research [\[24\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0024), fruits underwent processes like cleaning, washing, and precooling before data collection. The types of data utilized included moisture content, water activity, total soluble solids, total sugar levels, pH, and tannin.

Data collected from Al‐Ahsa International Airport (AIA) included various attributes such as wind speed and WD [\[25\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0025). The study applies a DT algorithm to analyze WD measurements, enhancing classification and regression efficiency while optimizing training time and memory use. WV is assessed based on the Beaufort Wind Force Scale (BWFS) using a one‐dimensional (1D‐CNN) [\[25\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0025). EI was also used to train the architecture described.

 

#### 18.3.1.2 Neural Networks and Structure Design

The research [\[24\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0024) applies an ANN. This ANN comprises several elements: Neurons process input and relay it; layers consist of an input layer for data reception, hidden layers for processing via weighted connections, and an output layer delivering final results. Types of ANNs include CNNs and recurrent neural networks (RNNs). EI utilizes the backpropagation algorithm and Adam optimizer for weight adjustment, effectively reducing error [\[24\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0024).

Another study uses 1D‐CNN and DT models to optimize training. The classification model includes over 3000 time‐series samples initially unlabeled. EI's data explorer assists in labeling and preprocessing the data with spectrograms. [Table 18.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0003) provides an insight into the architectures used in both studies.

### 18.3.2 Healthcare Systems

In today's world, health care has been and will be an important field to everyone. Not to consider harmful impact and consequences from coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19), our world is currently facing a phenomenon that still has only suggestions for solutions, that is, aging population. Old people mostly cannot do heavy works, and they are easier to catch illnesses than younger generations; thus, with the rise of the elders, healthcare systems must be developed and expanded faster to adapt to the group [\[26\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0026). Over many years, AI has played a crucial role in the field of health care. They have contributed significantly to imaging and diagnostics in medicine, remote patient care, research and discovery of new drugs, patient involvement and adherence, rehabilitation services, and other various administrative tasks in hospitals and medical centers [\[27\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0027). Moreover, involving machines that are combined with AI and physical objects can help interact with patients and doctors, work smartly in bio‐hazardous environments, and perform other dangerous tasks related to medical fields. Therefore, TinyML is a potential aspect for scientists to explore deeper in order to tackle the aging population problem and other issues such as COVID‐19. During the training process of ML models for those solutions, it involves many types of data, algorithms, and techniques, but mostly used are RFID, inertial measurement units (IMUs), supervised or unsupervised learning, CNN, ![upper K](images/c18-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means, etc. [\[20\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0020).

As previously mentioned, COVID‐19 continues to pose significant challenges to the healthcare system. Additionally, there are reports suggesting that mosquitoes, known for transmitting various diseases to both animals and humans, might also be capable of spreading COVID‐19 [\[28\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0028). Hence, it is pivotal to create a TinyML technology which can detect mosquitoes to prevent further disease transmission [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007).

In the proposed study, mosquito detection is reported to be using TinyML by examining their wingbeat sounds over intervals ranging from 0.5 to 3 seconds. The study's objective is to develop an affordable mosquito detection system, prioritizing efficiency and energy conservation. Two versions of the detection model are proposed: One uses a 1D‐CNN, while the other applies a 2D‐CNN. The models will be evaluated based on accuracy, F1 score, and other metrics to determine the most effective and efficient model for implementation on hardware and microcontrollers. The models are trained and tested using data stored on EI [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007).

For the implementation phase, the more efficient model is loaded onto an Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense microcontroller equipped with an external microphone to capture mosquito wingbeat sounds. The microcontroller is powered by a solar panel that charges its battery via a charge controller [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007). Lastly, the study utilizes the Arduino's Wi‐Fi capabilities to connect with mosquito repellent devices, which release chemicals to eliminate mosquitoes through a fog server [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007).

During the time of COVID‐19 worldwide spread, there have been many people suffered from the symptoms of the virus, and before that, they might have been affected by one of the most common ways, droplets from person‐to‐person communication [\[29\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0029). Therefore, wearing face masks has been an important activity that everyone, especially children, considered during the years 2022 and 2023. However, it is impossible to ensure that people we see and pass through do wear the mask properly; therefore, TinyML is a proper solution to detect those people. The study [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030) proposes a system for detecting properly worn masks using energy‐efficient and cost‐effective ML techniques such as K‐means and sliding windows. The models are implemented on the STM32F411 microcontroller, featuring a 100‐MHz ARM Cortex M4 chip to support low‐power computer vision tasks [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030). The K‐means algorithm is chosen for its minimal flash memory requirements compared to neural networks (NNs) and its potential to achieve 96% accuracy [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030). Image processing concepts such as bounding boxes and segmentation are explored; however, the study emphasizes the centroid approach for faster and more efficient object detection in static images.

Given the limited memory of microcontrollers like the 1 MB random access memory (RAM) available on the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense, reducing image size accelerates processing. The study resizes dataset images from 1024x1024px or 256x256px to 32x32px, preserving accuracy [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030). The paper applies the sliding window technique to reduce the dimension of 2D to 1D for easier detection [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030). [Figure 18.5](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0005) showcases an example of how sliding windows are used to convert the 2D bit array to 1D bit array.

![Figure 18.5 Sliding window technique from 3 times 3 2D array to 3 times 3 1D array.](images/c18f005.png)

**Figure 18.5** Sliding window technique from ![3 times 3](images/c18-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> 2D array to ![3 times 3](images/c18-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>3</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></math> 1D array.

Aside from COVID‐19, pollution is another massive issue to the field of health care; therefore, integrating TinyML will help interact with pollutants and reduce the harmful impacts. In an overall view, pollution is divided into many categories, such as water, light and noise, and mostly visible to daily life today is air pollution [\[31\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0031).

Air pollution primarily originates from harmful chemicals and emissions like ![CO Subscript 2](images/c18-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>CO</mtext><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, nitric oxide, gases, ash, and smoke. A TinyML paper proposed solutions for monitoring air quality in specific areas, which can tackle troubles in existing air pollution situations [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). The air quality monitoring system employs a Raspberry Pi Pico W microcontroller, including the RP2040's capability to run the TensorFlow Lite library [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). The device is powered by energy collected through a solar panel connected to a 18,650 mAh battery, with sensors providing input to the power manager to sustain the microcontroller [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018).

The microcontroller connects with various sensors, such as the SCD41, to collect air quality data [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). Specifically, it integrates the INA219, LC709203F, and SCD41 sensors [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). The INA219 measures the solar panel's current and voltage output, the LC709203F monitors battery capacity and voltage, and the SCD41 collects data on CO[2] levels, temperature, and humidity. Additionally, the Raspberry Pi Pico W microcontroller uses a DS3231 real‐time clock (RTC) module for precise timekeeping [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). The device integrates two ML models: one for prediction and another for data imputation. If real‐time data is missing, the microcontroller imputes the missing values before making predictions [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018).

As technology becomes more prevalent in hospitals and shared computerized resources are utilized more frequently, the risk of pathogen transmission has increased. This has led to a greater need for zero user interface (UI) solutions [\[32\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0032). First of all, zero UI means interacting with the world without actually touching even a screen or a button [\[32\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0032). Many solutions relate to this, for example, motion detection, eye tracking, and voice control [\[32\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0032). These solutions are becoming more and more necessary to the healthcare systems, and one of those is air writing [\[32\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0032). As described in the article, air writing is a method by which a user can write “in the air” to text messages or compose emails [\[32\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0032).

In a study, the air‐writing methodology is applied to detect Arabic characters [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). To be specific, the study employs TinyML with Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense microcontroller to identify numbers from 0 to 10 with several Arabic alphabets [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). Each character or numeral has 500 recordings, leading to a dataset comprising 11,000 samples [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). The model utilizes the accelerometer and magnetometer on the Arduino microcontroller to capture ![upper X](images/c18-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>X</mi></mrow></math>‐ and ![upper Y](images/c18-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi></mrow></math>‐axis data while writing gestures [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). These values are then displayed in the 2D plane [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). Moreover, the system in this study operates at a rate of 100 Hz [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033).

[Table 18.4](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0004) shortens the details of some papers and studies reviewed in the survey that are about TinyML applications in healthcare systems.

#### 18.3.2.1 Machine Learning Methods

In Kimutai and Förster [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007), the wingbeat sound dataset, sourced from Kaggle – a prominent online platform for data science and machine learning competitions – has been selected as a standard dataset for its contests. The dataset also includes samples recorded from low‐cost smartphones and high‐end recording devices in order for the model to be able to detect mosquitoes correctly from various acoustic sensors [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007). Moreover, other sounds are recorded in order for the model to categorize and classify sounds which are not mosquitoe wingbeat, such as silence, human voices, and noise from television (TV). The dataset also holds nearly 6,000 samples with a split rate of 80/20 for training/testing and 20% for validation.

In the study [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030), the data is got from two sources of dataset, the MaskedFace‐Net and Natural images. The MaskedFace‐Net dataset supports detecting people whether they are wearing the mask correctly [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030). It includes two subsets, one is a correctly worn face mask and the other one is incorrectly worn face mask; also, in the incorrectly worn face mask, there are three classes, which present three different faces of wearing mask incorrectly [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030). The Natural image dataset helps recognize human faces among other subjects such as cat, airplane, and fruit.

In the study [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018), a dataset was developed using real‐time measurements to train and evaluate the models. The involved parameters include ![CO Subscript 2](images/c18-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mtext>CO</mtext><mn>2</mn></msub></math>, air temperature, air humidity, solar panel output current, solar panel output voltage, battery voltage, temperature, and capacity [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). Moreover, to achieve the objective of building a cost‐effective air quality monitoring system, minimizing sensor power consumption was a key step [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). The device collects data with the interval of 10 minutes, resulting in a final dataset of 13,080 samples [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). The dataset was then divided, with 70% allocated for training and the remaining portion used for testing the models.

The study [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033) employs deep learning (DL), a branch of ML, for preprocessing data samples. Initially, the data collected is raw 3‐axis information, which is then transformed into a static 2D format suitable for the DL model [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). After this transformation, coordinates representing the actual writing location in the real world are incorporated into the 2D format [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). These coordinates are defined as two specific values: ![x](images/c18-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and ![y](images/c18-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). Once assigned, the data is normalized, scaling the coordinate values to fit within a range of 0 to 1 [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). [Figure 18.6](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0006) shows the procedure of data preprocessing in Pławiak and Alblehai [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033).

![Figure 18.6 Steps of fundamental data preprocessing. ¶ Source: Adapted from \[33\].](images/c18f006.png)

**Figure 18.6** Steps of fundamental data preprocessing. ¶ *Source:* Adapted from [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033).

The above procedures are the foundation of preprocessing data. After these procedures, the study continues to map the normalized coordinates to an image grid, which will then apply Bresenham's algorithm to colorize pixels in the image grid [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033).

 

#### 18.3.2.2 Neural Networks and Designing Structure

In the study [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007), two ML models are developed using 1D‐CNN and 2D‐CNN architectures. The first version, which uses the 2D‐CNN, incorporates only two convolutional layers (CLs), reducing the complexity compared to traditional models. In the second version, the model includes batch normalization and an identity shortcut layer to minimize overfitting. Additionally, a leaky rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function is applied between layers to enhance the training performance.

### 18.3.3 Military Systems

To protect itself and its people, a country must have military systems [\[34\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0034). Over many years, technological advancements have accelerated, allowing their integration into military applications [\[34\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0034). TinyML research within military domains often focuses on UAVs [\[34\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0034). UAVs serve multiple purposes, such as surveillance of hostile areas or direct engagement without endangering personnel [\[34\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0034). Small UAVs, or drones, often face constraints related to battery capacity [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). These devices, which can be used for surveillance or mapping terrain, often have a short operational time due to their small battery capacity [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). Therefore, it is essential to find a solution to maintain the intelligence of the drone but also make it consume less power for longer flying time [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035).

In [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035), it presents the integration of ML into GAP9Shield, which is a compact nano‐drone that fits within the palm of a hand [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). With this addition, the GAP9Shield achieves energy efficiency while maintaining intelligent functionality [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). To be particular, the nano‐drone is equipped with a 5MP OV5647 camera, a NINA W102 module supporting Wi‐Fi and BLE, and a VL53L1 ToF sensor for distance measurement [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). In comparison with other related studies, the drone achieves an red, blue, and green (RGB) sample rate of 20%, or 7 frames per second (FPS), higher while being lesser in weight. Using the You Only Look Once (YOLO) model, the drone operates below 100 mW of power consumption with minimal latency [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035).

The mentioned components above are added into a 6‐layer ![50 times 27](images/c18-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>50</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>27</mn></math> printed circuit board (PCB) [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). The proposed study's drone consists of a GAP9 system on chip (SoC), camera, Wi‐Fi module, and a 5‐direction ranging sensor [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). Specifically, the GAP9 SoC allows 330 μW per giga operation per second (GOP) of energy efficiency, which means that it saves up energy for every GOP in processing images [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). To other modules, the camera is high‐performance, low‐voltage‐consuming and can output 8‐ or 10‐bit RGB image formats [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). The NINA W102 module has an ESP32 MCU with 2.4‐GHz Wi‐Fi integrated in; the ESP32 microcontroller unit (MCU) is also a dual‐core SoC, which enables parallel activities for Wi‐Fi and Serial Communication Interface (SCI) to communicate with GAP9 SoC and also optimize the data throughput [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). Lastly, the VL53L1 sensor, which ranges in front, left, right, back, and up, can run at a maximum sampling rate of 60Hz [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035).

Besides UAVs, military systems also include cybersecurity threats. Attackers can effortlessly exploit these automated systems, particularly if there are even minor flaws in their design, coding, or any unpatched vulnerabilities [\[36\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0036). Moreover, adversarial attacks can happen not only on powerful computers but also on low‐power ones [\[37\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0037). This means that cyberattacks can still happen on microcontrollers [\[37\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0037). Therefore, it is crucial to create TinyML applications that can detect cyberattacks or at least deploy ML models capable of doing so.

In a study, similar difficulties are remarked \[42\]. Traffic security poses significant risks, and IoT devices with low power are inherently vulnerable [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). Consequently, the research proposes an ML approach for detecting and classifying different cyberattacks using edge IoT network traffic data [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). Although TinyML is not explicitly mentioned, optimizing the ML model for resource‐limited devices makes the approach viable. While IoT applications are increasingly deployed at the edge, they continue to encounter various threats, including denial of service (DoS)/distributed Dos (DDoS), information theft, Man‐in‐the‐ Middle (MITM), injection, and malware attacks [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038).

In the proposed paper, IoT device structures are structured into two tiers: the edge and the cloud layers [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). By performing all processes locally and eliminating the cloud layer, the security of IoT devices is refined [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). However, the edge layer still remains vulnerable, so adding a classifier for detection remains crucial [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). [Table 18.6](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0006) summarizes some TinyML studies in military systems.

**Table 18.6** Summary of studies on TinyML in military systems.

| Study || Purpose || Techniques/algorithms || Final result |

#### 18.3.3.1 Machine Learning Methods

The work [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038) uses the publicly available Edge‐IIoTset Cyber Security Dataset, containing 14 different attack types alongside normal data, to assess eleven ML models and determine which are most efficient at detecting edge IoT attacks [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). Furthermore, the study implements various algorithms within the edge IoT context, including RF, extreme gradient boosting (XGB), and Gaussian naive Bayes (GNB), to identify cyberthreats like DDoS Transmission Control Protocol (TCP), DDoS Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), and Structured Query Language (SQL) injection [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). This approach enhances the study's methodology when compared with previous research.

### 18.3.4 Wireless Systems

In fields such as agriculture, health care, and the military, wireless network has been an ultimate criterion to consider when applying TinyML in those fields. This is primarily due to the potential risks: If not protected properly, private data can be stolen or systems can be attacked via networks [\[39\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0039). Thus, researching TinyML in wireless networks has been a popular and essential aspect. In the mentioned field, there are many factors that can be applied with TinyML, such as WSNs, smart home automation, and cyberthreat detection, and those are very crucial to agriculture, health care, and military.

In paper [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040), it is said that agricultural events should be detected and noticed as it is very crucial; moreover, to create such a system with low‐latency, low‐power, and expansive data communication, there will be long‐range (LoRa)‐based WSNs integrated in the device [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040). In particular, the paper's goal is to create a device that can transmit data in a long range, while some traditional short range network technologies such as Zigbee or Bluetooth are not suitable, LoRa meets this criterion [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040). Moreover, to adapt to the criteria of low latency, the data transmitted to cloud platforms should not be large; therefore, the proposed study decides to analyze the data directly in the edge devices before transmitting it to the cloud platform [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040). Previously, there was a system called Safe for Food and Animal (SAF) implemented in agriculture, especially dairy production, to monitor livestock health, production, storage, and transportation [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040). With the addition of TinyML, the system will be able to detect anomalies or events. Moreover, the SAF system enables LoRa and can work with edge‐cloud model [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040).

The LoRa technology is deployed into the SAF system. For each hectare of agricultural lands, there are 100 LoRa T‐beam LilyGO (TTGO) nodes [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040) and each has three gateways, antennas to provide strong connectivity with the system [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040). Moreover, each node consumes 200 mAh of batteries for continuous operation [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040). The LoRa TTGO nodes are separated into two types, livestock ones rely on DS18B20 and MPU‐6050 sensors to measure temperature and movement, while the environmental nodes apply SHT31 and MQ‐4 sensors to collect humidity, temperature, and methane gas data [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040). Lastly, each node's gateways are connected to cloud with message queuing telemetry transport (MQTT) and transport layer security (TLS) protocol [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040).

When deployed, the system detects many events, such as unusual temperatures from animals, low humidity on the farm, and unusual pH values in tanks. To detect those, TinyML model is applied with anomaly detection, sensor fusion for holistic analysis, sheep fever detection, decision‐making, and more [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040).

Apart from WSN, many other modern wireless technologies significantly enhance the connectivity range of machine‐to‐machine (M2M) communication. These include Wi‐Fi, 4G, 5G, and low‐power wide area network (LPWAN) technologies such as LoRaWAN and NB‐IoT, which enable devices to connect and exchange data over various distances. In other studies, there are solutions that apply ML to network technologies to activate M2M communication faster; in other words, they work as “path finding” in networks. Paper [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041) demonstrates this idea.

Normally, like LoRa technology, the solution they provide is the ability to communicate M2M in different ranges, from long to short. However, these technologies include nodes between the main machine and the communicated machine, and they do not have the ability to find the shortest path to transmit information to that machine. Therefore, paper [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041) offers a solution for that. In the proposed study, an IoT device is created and considered as a decision‐making agent that can calculate the shortest transmission range for M2M and also reduce power consumption [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041). The architecture of multi‐devices works as follows: Firstly, the nearest relay node, or the IoT device, from the main machine will read its state, or the number of other IoT devices near it. Secondly, the IoT device will apply ML to decide to transmit information to the nearest node to the communicated machine. Finally, these two steps keep processing until communication is finished. [Figure 18.7](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0007) visualizes the working flow of the multi‐devices architecture where suitable IoT devices are connected to each other to transmit data in the fastest speed.

![Figure 18.7 Visualization for working flow of architecture. ¶ Source: Adapted from \[41\].](images/c18f007.png)

**Figure 18.7** Visualization for working flow of architecture. ¶ *Source:* Adapted from [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041).

To make decisions, the study relies on an ML process derived from the Markov decision process (MDP) framework that can determine the most optimized route path for M2M communication and also low‐power‐consuming consideration [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041). Moreover, each IoT device is promised to function well even if they do not know everything about the network [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041). Lastly, deep neural network (DNN) is used to help the ML models understand the long‐term benefits of taking certain actions in situations [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041). By doing this, the final system can be autonomous, be able to optimize energy consumption, and use only necessary IoT devices in the network to transmit information to destination devices [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041).

Besides network connection, TinyML can also be applied with other wireless sensors to recognize natural phenomena. In a particular study, TinyML is applied to a device which records and recognizes bird song using acoustic sensors [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). Not only does the final device achieve a high precision metric score, but it can also run within two weeks for a single battery charge, satisfying the low‐cost criteria proposed in the paper [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). Unlike previous machine learning models like BirdNet, the model in this study is designed to record and detect bird sounds directly in natural environments, rather than being limited to laboratory settings [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042).

The dataset in the proposed study includes over 500,000 audio samples from more than 10,000 species, and there are nearly 3,000 samples recording bird sounds to be used to detect sounds from 17 bird species [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). Moreover, it encompasses data from other public datasets such as Oxfordshire Corn Buntings, Xeno‐Canto, and Google AudioSet [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). To evaluate the TinyML model, the study measures the accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042).

[Table 18.8](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0008) displays an overview of proposed studies in this subsection.

**Table 18.8** Summary of machine learning approaches and results in wireless systems studies.

| Study || Purpose || Machine learning algorithms/models || Techniques || Results |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Karras et al. [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040) || Detect agricultural events using TinyML with LoRa || Anomaly detection, sensor fusion, edge‐cloud model || LoRa, TinyML, edge computing || Accuracy: 92.3%–95.1% |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Kwon et al. [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041) || Optimize M2M communication by finding the shortest path || Markov decision process (MDP), deep reinforcement learning (DRL), double deep Q‐network (DDQN) || Path finding, Energy optimization || Improved M2M communication, Reduced power consumption |
| Huang et al. [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042) || Recognize bird songs using acoustic sensors with TinyML || Convolutional neural networks (CNN), Residual Neural Networks (ResNet), Mel‐Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), transformer || Spectrogram analysis, Time‐series analysis || Average accuracy: 92.8%, Average Precision: 86.2%, Average Recall: 97.6%, Average F2 Score: 94.4% |

 

#### 18.3.4.1 Machine Learning Methods

In the proposed study [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041), a decision‐making model is formulated by an MDP, shown as a tuple <S,A,R,![gamma](images/c18-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math>\>, where S is the state or the range an IoT device scans for the next optimal node, A is an action space, R is a reward, and ![gamma](images/c18-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> is a discount factor [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041). Problems from the MDP framework include S, A, R, and the probabilities of moving from one state to another after taking an action can affect the decision‐making feature of MDP; therefore, the study uses deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to tackle these issues [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041). In particular, DRL allows IoT devices to observe nodes within its state, taking necessary actions such as transmitting data, and receives rewards [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041). Furthermore, to optimize DRL, the paper also applies Q‐function to predict the expected dissipate rewards for taking different actions. Lastly, the terminologies above, especially ![upper Q](images/c18-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐function, are applied in a small network with a few nodes, so a double deep Q‐network (DDQN) is used to optimize ![upper Q](images/c18-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐function in circumstances such as large‐scale network [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041).

In paper [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042), the data is recorded over a season. Particularly, researchers place battery‐powered sensors in fields to record natural sounds. After an entire season, they retrieve the collected data and analyze it; in other words, they only keep data which makes birds sound, and others are discarded.

After filtering the dataset, each sample is processed with two dissipate approaches. The initial step involves applying a short‐time Fourier transform (STFT) as a preprocessing block, transforming the sound sample into a spectrogram, which is then treated as an image [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). Consequently, TinyML utilizes CNNs and residual neural networks (ResNets) to learn patterns through image recognition tasks. In another approach, the audio sample is analyzed by Mel‐frequency Cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) preprocessing block, and this will extract the features from the audio and can be used by TinyML to learn patterns from those features in a different approach such as classification [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). To conclude, one approach applies computer vision, while the other one relies on audio analysis.

To enhance performance and minimize the risk of misprediction during the inference of bird sounds, the raw data must first pass through a “baseline” filter [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). This baseline acts as a filter for the raw data by calculating the power signal (![upper P](images/c18-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>) and comparing it against two thresholds to determine whether to proceed with further inference steps [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). In short, [Figure 18.8](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0008) demonstrates the working strategy of the bird sound detecting device.

![Figure 18.8 Inferencing process of bird sound detector.](images/c18f008.png)

**Figure 18.8** Inferencing process of bird sound detector.

 

#### 18.3.4.2 Neural Networks and Designing Structure

In the proposed paper [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040), the overall architecture of the system is described in [Figure 18.9](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0009). In the graph, the microcontroller uses application programming interfaces (APIs) from the SAF system to interact with cloud and application interface.

![Figure 18.9 SAF's architecture with TinyML.](images/c18f009.png)

**Figure 18.9** SAF's architecture with TinyML.

In Kwon et al., the procedure occurred between each IoT device is shown in [Figure 18.10](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0010).

![Figure 18.10 An example of two nodes, or IoT devices, interacting to transmit data. ¶ Source: Adapted from \[41\].](images/c18f010.png)

**Figure 18.10** An example of two nodes, or IoT devices, interacting to transmit data. ¶ *Source:* Adapted from [\[41\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0041).

First of all, the node gets the action ![upper A](images/c18-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math> from the ![epsilon](images/c18-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐greedy action selection from DDQN of node ![v Subscript i](images/c18-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> procedure. Then, the node adjusts the transmission range based on the returned action, which means this step determines whether the path should be shorter. After adjusting, the node transmits the data away and evaluates its throughput, which means the node considers its rewards based on its recent action. Consequently, the node will update its state based on the evaluation result and update DDQN, so the node will improve its decision‐making ability in the future.

The proposed study of Huang et al. applies two approaches, one for computer vision and one for audio analysis, particularly using spectrogram and time‐series data [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). These two approaches also rely on different classification models [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). The following gives a summary of the models used in two approaches.

*   **CNN‐Mel:** This model is used for spectrogram analysis, which involves 2D layers with activation functions such as ReLU and Softmax [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042).
*   **SqueezeNet‐Mel:** This model is applied to spectrogram analysis and is based on the original SqueezeNet model [\[43\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0043). However, this model has fewer parameters than the original one and ensures faster processing speed [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042).
*   **CNN‐Time:** The paradigm includes 1D layers with activation functions like ReLU and Softmax. It is used to extract and learn the patterns from time‐series data's features [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042).
*   **Transformer‐Time:** The approach employs a 1D layer, along with ReLU and Softmax activation functions, and a SingleHeadTransformer to convert raw data into embeddings for the transformer [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042).
*   **SqueezeNet‐Time:** Like SqueezeNet‐Mel, this model is based on the SqueezeNet model \[[42](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042), [43](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0043)\]. However, all 2D layers in the original model are replaced with 1D layers, and this significantly lowers the filter number by up to 70% [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042).

After learning the pattern, two approaches are optimized through model quantization and partial convolution [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042).

 

## 18.4 Case Study: New Insights on Air Writing from Pławiak and Alblehai [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033)

 

### 18.4.1 Introduction

As introduced in the “Healthcare systems” section, air writing is an important aspect in healthcare systems. Moreover, air writing can rely on TinyML for benefits such as cost savings and reduced energy consumption [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). However, the study of Pławiak P. and Alblehai F. et al. makes use of computer vision; that is, the collected raw 3D data is transformed into grid cell images for detection [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). This can take more time as after basic preprocessing data steps, the computer has to convert those normalized numbers into pixels in images. Therefore, this case study reveals a simpler way. After normalization, the extracted data features will then be given to the model for learning, and the post‐training model will detect classes of data from numbers directly, which does not require any image conversion.

Different from the study in [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033), this case study detects Vietnamese alphabets, not Arabic ones. Nevertheless, the case study will use the same microcontroller, Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense, like the one in the study, and some similar parameters in CNN architecture for performance comparison at the case study's “Discussion” section.

 

### 18.4.2 Methodology

In this section, the survey talks about the data, the architecture and the techniques, and algorithms of the model. The data preparation, model training, optimization, and deployment steps are initiated on the EI platform due to its straightforward support for CNN use cases.

 

#### 18.4.2.1 Case Study – Dataset

To collect data, the case study connects Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense microcontroller to EI via its API to start collecting 3D raw data. The reason for this is because the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense microcontroller has an IMU sensor integrated, which is also the data type in the study in Pławiak and Alblehai [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). The characters for detection encompass á, à, ![ModifyingAbove Above ModifyingAbove normal a With breve With acute](images/c18-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover><mo>&#180;</mo></mover></math>, ![ModifyingAbove Above ModifyingAbove normal a With breve With grave](images/c18-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">a</mi><mo>&#728;</mo></mover><mo>&#96;</mo></mover></math>, é, è, ![ModifyingAbove Above ModifyingAbove normal e With Ì‚ With acute](images/c18-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mover accent="true"><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">e</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>&#180;</mo></mover></math>, and idle. The “idle” is detected whenever someone is writing something or not. The case study prepares a dataset of 215 samples in total. Moreover, it is split into train/test rate of 83/17. Additionally, most characters have a number of 24 samples, é character has 36 samples, and idle state has 35 samples. Additionally, the sampling rate is similar to Pławiak and Alblehai [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033): 100 Hz.

 

#### 18.4.2.2 Case Study – Preprocessing, Training, and Testing Model

As mentioned above, the preprocessing step is simpler than the one in Pławiak P. and Alblehai F. et al. Before normalization, the raw data is rasterized like the one in Pławiak and Alblehai [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). Then, the case study uses the EI's “spectral analysis” block to handle the normalizing process [\[44\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0044). The parameters are listed in [Table 18.9](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0009).

**Table 18.9** Filter and analysis settings in “spectral analysis” block.

| Filter || Analysis |
| --- | --- |
| Scale: 3 || Type: FFT |
| --- | --- |
| Input decimation ratio: 10 || FFT length: 16 |
| Type: none || Take log of spectrum?: Yes |
|  || Overlap FFT frames?: Yes |
|  || Improve low‐frequency resolution?: No |

The formulas for normalization are given by ([18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0001)):

(18.1)![x Subscript n o r m Baseline equals StartFraction x minus min left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis Over max left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis minus min left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis EndFraction comma y Subscript n o r m Baseline equals StartFraction y minus min left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis Over max left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis minus min left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis EndFraction](images/c18-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>min</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>min</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>min</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>min</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math> 

where ![x](images/c18-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> and ![y](images/c18-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> are the original data values, ![min left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c18-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>min</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![min left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis](images/c18-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>min</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are the minimum values in the datasets, and ![max left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c18-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>max</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> and ![max left-parenthesis y right-parenthesis](images/c18-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>max</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></math> are the maximum values in the datasets.

Consequently, Vietnamese characters contain accent marks, such as circumflex or grave accent, that can present a special feature of each of its characters. Therefore, the solution to increase accuracy for detection is “highlighting” the values in 2D data that represents these marks. The “Scale” setting in “Filter” settings in spectral analysis block affects this. Instead of normalizing data values to the range of 0 to 1, this block normalizes values from 0 to 3, and this can enhance the presence of accent marks in each Vietnamese character.

The model used in this case study is classification. The set epoch is 1,000, and the learning rate is 0.01. [Table 18.10](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0010) reveals the parameters of the model and its CNN architecture.

**Table 18.10** Filter and analysis settings in “spectral analysis” block.

| --- | --- |
| Model type || Sequential |
| --- | --- |
| *CNN architecture* ||  |
| Dense layer || 400 neurons |
| Activation function || ReLU |
| L1 regularization strength || 0.00001 |

After preprocessing with “spectral analysis” block, data samples in the training section are clustered but not in particular feature groups [\[44\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0044). Therefore, the case study relies on ![upper K](images/c18-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means algorithms to not only group the clusters but also help detect anomalies [\[44\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0044). Since the total number of classes, or characters, in the dataset is 8, it will be the ![k](images/c18-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> number in the algorithm to detect 8 specific features from the preprocessing stage.

After training with the classification model and ![upper K](images/c18-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means algorithm, the results are positive and are shown in the consequent part of this survey.

 

### 18.4.3 Discussion and Conclusion

As said, the achieved results are promising. [Table 18.11](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0011) presents the confusion matrix, which is displayed on the EI platform.

![Table 18.11 EI confusion matrix of case study model.](images/c18-i0038.png)

**Table 18.11** EI confusion matrix of case study model.

The ![upper K](images/c18-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>‐means algorithm also groups the clusters successfully. Some variables needed to be detect, according to EI analysis, are acceleration and gyroscope values, root‐mean square (RMS). Nevertheless, the inferencing accuracy only achieves 77.5% and still needs to be improved further. Additionally, the dataset is manually created by an individual, which means that it lacks diversity in writing styles. Hence, there are numerous factors needed to be considered to improve the inferencing accuracy of this TinyML model.

The post‐training model is also suitable with Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense memory capacity. With the conversion of TensorFlow Lite library, the trained model only uses 2.8 Kb of RAM and 36.6 Kb of flash RAM. ## 18.5 Results and Discussion

In this chapter, the paper provides results of discussed works and also explains a deeper insight to clarify concepts and strategies in previous studies.

 

### 18.5.1 Smart Agriculture Results and Discussion

To rate the model in study [\[24\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0024), the paper uses root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) to assess the TinyML model:

After training, the model uses 1.8 KB in Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense RAM usage out of 256 KB to store model parameters. Under different conditions, 5 and ![2 4 Superscript ring Baseline normal upper C](images/c18-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mn>2</mn><msup><mrow><mn>4</mn><mspace width="0.15em"/></mrow><mo>&#8728;</mo></msup><mi mathvariant="normal">C</mi></math>, metrics, and packaging type, the average MAPE across threshold parameters is 94.11, while the average RMSE are 0.43 [\[24\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0024).

In study [\[25\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0025), the proposed model is evaluated using multiple criteria such as overall accuracy (OA) and F1 score. In ML, **F1 score** is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, providing a balance between the two, and this is usually useful when tackling imbalanced datasets. **Precision** measures the proportion of true‐positive predictions among all positive predictions. **Recall** measures the proportion of true‐positive predictions among all positive instances [\[25\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0025):

### 18.5.2 Healthcare System Results and Discussion

Proposed in paper [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007), the 1D‐CNN model achieves 100% of validation accuracy at epoch 28, and 2D‐CNN achieves it after 30 epochs. Although the 2D‐CNN has greater space to train with more parameters, 1D‐CNN reaches peak accuracy in shorter time than 2D‐CNN, predominantly because of the replacement of some CNN layers with batch normalization and the identity shortcut. Initially, the paper wants to create a low‐cost and efficient detector; thus, choosing 1D‐CNN will be a good choice as it runs faster than 2D‐CNN version and is able to prevent overfitting [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007). [Table 18.13](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0013) shows the final accuracy from validating the model and its loss of the two different versions after training.

![Table 18.13 Final accuracy and loss from validation. ¶ Source: Adapted from \[7\].](images/c18-i0051.png)

**Table 18.13** Final accuracy and loss from validation. ¶ *Source:* Adapted from [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007).

Although validation accuracy is considerably high, the inferencing accuracy might vary based on circumstances, such as mosquitoe types. For example, for mosquitoes from the domestic environment in the paper, the accuracy of 2D‐CNN and 1D‐CNN versions is, respectively, 0.9444 and 0.9065, while for Culex quinquefasciatus, another type of mosquito, reach only 0.7667 and 0.7222 in general performance. Moreover, the 2D‐CNN always has a better inferencing performance than the 1D‐CNN version, and this is because of the ability to provide more parameters during the training process of 2D‐CNN model [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007). To satisfy the criteria of low cost and efficiency, the deployment process also makes use of solar energy and ML, which has been discussed, and after 50 days, the detector uses less than the traditional mosquitoe repellent method 2,995 Watts (W) of energy [\[7\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007).

In study [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030), the system detects overall well with accuracy points all over 79%. Particularly, the accuracy of detecting a person wearing face mask is 79.51% and not wearing face mask is 79.13% [\[30\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0030).

In paper [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018), the model predictor returns a good predicting rate for air humidity with an ![upper R](images/c18-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>‐squared score of approximately 0.9 [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). This score is also applied for air temperature, humidity, solar panel voltage, etc., before quantization. To quantize the two models, the paper applies TensorFlow Lite library to reduce the size of two models: 47.7% reduced in size for model predictor and 56.6% for model imputer [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). Despite the large degradation of the two models, they only suffer little degradation in accuracy [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018). Particularly, before quantization, the model predictor achieves a coefficient of determination higher than 0.7 and the model imputer runs correctly when missing rates are smaller than 0.8 [\[18\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018).

Before discussing about results, the study in Pławiak and Alblehai [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033) converts and transforms the ML TensorFlow model to a TensorFlow Lite model, and this will help reduce memory usage in microcontrollers [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). The converted version is deployed into the Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense microcontroller [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). Moreover, the study also applies algorithms for image recognition such as ResNet to recognize Arabic characters from proposed grid images [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033). With the high accuracy and the ability to be deployed on microcontrollers, the model is believed to be successful in real‐world applications, especially in health care as it achieves cost‐effectiveness in computation and consumes less energy because of low‐power required microcontroller (Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense) [\[33\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0033).

 

### 18.5.3 Military System Results and Discussion

According to the study [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035), the nano‐drone developed is approximately 15% lighter and 30% smaller compared to the Crazyflie model, which weighs 29 g and measures 10 cm. The OV5647 camera operates at 45 FPS while maintaining power usage below 150 mW [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035). Additionally, the system referenced in the research achieves acceptable performance, with a latency of 17 ms and an energy consumption of 1.59 mJ [\[35\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0035).

The study [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038) divides the dataset into 70% for training, 10% for validation, and the rest for testing. Additionally, the dataset file includes 70 features representing 14 types of cyberattacks and 13 types of conventional IoT traffic data [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). The study evaluates the performance of eleven models using metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). [Table 18.14](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0014) displays the F1 score analysis, ranking the models from best to worst for edge IoT cyberattacks detection.

**Table 18.14** Performance between 14 ML cybersecurity models being discussed.

*Source:* [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038) / IEEE.

| Models || F1 score |
| --- | --- |
| AB || 0.999 |
| --- | --- |
| RF || 0.986 |
| DT || 0.970 |
| XGB || 0.933 |
| CART || 0.912 |
| CNN || 0.923 |
| ANN || 0.825 |
| GNB || 0.766 |
| KNN || 0.698 |
| SVM || 0.511 |
| LR || 0.275 |

The models displayed various success rates for different attacks, regardless of overall accuracy [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). However, there are limitations in the study, such as the reliance on static IoT traffic data and the use of only one dataset for evaluation [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038). Despite these limitations, the AdaBoost (AB) model proved to be the most effective for detecting and classifying edge IoT device attacks in the dataset [\[38\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0038).

Based on its performance, the model could be optimized and deployed on resource‐limited microcontrollers, such as Raspberry Pi models, to enhance security in low‐power IoT systems. This research has potential applications in improving military systems to safeguard against cyberthreats.

 

### 18.5.4 Wireless System Results and Discussion

As presented in paper [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040), the TinyML models rely on many detections, and [Table 18.15](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0015) includes all of the TinyML models and the overall performance [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040).

| Event detection || Accuracy || Precision || Recall || F1 score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Anomaly detection || 92.3 || 91.7 || 90.9 || 91.3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Integrated sensor analysis || 93.5 || 94.1 || 92.9 || 93.5 |
| Predictive packet transmission || 88.4 || 87.9 || 88.9 || 88.4 |
| Predictive trajectory analysis || 89.9 || 88.4 || 90.1 || 89.2 |
| Sheep fever detection || 95.1 || 94.8 || 95.5 || 95.1 |

With decent results, the system is promising to be deployed in agricultural fields [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040). However, it still needs further refinements. In the future, the system will be integrated with more exterior sensors and networks to be able to perform real‐time analysis; moreover, prioritize improving the energy efficiency of the system so that the long life of the system is ensured [\[40\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0040).

There are five models used in two circumstances: computer vision and audio analysis. These paradigms are evaluated in different metrics, particularly accuracy, precision, recall, and F2 score from paper [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). Particularly, the five models have an average accuracy of 0.928, an average precision of 0.862, an average recall of 0.976, and an average of F2 score of 0.944 [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). Like F1 score, F2 score also combines precision and recall, but it emphasizes more on recall [\[45\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0045). The formula for F2 score [\[45\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0045) is displayed in equation ([18.8](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0008)):

(18.8)![upper F Baseline 2 minus upper S c o r e equals StartFraction 5 dot upper P r e c i s i o n dot upper R e c a l l Over 4 dot upper P r e c i s i o n plus upper R e c a l l EndFraction](images/c18-math-0008.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>F</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>&#8208;</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> 

Due to the latency caused from additional steps to convert into spectrogram models, time‐series model, specifically Transformer‐Time, is claimed to be the most suitable for the final TinyML model [\[42\]](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042). The final device, named TinyChirp, operates for periods ranging from two to eighteen weeks, ensuring its applicability in various real‐life bio‐acoustic scenarios \[[42](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0042), [45](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0045)\].

 

## 18.6 Conclusion and Future Scope

Overall, this survey reviews several studies on TinyML applications related to smart agriculture, smart healthcare systems, military systems, and wireless systems. Unlike previous surveys, this one includes a case study examining a specific paper. Additionally, it provides detailed information about the methodology and results of each study for profound insights, making the survey easy to read and coherent. The study also demonstrates the potential of TinyML to enable efficient and effective machine learning on resource‐constrained devices, paving the way for innovative solutions in these fields.

This paper aims to provide insights into TinyML applications across multiple fields (agriculture, health care, military systems, and wireless systems). Additionally, the inclusion of a case study compared to one of the referenced papers offers a deeper understanding of the methodologies and results of a particular application, providing valuable insights for future research.

Despite these features, the paper only reviews studies in four proposed fields. Therefore, more papers in each field need to be reviewed for further insights into applications. Additionally, the survey must clarify the workflow of paradigms presented in some studies to elucidate the logic of those studies.
